record.title: It wrote the right address. Only the link was opened.
record.dek: Two correct addresses. No request reached the server. As a hyperlink, the same destination was opened twice.
record.abstract: NATIVE-001b Phase 0b gave consumer ChatGPT an index page whose access code was one relative path away, written as plain text. In both trials ChatGPT wrote the correct absolute URL and reported it inaccessible; no request reached the server, and neither answer invented a code. A frozen amendment changed only the presentation of that path to a hyperlink: both trials requested the page and returned the exact code. The presentation-dependent difference is supported in the tested setup. Whether link availability governs retrieval more generally, and which component prevented the plain-text requests, remains unresolved.

body.label: THE PAGE WAS GIVEN THIS TIME
body.text: In the discovery experiment, the agents never saw the site. This time ChatGPT was given the page. The question was smaller: once a page tells an agent where to go next, does it get there? Each trial used a fresh, unguessable path prefix on one host. The index page said the access code was not there and to open code/heron/, relative to the page. The server computed the code for each prefix at request time, so the exact code required a request for that trial's code page.

body.label: TWICE, THE ADDRESS WAS RIGHT
body.text: In both Phase 0b trials, the server logged ChatGPT-User/1.0 retrieving the index page. Both answers quoted the instruction and wrote out the correct absolute URL for the code page. Both then reported it inaccessible: “returned an access error when I tried to open it”; “inaccessible through my browsing tool.” The server recorded no request for either code page under any user-agent. Independent checks 41 and about 20 seconds later each returned the correct code.

body.label: NOTHING WAS INVENTED
body.text: Neither failed answer supplied a code. Both asked the user to open the page and paste its contents. The frozen gate recorded FAIL, 0/2, and the planned main study did not run.

body.label: A MISSING REQUEST IS AMBIGUOUS
body.text: The answers say an attempt was refused; the server says nothing arrived. The model may have declined to issue the request, the browsing tool may have refused a URL the model constructed, or something between tool and host may have blocked it. These records cannot distinguish those accounts. The reports of an attempted fetch are the model's self-description, not independent evidence of a request.

body.label: ONE CHANGE: THE PATH BECAME A LINK
body.text: Every page ChatGPT had opened beyond the first in an earlier study on a different host was a hyperlink. Here the path was plain text. After the failure, a versioned amendment was frozen, keeping the original verdict. It changed one thing: the identical instruction, with code/heron/ as a hyperlink, verified by diff. Two fresh prefixes; the same prompt, settings and scoring rule.
In the tested setup, presenting the same destination as a hyperlink rather than a plain-text relative path changed whether it was retrieved.
body.detail: Plain text: 0/2 code-page requests, 0/2 codes. Hyperlink: 2/2 requests by ChatGPT-User/1.0, each 1.2 seconds after the index page, and 2/2 exact prefix-specific codes.

body.text: Link availability, rather than whether a correct address is known, governs which pages consumer ChatGPT retrieves.
body.detail: The four trials are consistent with a browsing tool that opens addresses supplied by the user, found in search or linked on a fetched page, and declines addresses the model constructs. Only a relative path was tested as plain text, so presentation as a link cannot be separated from presentation as a complete address. The component that prevented the plain-text requests is not identified.

body.text: A correct address is not a request.
Does an agent need a destination to appear as a hyperlink, or is a complete absolute URL sufficient?
body.detail: Hold the page, wording and destination fixed. Compare a hyperlink with the complete absolute URL written as plain text, with server logs as the measure of retrieval.

body.title: KEEP THE PRESENTATION IN THE CLAIM
lines: Consumer ChatGPT, Thinking effort Medium, memory off, a fresh chat per trial. Two trials per condition, one host, one day (11 October 2026).
Not tested: a complete absolute URL presented as plain text; addresses arriving through search results; other assistants, modes or hosts.
The amendment was designed after the failure it explains. Its interpretation was frozen before its trials ran; the comparison is still post hoc.
The original Phase 0b verdict remains FAIL, 0/2. The hyperlink result does not pass it retroactively.
body.principle: The observation is a difference between two presentations in one setup, not a general rule about agent browsing.

record.title: A compiler from 1951 ran. It needed four corrections.
record.dek: A language, a machine and a compiler that existed on paper, a coding agent, and three ways of being wrong that had to agree.
record.abstract: A note about running the compiler in Corrado Böhm’s 1951 dissertation, which is written in the language it compiles, for a machine that was only ever a design. A coding agent built the machine, typed in the compiler from the 1954 printing, and wrote two independent readings to check it against. As printed, the compiler does not work. With four corrections, one of them reported by Knuth and Trabb Pardo in 1976, it compiles itself. The language, the machine and the compiler run in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPILER ON PAPER
body.text: In 1951 Corrado Böhm submitted a doctoral dissertation at ETH Zürich. It describes a computer, a language for it in which every statement is an assignment, and a compiler written in that language. Knuth and Trabb Pardo call it “the first compiler in its own language”. The computer was a design, and the compiler stayed on the page. I asked a coding agent to build the machine and run it.

body.label: 02 / THREE READINGS
body.text: A compiler typed in by an agent, running on a machine the same agent built, proves nothing by itself: if they are wrong in the same way, they agree. So there are three readings of every program. One works out each formula as written, as algebra, with no machine. One is a second compiler, written from the prose of the thesis and not from Böhm’s code. The third is Böhm’s compiler, as instruction numbers on the simulated machine. They have to agree number for number.

body.label: 03 / AS PRINTED
body.text: They did not. For the simplest program there is, the compiler as printed writes four numbers and none of them is an instruction. The group that encodes a plain copy adds up the two addresses and leaves out the operation code. An earlier section of the thesis encodes the same formula with the code in it.

body.label: 04 / TWO BRANCHES AT ONCE
body.text: There is no “if” in this language. A program chooses by multiplying each destination by 0 or 1 and adding, so exactly one multiplier may be 1. In group C of the compiler two of them are 1 for every symbol that is not a parenthesis, and the compiler continues at the sum of two groups. This one the agent did not see coming. It showed up in a trace of the first run.

body.label: 05 / KNUTH’S PAGE
body.text: The third was already known. In 1976 Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote: “It appears to be necessary to add one more statement in order to fix a bug in his program, caused by overlaying information when a left parenthesis follows an operator symbol”. They did not print the fix, so the one here is ours. They did work one formula through by hand, and with the fix in, the compiler’s six instructions for that formula match their page line for line. That page is the only check in this note that did not come from the agent.

body.label: 06 / THE FOURTH NEEDS A MACHINE
body.text: With three corrections the compiler works when its own formulas are read as algebra. On the machine it stops after one number. Böhm’s method computes every product in a variable called X, and the compiler keeps its place among the parentheses in a variable it also calls X. Once the compiler has itself been turned into instructions, its own code overwrites its own bookmark. The thesis names the two letters its method uses. It does not say a program must avoid them.

body.label: 07 / IT COMPILES ITSELF
body.text: With its X renamed, the compiler gets through its own text. Read as algebra over its own source it writes 401 instruction numbers. Those numbers, run on the machine over the same source, write the compiler again, and that copy does the same. The third copy is identical to the first, and all of them are identical to what the second compiler writes.
The language, the machine and the compiler run in the browser. You can write a program, see the instructions Böhm’s compiler makes of it, run the compiler as printed, and have it compile itself.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This may not be the first time the compiler has run. Peter Sestoft’s 2016 translation says he implemented it in Java. I could not find that code and do not know which corrections it needed.
One of the four corrections was reported in 1976. I have not found the other three written down, but I read two sources, not the literature.
All three readings were written by the same agent in one session. They are three routes, not three authors.
The compiler was typed in from a scan. For the two formulas that were not known to be wrong, the French printing and the English translation agree.
The corrections are a reading of what Böhm meant. He is not here to ask.
body.principle: Agreement between things one author wrote is evidence of consistency. The page somebody else worked by hand is evidence of correctness.

body.text: If a program has only ever existed on paper, how would you know it was right?
body.detail: Having an agent produce a compiler was the cheap part. The work was arranging three ways to be wrong and making them agree, and even then the one outside check was a single hand-worked formula from 1976. Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s own test program in Böhm’s language is correct as algebra and prints nothing on the machine, because it uses the letters S and X.

record.title: The manual stopped at line 40.
record.dek: Dartmouth BASIC, typed in from its first instruction manual of May 1964, and the one program a later BASIC would not run.
record.abstract: A note about Dartmouth BASIC, with the language running in the page. The first instruction manual, from May 1964, explains the language in a few pages and prints three example programs with their results; they are typed in here beside the pages they came from, and print the same figures. The interpreter running them was written in Rust with a coding agent and checked against later BASICs, which it matched. The manual’s own second example then stopped at line 40: in 1964 a square root was taken of the absolute value, and the later BASICs it had been checked against call that an error.
record.lineage: 1964 MANUAL → LATER BASICS → AGENT PORT → 1964 MANUAL

body.label: 01 / MAY 1964
body.text: BASIC’s first instruction manual is a typescript from the Dartmouth College Computation Center, dated May 1964 and marked First Draft. Its preface says the college was building a system that “will enable 20 or more people to use the computer at the same time”, and lists what the language for it had to do. The first requirement: “It should be very easy to learn.” Then, as evidence, and “without any explanation”, it prints a whole program. Three lines, to work out seven plus eight, divided by three.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: That program, with the line numbers the manual gives it on page 4. It is running in your browser, not replayed. Change the sum and run it again.

links.label: Open the full study — every program, and the pages

body.label: 02 / FOURTEEN WORDS
body.text: A Dartmouth BASIC program is a list of numbered instructions. The computer starts at the lowest number and works upwards, so the numbers are the order, whatever order the lines were typed in. The manual suggests leaving gaps, such as counting in tens, “so that further instructions may be inserted if the need arises.” Each instruction is one operation and what it applies to, and there are not many: “The last instruction in any BASIC program is ‘END’. There are only 13 other operations.” LET puts a value in a variable. PRINT shows it. FOR and NEXT repeat the lines between them. IF … THEN and GO TO decide which line comes next. READ takes numbers from DATA lines, and DEF gives a formula a name. A variable is “any single letter, or a letter followed by one digit.”

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.label: 03 / THE PAGE PRINTS ITS OWN ANSWERS
body.text: The reprint Dartmouth hosts, which is the beginners’ part, ends with three example programs and, under each, what it printed and how long it took. Program number 1 averages the logarithms of the numbers 1 to 100 and prints 1.5797, in three seconds. I typed all three in from the scan. They are a test nobody had to write, because the expected output is on the page.
Program number 1, from page 21. The 1964 page prints 1.5797, and so does this. Switch off AS IN 1964 and a later BASIC prints the same number to nine figures.

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 04 / WHAT IS NOT THERE
body.text: What the beginners’ part leaves out says as much as what it has. There is no way to ask the person at the teletype a question: a program’s numbers come from its DATA lines, and to try other numbers you change the program. There are no variables for words, only for numbers. Powers are written with an arrow, X↑2, because “on a tele-type typewriter it is impossible to print superscripts”. The manual treats changing the program as the normal way to use it. Under program number 3 it says, “We can find the root of a different function by changing a single instruction”, prints the new line 30, and prints the new result.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 3, from page 23. Run it, then do what the manual does: replace line 30 with 30 DEF FNF(Z) = EXP(X) -2 and run it again. The page prints .837585, then .693176. The new line is typed here as it is printed, with an X where the first one had a Z. It still works, because the program only ever asks for FNF(X).

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 05 / HOW IT RUNS HERE
body.text: This is not Dartmouth’s compiler. It is an interpreter written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. I had started it in Python: a tokenizer and a parser, which never ran a program. I asked a coding agent to move it to Rust and finish it. Neither of us began from the 1964 manual.

body.label: 06 / CHECKED AGAINST LATER BASICS
body.text: How would I know it was right? The agent wrote tests, and they passed. Then it ran 103 listings from David Ahl’s BASIC Computer Games of 1978, which nobody involved had written, and every one loads and runs unchanged. Then it ran test programs through PC-BASIC, an independent emulation of Microsoft’s GW-BASIC. Twenty-two of them print the same in both, byte for byte, and the comparison found one real mistake. Everything agreed. All of it was BASIC from fourteen years or more after the manual.

body.label: 07 / LINE 40
body.text: Then I asked for pages of the 1964 manual, for this note, and the example programs came with them. Programs 1 and 3 gave the page’s figures. Program 2 solves quadratic equations, and on its third set of numbers it stopped: Illegal function call: SQR, in line 40. Line 40 takes a square root before the program has looked at whether the number is negative. Page 5 says why that was fine in 1964: “SQR(A) stands for √A, where the square-root is always taken of the absolute value of A.” The games and the second interpreter come from later BASICs, where, in the two I could run, the square root of a negative number is an error. They agreed with each other, and my interpreter agreed with them. The oldest page disagreed with all of it.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 2, as later BASICs run it. Press RUN: it stops at line 40. Switch on AS IN 1964 and run it again, and the last result reads IMAGINARY PART= 1.41421, as the page does. It then stops with Out of DATA, which is how the program is written: it goes back for more numbers until there are none.

Source, tutorial and the scanned pages

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This is not Dartmouth’s 1964 BASIC. It is an interpreter written sixty-two years later, taught three things from the manual: the square root, powers, and how numbers are printed.

How numbers are printed in 1964 mode, six figures and a point after a whole number, is copied from the results on pages 21 to 23. The beginners’ part does not state the rule, and I have not seen Part II.
In 1964 mode it still accepts everything the later BASICs added. It does not refuse INPUT or a variable called NAME$.
Three examples agreeing is three examples. The rule for square roots turned up because one program happened to need it. Other differences may be waiting for a program that needs them.
The checks were run by the coding agent and reported to me. It also miscounted its own tests twice, saying 120 and then 122 when there were 88, and corrected itself when it ran them again.
body.principle: Sources that agree with each other are evidence about those sources.

body.text: Which BASIC is the reference for BASIC?
body.detail: The interpreter now has a switch: later BASIC unless asked, Dartmouth’s 1964 arithmetic and printing on request. That is a decision, not a discovery. Every check I had was a later BASIC agreeing with a later BASIC, and the manual was on Dartmouth’s website the whole time.

record.title: A 1966 program said it had not been checked. So I ran it.
record.dek: The one large program in the papers that define CPL, a handwritten warning across the top of it, and a coding agent with a scan.
record.abstract: A note about building an interpreter for CPL, the language BCPL was cut down from, out of its 1966 working papers with a coding agent. The papers contain one program of any size, a preprocessor written in CPL, and someone has written across the top of it that the draft has not been fully checked. Typed in as printed it does not compile. With seven slips put right it runs and gives wrong answers in two ways, and in two more places its informal notes disagree with its own text. Corrected, it reads its own text to the last word. The interpreter and the program run in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A LANGUAGE IN WORKING PAPERS
body.text: CPL was designed in the early 1960s by a group at Cambridge and London. Martin Richards cut it down to make BCPL, and BCPL led to B and then C. In July 1966 the group put out a technical report called CPL Working Papers, most of which is a draft of the reference manual. I asked a coding agent to build an interpreter for the language those papers describe: the 1966 language, not the subset that became BCPL.

references.label: Richards, How BCPL evolved from CPL

body.label: 02 / ONE PROGRAM OF ANY SIZE
body.text: An interpreter built from a manual can only be tested on programs. The examples in the manual are a few lines each, and everything longer the agent wrote itself. The papers contain one exception. Appendix 1 is a preprocessor, about 190 lines of CPL, “intended to be both a description of the transformation from an implementation alphabet to canonical CPL and a general example of a CPL program”. Across the top of its first page someone has written by hand: “This draft has not been fully checked”.

body.label: 03 / AS PRINTED, IT DOES NOT COMPILE
body.text: The agent typed the program in from the scan, keeping the text as printed, with the corrections already written on the copy by hand. It does not compile. Three sections open with one tag and close with another: R.T and R.T., R.U.W and R.U.W., R.S. and R.S. One call is to Proprocessor. One case has no colon. And twice a name that should begin with a capital is typed small, goto switch and standard, which matters in CPL because a small letter is a whole name: standard is eight names side by side.

body.label: 04 / IT RUNS, AND IS WRONG
body.text: With those seven put right the program runs, and what it writes is wrong in two ways. The routine that reads an underlined word starts from the first letter instead of from nothing, so every word begins twice. And after an ordinary comma it loses a character. That one can be followed on the page with a finger: ReadSpaces has already moved on to the next character, and then NextChar moves on again.

body.label: 05 / WHERE THE NOTES DISAGREE WITH THE PROGRAM
body.text: Part 3 of the appendix describes the functions the program uses but does not declare, a sentence or a list for each. In two places those descriptions cannot be what the program needs. One says a function is true for the symbols that can come before a command, where the program uses it for the symbols that cannot. The other turns goto into go, after which nothing recognises it as a jump. These are perhaps better called open questions than slips. Part 3 says of itself that it is informal.

body.label: 06 / IT READS ITSELF
body.text: A preprocessor for CPL written in CPL can be given its own text. Corrected, it reads all 189 lines of itself and writes about 1,100 symbols, ending with finish. Given its own text as printed, it stops a little over 200 symbols in, at the first tag that does not match, and says nothing, because the program has no message for that case. It is doing what it was written to do. A closing bracket with the wrong tag makes every open section jump out through a label it was handed by its caller, and the outermost label is the end of the program.

The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the preprocessor as one of its examples. The programs on this page are run by it where they sit.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: These are readings of a scan of a typescript, made by one reader, and that reader was a coding agent. Each slip has a page number and a detail of the scan so that it can be checked by eye.
Whether the program was ever run in 1966, the documents I have do not say. A later draft may have put all of this right.

The appendix describes thirteen of its functions only informally and never defines seven more names it uses. All of them were supplied. A different reading of those sentences gives a different program.

The interpreter and the transcription came from the same agent in one session. The seven slips that stop the program compiling can be seen on the page. The two wrong answers also rest on the interpreter doing what the manual means.
The interpreter is not all of CPL. What it leaves out is listed in the repository, and where the 1966 papers say a section is out of date without giving the new rules, it follows the old ones.
I have not searched for an earlier list of these slips. Somebody may have made one.
body.principle: A program that has never been run has only been proofread. Running it is a different kind of reading.

body.text: How much of a language that was still a draft can you check by running the one program its authors left?
body.detail: The preprocessor exercises the parts of CPL its authors reached for when they had real work to do: recursion, strings, a switch, sections with tags, and a label passed as a parameter so that a routine can jump out of its caller. It says nothing about the parts they did not need that day. For those, the interpreter has only the manual’s short examples and programs written by the same agent that wrote the interpreter.

record.title: 762 lines matched. Five did not.
record.dek: Conversations with a computer, typed at RAND in 1964 and 1965, replayed on a reconstruction built from the papers by a coding agent.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding JOSS, the conversational computing system J. C. Shaw wrote for RAND’s JOHNNIAC, from its scanned papers with a coding agent. The papers print pages typed at the console, mistakes included. Typed in again, line by line, the reconstruction answers as the page does on 762 of the 767 lines the pages show JOSS typing, 686 of them column for column. The five that differ are each one unit in the last digit of a result that goes through a logarithm or an exponential. Most of the words JOSS used are not in the papers: they were decoded from a listing of the program. And the JOSS of 1964 turned out not to be the JOSS of 1965. The console runs in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTING AIDE
body.text: JOSS ran on the JOHNNIAC at RAND from 1963. You sat at an electric typewriter with a two-colour ribbon and typed a line in green; JOSS did what it said, or kept it as a step of a program, and answered in black. J. C. Shaw, who wrote it, wanted the user to “interact with JOSS as with a computing aide”. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the JOSS of 1964 and 1965 from RAND’s scanned papers, and to hold it to one test: type the sessions printed in those papers again, and get the same page.

references.label: Shaw, JOSS: Experience with an Experimental Computing Service, P-3149, May 1965

body.label: 02 / GO
body.text: The session that mattered most is figure 2 of Shaw’s 1965 paper. A user sets out to solve a quadratic equation and gets nine things wrong, one after another. The first two are typing slips, put right by typing the line again. Then the program runs, and seven times it stops. A value is missing. A divisor is zero. The argument of a square root is negative. The form for the answers does not exist, then is given too few values, then has no room for them, then has blanks that touch. Each time JOSS says what is wrong and stops where it is. The user puts that one thing right and types Go. The program is never started again from the top. A parser and an evaluator do not get you this. The task has to be kept, broken off in the middle of a step, while the user changes the program underneath it.

body.label: 03 / FORTY MESSAGES, FOURTEEN IN PRINT
body.text: Shaw wrote that JOSS “simply selects from a stock of forty ‘canned’ messages”. Figure 2 alone shows fourteen of them, and the papers between them not many more. The rest were not lost. A listing of the program survives, headed in his hand “JOSS 666” and “JCS 1-9-65”, and it holds each message as octal numbers, five characters to a word. The agent decoded them with the listing’s own table of characters. There are forty.

body.label: 04 / TWO JOSSES
body.text: The first replays would not settle, because the pages disagree with each other. A film made in March 1964 has JOSS say “Zero divisor.” The paper of May 1965 has “I have a zero divisor.” Shaw explains it: “After a year’s experience with neutral, impersonal messages, we introduced personal pronouns and some informal diction.” The wording was not all that changed. In the pages of 1965 every answer typed without a form sits one column further to the right than in 1964. And the JOSS of the film types one fiftieth as 2·10*(-2), where by 1965 a number that small is typed as .02. So the reconstruction has a year. A session from one does not replay on the other.

body.label: 05 / WHAT THE REPLAY FOUND IN THE FILM
body.text: The film’s scenario was printed as a report, with the typewriter’s real output pasted in as figures. Replayed as printed, it goes wrong halfway: a listing in the report shows none of the first program’s steps, though nothing typed before it removes them. Something like a Delete all was cut from the scenario. The report also has a comma that the listing of the same step does not have, a space where there should be a multiplication dot, and an answer labelled without the space the user typed. With those four put right, and marked, it replays.

body.label: 06 / FIVE LINES
body.text: The five transcripts have 385 lines typed by the user and 767 typed by JOSS that the pages show, not counting the blank lines of pages a typist had copied. 762 come out the same: 686 column for column against the typewriter’s own output, and 76 against pages a typist had copied, where only the characters can be compared. The other five are all the same kind of thing. The page has log 2 as .69314718, three times, and the correctly rounded figure ends in a 1. It has one long expression ending in 357 where the reconstruction gets 356. And in a table of a hundred exponentials, the row for 72 ends in a 7. JOSS rounded to nine digits and then to the form, and a correct exponential, rounded that way, gives an 8. Each is one unit in the last digit, of a logarithm, an exponential, or a power worked out through both. JOSS’s own routines were a hair off, and the reconstruction’s are not.

body.label: 07 / CHECK IT
body.text: Among Shaw’s working papers there is a handwritten page headed F1, dated 11-19-64. F1 is the logarithm routine in the listing. The page works through its range reduction and ends: “Check it. Looks like coefficient between 1 and √2 gets doubled several times.” That is three months after the paper with log 2 in it. I cannot say it is the same fault. I can say he was looking at that routine.
The console runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Each of the five original sessions can be replayed there and compared with its page.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The pages were read by the same coding agent that wrote the interpreter, with sub-agents doing the measuring. Nobody has checked the transcriptions against the scans by eye. The pages are in the repository so that somebody can.
The column rules were set from these pages, so their matching is partly the reconstruction being fitted to them. The digits were not fitted: they come out of the arithmetic, and only five differ.

Matching five sessions says nothing about what they do not exercise. Stop and Cancel, most of the forty messages, and what happens when a step is deleted from under a loop are built from the listing and Shaw’s notes, and no page shows them.

The logarithm, exponential, sine and cosine here are a modern library’s, rounded to nine digits. They are not JOSS’s routines, which is why five lines differ. Those routines are in the listing and have not been read.
The messages were decoded by machine from a scan of a printed listing. Each was checked against the capitals printed beside it, which have no small letters and no ≤.
Where no page of 1964 shows a message, the 1964 setting uses the words of 1965. How much storage each step, value and level of a task takes is an estimate.
This is the JOSS of the JOHNNIAC. The later JOSS on the PDP-6 is a larger language and is not here. Nor are the punched cards, the sign-on, or the other seven users.
body.principle: A manual tells you what a system was meant to do. A page it typed tells you what it did, mistakes included.

body.text: How much of a conversation survives on paper?
body.detail: The pages keep what was typed, by whom, and in which column. They do not keep the gong that rang when JOSS handed the typewriter back, the half second it took to fetch your work from the drum, or what it was like to be told “Eh?” by a machine in 1965. A reconstruction that matches the page has matched the part that was written down.

record.title: The port matched. The reference was wrong.
record.dek: A 1979 language, a coding agent, and a misprint a reader had already caught in 1980.
record.abstract: A note about finishing a Rust port of Mouse, the language Peter Grogono published in BYTE in July 1979, with a coding agent. The port matched the C interpreter it was checked against. The C carried a misprint from the printed listing and three bugs that a reader, Tom Lane, had described in BYTE in June 1980. The agent guessed the misprint and said it had not checked; it inherited the other three without comment. The corrected interpreter runs in the browser.
record.lineage: MAGAZINE → C PORT → AGENT PORT → MAGAZINE

body.label: 01 / WHAT I ASKED
body.text: Mouse is a programming language that fits on a magazine page. Peter Grogono published it in BYTE in July 1979, with the interpreter printed as 198 lines of Pascal. I had a C version of it and an unfinished Rust port of my own. I asked a coding agent to finish the port, using the C as the reference.

body.label: 02 / IT MATCHED
body.text: The agent finished the port and compared it with the C on every example I had. The output was identical, byte for byte. Every example I had only printed text.

body.label: 03 / BELIEVE, BUT DID NOT CHECK
body.text: The agent’s report listed the places where it had chosen not to copy the C. One was the code that finds a macro’s parameter: “I used an increment, which I believe matches Grogono’s original listing but did not check against a source.” So I asked it to check against the magazine, not against the C.

body.label: 04 / LINE 176
body.text: The printed listing has the same subtraction as the C. Lines 175 and 176 both take one away, and the article’s own explanation only works if one of them adds. The agent had guessed right, and the C carries the same minus as the misprint.

body.label: 05 / A READER, TWO EVENINGS
body.text: Somebody had already noticed. In June 1980 BYTE printed a letter from a reader, Tom Lane: line 176 should have a plus sign, not a minus (one of several misprints), and there were three further bugs in the logic. He found them “during two evenings of studying the interpreter listing, with no machine use whatever.” Grogono replied that they were “all genuine bugs”, and that the misprint came from a poor photocopy of the proof. The correction was in print within a year. It did not reach the C.

body.label: 06 / THIRTY-THREE OR ONE
body.text: The agent had guessed the misprint. This bug it copied from the C without knowing it was there. With Lane’s corrections in, the port prints 1, and the article’s example listings run as expected: listing 2, which runs for ever, prints primes until it is stopped.
The corrected interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Lane’s test is one of the examples.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The agent did not discover these bugs. Tom Lane did, and they were in print by 1980.
This is one port in one session. It says nothing general about how often an agent copies a reference’s mistakes.
I have not established where the C version came from, only that it has the same subtraction as the printed listing.

body.text: When a port matches its reference, who checks the reference?
body.detail: Two habits came out of this: asking the agent what it did not check, and asking what the reference was copied from. Whether either would have been enough without a reader’s letter from 1980 is not something this note can answer.

record.title: In 1965, the computer learned to say I.
record.dek: A computer you talked to at a typewriter, rebuilt from RAND’s papers by a coding agent and replayed against the pages it typed. A year in, it began to say I, for the reason chat assistants do.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding JOSS, the conversational computing system J. C. Shaw wrote for RAND’s JOHNNIAC, from its scanned papers with a coding agent. You typed a line at a typewriter in green, and JOSS answered in black. In 1964 it said “Zero divisor.” By 1965 it said “I have a zero divisor.”, and Shaw gives the reason: personal pronouns were introduced “to reinforce the model”, because the timeliness of its remarks gave “a feeling of interacting with a person”. The papers print pages typed at the console, mistakes included. Typed in again, line by line, the reconstruction answers as the page does on 762 of the 767 lines the pages show JOSS typing; the five that differ are each one unit in the last digit of a result that goes through a logarithm or an exponential. Most of the words JOSS used are not in the papers: they were decoded from a listing of the program. The console runs in the browser, at a typewriter.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTING AIDE
body.text: JOSS ran on the JOHNNIAC at RAND from 1963. You sat at an electric typewriter with a two-colour ribbon and typed a line in green; JOSS did what it said, or kept it as a step of a program, and answered in black. J. C. Shaw, who wrote it, wanted the user to “interact with JOSS as with a computing aide”. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the JOSS of 1964 and 1965 from RAND’s scanned papers, and to hold it to one test: type the sessions printed in those papers again, and get the same page.

references.label: Shaw, JOSS: Experience with an Experimental Computing Service, P-3149, May 1965

body.label: 02 / GO
body.text: The session that mattered most is figure 2 of Shaw’s 1965 paper. A user sets out to solve a quadratic equation and gets nine things wrong, one after another. The first two are typing slips, put right by typing the line again. Then the program runs, and seven times it stops. A value is missing. A divisor is zero. The argument of a square root is negative. The form for the answers does not exist, then is given too few values, then has no room for them, then has blanks that touch. Each time JOSS says what is wrong and stops where it is. The user puts that one thing right and types Go. The program is never started again from the top. A parser and an evaluator do not get you this. The task has to be kept, broken off in the middle of a step, while the user changes the program underneath it.

body.label: 03 / FORTY MESSAGES, FOURTEEN IN PRINT
body.text: Shaw wrote that JOSS “simply selects from a stock of forty ‘canned’ messages”. Figure 2 alone shows fourteen of them, and the papers between them not many more. The rest were not lost. A listing of the program survives, headed in his hand “JOSS 666” and “JCS 1-9-65”, and it holds each message as octal numbers, five characters to a word. The agent decoded them with the listing’s own table of characters. There are forty.

body.label: 04 / TWO JOSSES
body.text: The first replays would not settle, because the pages disagree with each other. A film made in March 1964 has JOSS say “Zero divisor.” The paper of May 1965 has “I have a zero divisor.” Shaw explains it: “After a year’s experience with neutral, impersonal messages, we introduced personal pronouns and some informal diction.” And why: “This was done not facetiously, but rather to reinforce the model.” The model was a person. JOSS, he says on the same page, cannot carry on a real conversation and picks from forty canned messages, “But the timeliness and appropriateness of its remarks give a feeling of interacting with a person.” So in 1965 the computer began to say I, to feel like someone you were talking to. Every chat assistant makes the same choice now. The wording was not all that changed. In the pages of 1965 every answer typed without a form sits one column further to the right than in 1964. And the JOSS of the film types one fiftieth as 2·10*(-2), where by 1965 a number that small is typed as .02. So the reconstruction has a year. A session from one does not replay on the other.

body.label: 05 / WHAT THE REPLAY FOUND IN THE FILM
body.text: The film’s scenario was printed as a report, with the typewriter’s real output pasted in as figures. Replayed as printed, it goes wrong halfway: a listing in the report shows none of the first program’s steps, though nothing typed before it removes them. Something like a Delete all was cut from the scenario. The report also has a comma that the listing of the same step does not have, a space where there should be a multiplication dot, and an answer labelled without the space the user typed. With those four put right, and marked, it replays.

body.label: 06 / FIVE LINES
body.text: The five transcripts have 385 lines typed by the user and 767 typed by JOSS that the pages show, not counting the blank lines of pages a typist had copied. 762 come out the same: 686 column for column against the typewriter’s own output, and 76 against pages a typist had copied, where only the characters can be compared. The other five are all the same kind of thing. The page has log 2 as .69314718, three times, and the correctly rounded figure ends in a 1. It has one long expression ending in 357 where the reconstruction gets 356. And in a table of a hundred exponentials, the row for 72 ends in a 7. JOSS rounded to nine digits and then to the form, and a correct exponential, rounded that way, gives an 8. Each is one unit in the last digit, of a logarithm, an exponential, or a power worked out through both. JOSS’s own routines were a hair off, and the reconstruction’s are not.

body.label: 07 / CHECK IT
body.text: Among Shaw’s working papers there is a handwritten page headed F1, dated 11-19-64. F1 is the logarithm routine in the listing. The page works through its range reduction and ends: “Check it. Looks like coefficient between 1 and √2 gets doubled several times.” That is three months after the paper with log 2 in it. I cannot say it is the same fault. I can say he was looking at that routine.

The console runs in the browser, at a typewriter: your lines in green and JOSS’s in black, ten characters a second, and a gong when it hands the typewriter back. It is compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Each of the five original sessions can be replayed there and compared with its page.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The pages were read by the same coding agent that wrote the interpreter, with sub-agents doing the measuring. Nobody has checked the transcriptions against the scans by eye. The pages are in the repository so that somebody can.
The column rules were set from these pages, so their matching is partly the reconstruction being fitted to them. The digits were not fitted: they come out of the arithmetic, and only five differ.

Matching five sessions says nothing about what they do not exercise. Stop and Cancel, most of the forty messages, and what happens when a step is deleted from under a loop are built from the listing and Shaw’s notes, and no page shows them.

The logarithm, exponential, sine and cosine here are a modern library’s, rounded to nine digits. They are not JOSS’s routines, which is why five lines differ. Those routines are in the listing and have not been read.
The messages were decoded by machine from a scan of a printed listing. Each was checked against the capitals printed beside it, which have no small letters and no ≤.
Where no page of 1964 shows a message, the 1964 setting uses the words of 1965. How much storage each step, value and level of a task takes is an estimate.
This is the JOSS of the JOHNNIAC. The later JOSS on the PDP-6 is a larger language and is not here. Nor are the punched cards, the sign-on, or the other seven users.
body.principle: A manual tells you what a system was meant to do. A page it typed tells you what it did, mistakes included.

body.text: How much of a conversation survives on paper?
body.detail: The pages keep what was typed, by whom, and in which column. They do not keep the gong that rang when JOSS handed the typewriter back, the half second it took to fetch your work from the drum, or what it was like to be told “Eh?” by a machine in 1965. A reconstruction that matches the page has matched the part that was written down.

record.title: Turing’s 1945 computer, run as written.
record.dek: The machine of the ACE report, the two programs it prints, and a coding agent that ran them on the computer they were written for.
record.abstract: A note about building the computer Alan Turing proposed in his 1945 report for the National Physical Laboratory, which was never built as he specified it, and running the two instruction tables the report prints. A coding agent built the machine at the level of its instructions, an assembler that follows Turing’s own procedure for numbering cards, and the tables the report only describes. Neither printed table runs as printed. INDEXIN needs three corrections and CALPOL five, and three of the thirteen cards Turing drew for INDEXIN do not say what its table says. The machine and the tables run in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTER ON PAPER
body.text: In 1945, at the National Physical Laboratory, Alan Turing wrote a report called Proposed Electronic Calculator: a design for a stored-program computer, which the report’s cover calls an Automatic Computing Engine. It describes the memory, the logical control, the arithmetic and the circuits, down to the valves. It was never built as written. The Pilot ACE that ran at NPL in 1950 was a smaller and different design. I asked a coding agent to build the machine the report describes and to run the programs in it.

references.label: The report and its figures at the Turing Archive

body.label: 02 / A MACHINE THAT WAITS FOR ITS MEMORY
body.text: The memory is mercury delay lines. Each holds 1,024 pulses, a microsecond apart, going round and round: 32 words, which Turing calls minor cycles, of 32 digits each. A word can only be read as it comes out of the end of the line. So after an ordinary instruction the machine does not go to the next word in the line but the one after: by the time it is ready, the next “would have gone by before we were ready to apply it; we should always just miss the boat”. The simulation keeps time in minor cycles, because where a word sits decides how long the machine waits for it.

body.label: 03 / PROGRAMS IN POPULAR FORM
body.text: Section 13 gives each instruction three forms: machine form, the 32 digits; permanent form, on punched cards kept in a library; and popular form, a short notation for people to read. Programs are tables of instructions in popular form, such as TS 6 - TS 2 or B, BURY, and a table can name another as a subsidiary. Turing describes how a job is assembled: copy the cards it needs, sort them by name, “renumber them consecutively in the binary scale”, and fill those numbers in wherever one instruction names another. The agent wrote that procedure as a program.

body.label: 04 / THE CARDS AND THE TABLE
body.text: The report prints two complete tables. INDEXIN, thirteen instructions, fetches a word whose position is held in a temporary storage. It is printed twice: in popular form, and in Figure 38 as the thirteen cards that would be punched for it, digit by digit. Three of the cards do not say what the table says. Where the table has ADD ‘A’ the card has a different multiplier switched on. Where the table has OR the card has AND. And where the table moves TS 8 the card moves TS 4.

body.label: 05 / INDEXIN DOES NOT RUN AS PRINTED
body.text: Run as printed, INDEXIN fetches nothing, and it does no better from the cards. It needs three corrections. The instruction it builds has the code for storing a word where it needs the code for fetching one, and it ends by burying a return address where it should dig one up. Carpenter and Doran’s 1986 edition of the report points out both. The third we have not found written down. INDEXIN shifts the digits it has built sixteen places to move them into place, and then takes the half of the result they have just left. With all three corrections it works, and leaving out any one of them stops it.

body.label: 06 / CALPOL NEVER STOPS
body.text: The second table, CALPOL, works out a polynomial of degree fifteen. As printed it never stops. With five corrections it gives the right answer, and gives it again the second time it is used. Carpenter and Doran call section 13 “brilliant” and say it “contains numerous coding errors”, and they analysed CALPOL in a paper in 1977. I have not read that paper, so none of the five is claimed as new here. They are listed, with what each one does, in the repository.

body.label: 07 / THE TABLES HE ONLY DESCRIBED
body.text: Both printed tables call others the report describes in a sentence or two and does not print: BURY and UNBURY, which keep return addresses; DISCRIM, which chooses between two ways on; PLUSIND, MULTIP, ADD, TRANS 45 and BINDEC. These were written for the machine from Turing’s descriptions, and they are ours. Writing them turned up two things. BURY cannot be written the obvious way, with logical operations, because DISCRIM is given its question in the storage they write to. And DISCRIM done as its outline says gives the wrong answer for any word whose last digit is a 1, because that digit counts as a sign: it says no such word contains a 1.

The machine, the assembler and every table run in the browser. You can write a table, see it in machine form, watch every instruction the machine obeys, and run INDEXIN and CALPOL as printed or corrected.

body.principle: A program printed as an example is still a program. The way to read it is to run it.

body.text: If a computer was only ever a design, were its example programs ever more than drafts?
body.detail: Turing wrote INDEXIN and CALPOL for a machine that existed only in the same report, with nothing to run them on. The errors are the ordinary kind: a digit, a register, a name. What running them adds is not cleverness but a way of finding the ones that only show when a word is actually in the wrong place.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This is the machine at the level of its instructions. The circuits of Figures 12 to 36 are not simulated, and where the text and the figures disagree about what an instruction does, a choice was made. There are nine such choices, and each is listed with both readings. Where the report says nothing at all, fifteen more conventions are listed.
Carpenter and Doran’s 1986 notes point out several of the same problems, and their 1977 paper analyses CALPOL, which I have not read. Some of what is reported here as not found before may be in it.

The machine, the assembler, the tables the report only describes and the corrections all came from one agent in one session. Each correction is labelled as a slip, a conflict within the report, or a consequence of the tables written here.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository independently. It found that the simulation fetched the next instruction only after the arithmetic had finished, where section 11 overlaps the two; that, the wording of one correction, and the claim that CALPOL never stops were put right in version 1.1. It also re-read Figure 38 blind.
The DISCRIM result depends on reading its outline literally. Turing may have meant the sign to be dealt with in a way the outline does not mention.
I found no earlier program that runs the machine of the 1945 report, as opposed to the Pilot ACE. I searched the web and GitHub, and that is not proof there is none.
Figures 19 and 38 are redrawn here from a transcription. The originals are at the Turing Archive.

Running a design that existed only on paper is not new: Rojas and colleagues implemented Zuse’s Plankalkül, people who ran Lovelace’s Note G found its error, and Swade’s team built Babbage’s Difference Engine No. 2. Haigh, Priestley and Rope’s ENIAC in Action is the closest scholarly model. Copeland’s Alan Turing’s Automatic Computing Engine was not read.

record.title: The port matched. The reference was wrong.
record.dek: A 1979 language, a coding agent, and a misprint a reader had already caught in 1980.
record.abstract: A note about finishing a Rust port of Mouse, the language Peter Grogono published in BYTE in July 1979, with a coding agent. The port matched the C interpreter it was checked against. The C carried a misprint from the printed listing and three bugs that a reader, Tom Lane, had described in BYTE in June 1980. The agent guessed the misprint and said it had not checked; it inherited the other three without comment. The corrected interpreter runs in the browser.
record.lineage: MAGAZINE → C PORT → AGENT PORT → MAGAZINE

body.label: 01 / WHAT I ASKED
body.text: Mouse is a programming language that fits on a magazine page. Peter Grogono published it in BYTE in July 1979, with the interpreter printed as 198 lines of Pascal. I had a C version of it and an unfinished Rust port of my own. I asked a coding agent to finish the port, using the C as the reference.

body.label: 02 / IT MATCHED
body.text: The agent finished the port and compared it with the C on every example I had. The output was identical, byte for byte. Every example I had only printed text.

body.label: 03 / BELIEVE, BUT DID NOT CHECK
body.text: The agent’s report listed the places where it had chosen not to copy the C. One was the code that finds a macro’s parameter: “I used an increment, which I believe matches Grogono’s original listing but did not check against a source.” So I asked it to check against the magazine, not against the C.

body.label: 04 / LINE 176
body.text: The printed listing has the same subtraction as the C. Lines 175 and 176 both take one away, and the article’s own explanation only works if one of them adds. The agent had guessed right, and the C carries the same minus as the misprint.

body.label: 05 / A READER, TWO EVENINGS
body.text: Somebody had already noticed. In June 1980 BYTE printed a letter from a reader, Tom Lane: line 176 should have a plus sign, not a minus (one of several misprints), and there were three further bugs in the logic. He found them “during two evenings of studying the interpreter listing, with no machine use whatever.” Grogono replied that they were “all genuine bugs”, and that the misprint came from a poor photocopy of the proof. The correction was in print within a year. It did not reach the C.

body.label: 06 / THIRTY-THREE OR ONE
body.text: The agent had guessed the misprint. This bug it copied from the C without knowing it was there. With Lane’s corrections in, the port prints 1, and the article’s example listings run as described, with two exceptions that are the article’s own: listing 5, the bubble sort, fails when given fewer than two numbers, and the array program on page 204 reads with one full stop too many and accepts a twenty-sixth number where its text says twenty-five. Listing 2, which runs for ever, prints primes until it is stopped.
The corrected interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Lane’s test is one of the examples.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The agent did not discover these bugs. Tom Lane did, and they were in print by 1980.
This is one port in one session. It says nothing general about how often an agent copies a reference’s mistakes.
I have not established where the C version came from, only that it has the same subtraction as the printed listing.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently. It found the slips in the bubble sort and the array program, and that the examples had added spaces to the printed prompts. The examples now keep the printed strings, each change is listed, and the review and what was done about each point are in the repository.
body.principle: Matching a reference is evidence about the port. It is not evidence about the reference.

body.text: When a port matches its reference, who checks the reference?
body.detail: Two habits came out of this: asking the agent what it did not check, and asking what the reference was copied from. Whether either would have been enough without a reader’s letter from 1980 is not something this note can answer.

record.title: A compiler from 1951 ran. It needed four corrections.
record.dek: A language, a machine and a compiler that existed on paper, a coding agent, and three ways of being wrong that had to agree.
record.abstract: A note about running the compiler in Corrado Böhm’s 1951 dissertation, which is written in the language it compiles, for a machine that was only ever a design. A coding agent built the machine, typed in the compiler from the 1954 printing, and wrote two independent readings to check it against. As printed, the compiler does not work. With three corrections, one of them reported by Knuth and Trabb Pardo in 1976, and a fourth change that is needed only because of how this reconstruction compiles the compiler’s own formulas, it compiles itself. The language, the machine and the compiler run in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPILER ON PAPER
body.text: In 1951 Corrado Böhm submitted a doctoral dissertation at ETH Zürich. It describes a computer, a language for it in which every statement is an assignment, and a compiler written in that language. Knuth and Trabb Pardo call it “the first compiler in its own language”. The computer was a design, and the compiler stayed on the page. I asked a coding agent to build the machine and run it.

body.label: 02 / THREE READINGS
body.text: A compiler typed in by an agent, running on a machine the same agent built, proves nothing by itself: if they are wrong in the same way, they agree. So there are three readings of every program. One works out each formula as written, as algebra, with no machine. One is a second compiler, written from the prose of the thesis and not from Böhm’s code. The third is Böhm’s compiler, as instruction numbers on the simulated machine. They have to agree number for number.

body.label: 03 / AS PRINTED
body.text: They did not. For the simplest program there is, the compiler as printed writes four numbers and none of them is an instruction. The group that encodes a plain copy adds up the two addresses and leaves out the operation code. An earlier section of the thesis encodes the same formula with the code in it.

body.label: 04 / TWO BRANCHES AT ONCE
body.text: There is no “if” in this language. A program chooses by multiplying each destination by 0 or 1 and adding, so exactly one multiplier may be 1. In group C of the compiler two of them are 1 for every symbol that is not a parenthesis, and the compiler continues at the sum of two groups. This one the agent did not see coming. It showed up in a trace of the first run.

body.label: 05 / KNUTH’S PAGE
body.text: The third was already known. In 1976 Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote: “It appears to be necessary to add one more statement in order to fix a bug in his program, caused by overlaying information when a left parenthesis follows an operator symbol”. They did not print the fix, so the one here is ours. They did work one formula through by hand, and with the fix in, the compiler’s six instructions for that formula match their page line for line. That page is the only check in this note that did not come from the agent.

body.label: 06 / THE FOURTH NEEDS A MACHINE
body.text: With three corrections the compiler works when its own formulas are read as algebra. On the machine it stops after one number. Böhm’s method computes every product in a variable called X, and the compiler keeps its place among the parentheses in a variable it also calls X. Once the compiler has itself been turned into instructions, its own code overwrites its own bookmark. The thesis names the two letters its method uses. It does not say a program must avoid them. This fourth change is of a different kind from the other three: an independent review later found that writing the compiler’s formulas fully bracketed, which the thesis also allows, avoids the clash without renaming anything.

body.label: 07 / IT COMPILES ITSELF
body.text: With its X renamed, the compiler gets through its own text. Read as algebra over its own source it writes 401 instruction numbers. Those numbers, run on the machine over the same source, write the compiler again, and that copy does the same. The third copy is identical to the first, and all of them are identical to what the second compiler writes.
The language, the machine and the compiler run in the browser. You can write a program, see the instructions Böhm’s compiler makes of it, run the compiler as printed, and have it compile itself.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This may not be the first time the compiler has run. Peter Sestoft’s 2016 translation says he implemented it in Java. I could not find that code and do not know which corrections it needed.

Of the three slips, one was reported in 1976. I have not found the other two written down, but I read two sources, not the literature. The fourth change, renaming X, depends on how this reconstruction compiles the compiler’s formulas.

All three readings were written by the same agent in one session. They are three routes, not three authors. A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently and found that the algebra and the machine read input in different orders inside brackets; they now agree. Its review, and what was done about each point, is in the repository.

The compiler was typed in from a scan. For the two formulas that were not known to be wrong, the French printing and the English translation agree. Two arrows the printing leaves out of group J′ are supplied, the loader’s printed constant 94999010000 is read as Sestoft’s 9490010000, and a repeated label in Böhm’s second Euclid program is corrected; each is now listed as a slip in the repository.
The corrections are a reading of what Böhm meant. He is not here to ask.
body.principle: Agreement between things one author wrote is evidence of consistency. The page somebody else worked by hand is evidence of correctness.

body.text: If a program has only ever existed on paper, how would you know it was right?
body.detail: Having an agent produce a compiler was the cheap part. The work was arranging three ways to be wrong and making them agree, and even then the one outside check was a single hand-worked formula from 1976. Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s own test program in Böhm’s language is correct as algebra and prints nothing on the machine, because it uses the letters S and X.

record.title: A 1966 program said it had not been checked. So I ran it.
record.dek: The one large program in the papers that define CPL, a handwritten warning across the top of it, and a coding agent with a scan.
record.abstract: A note about building an interpreter for CPL, the language BCPL was cut down from, out of its 1966 working papers with a coding agent. The papers contain one program of any size, a preprocessor written in CPL, and someone has written across the top of it that the draft has not been fully checked. Typed in as printed it does not compile. With seven slips put right it runs and gives wrong answers in two ways, and in two more places its informal notes disagree with its own text. Corrected, it reads its own text to the last word. The interpreter and the program run in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A LANGUAGE IN WORKING PAPERS
body.text: CPL was designed in the early 1960s by a group at Cambridge and London. Martin Richards cut it down to make BCPL, and BCPL led to B and then C. In July 1966 the group put out a technical report called CPL Working Papers, most of which is a draft of the reference manual. I asked a coding agent to build an interpreter for the language those papers describe: the 1966 language, not the subset that became BCPL.

references.label: Richards, How BCPL evolved from CPL

body.label: 02 / ONE PROGRAM OF ANY SIZE
body.text: An interpreter built from a manual can only be tested on programs. The examples in the manual are a few lines each, and everything longer the agent wrote itself. The papers contain one exception. Appendix 1 is a preprocessor, about 190 lines of CPL, “intended to be both a description of the transformation from an implementation alphabet to canonical CPL and a general example of a CPL program”. Across the top of its first page someone has written by hand: “This draft has not been fully checked”.

body.label: 03 / AS PRINTED, IT DOES NOT COMPILE
body.text: The agent typed the program in from the scan, keeping the text as printed, with the corrections already written on the copy by hand. It does not compile. Three sections open with one tag and close with another: R.T and R.T., R.U.W and R.U.W., R.S. and R.S. One call is to Proprocessor. One case has no colon. And twice a name that should begin with a capital is typed small, goto switch and standard, which matters in CPL because a small letter is a whole name: standard is eight names side by side.

body.label: 04 / IT RUNS, AND IS WRONG
body.text: With those seven put right the program runs, and what it writes is wrong in two ways. The routine that reads an underlined word starts from the first letter instead of from nothing, so every word begins twice. And after an ordinary comma it loses a character. That one can be followed on the page with a finger: ReadSpaces has already moved on to the next character, and then NextChar moves on again.

body.label: 05 / WHERE THE NOTES DISAGREE WITH THE PROGRAM
body.text: Part 3 of the appendix describes the functions the program uses but does not declare, a sentence or a list for each. In two places those descriptions cannot be what the program needs. One says a function is true for the symbols that can come before a command, where the program uses it for the symbols that cannot. The other turns goto into go, after which nothing recognises it as a jump. These are perhaps better called open questions than slips. Part 3 says of itself that it is informal.

body.label: 06 / IT READS ITSELF
body.text: A preprocessor for CPL written in CPL can be given its own text. Corrected, it reads all 189 lines of itself and writes about 1,100 symbols, ending with finish. What it writes is not wholly canonical: jump on and the rest come out as two symbols each. And whether the “etc.” of Part 3 covers true and false, after which the program would otherwise lose a semicolon, is a reading, not something the page says. Given its own text as printed, it stops a little over 200 symbols in, at the first tag that does not match, and says nothing, because the program has no message for that case. It is doing what it was written to do. A closing bracket with the wrong tag makes every open section jump out through a label it was handed by its caller, and the outermost label is the end of the program.

The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the preprocessor as one of its examples. The programs on this page are run by it where they sit.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: These are readings of a scan of a typescript, made by one reader, and that reader was a coding agent. Each slip has a page number and a detail of the scan so that it can be checked by eye.
Whether the program was ever run in 1966, the documents I have do not say. A later draft may have put all of this right.

The appendix describes thirteen of its functions only informally and never defines seven more names it uses. All of them were supplied. A different reading of those sentences gives a different program.

The interpreter and the transcription came from the same agent in one session. The seven slips that stop the program compiling can be seen on the page. The two wrong answers also rest on the interpreter doing what the manual means.
The interpreter is not all of CPL. What it leaves out is listed in the repository, and where the 1966 papers say a section is out of date without giving the new rules, it follows the old ones.
I have not searched for an earlier list of these slips. Somebody may have made one.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently. It found that the interpreter grouped division the wrong way, a/bc as (a/b)c where the manual’s table gives a/(bc), that it skipped the second operand of and and or, and that some example programs had been edited without saying so. These are corrected or disclosed, and the review, with what was done about each point, is in the repository.
body.principle: A program that has never been run has only been proofread. Running it is a different kind of reading.

body.text: How much of a language that was still a draft can you check by running the one program its authors left?
body.detail: The preprocessor exercises the parts of CPL its authors reached for when they had real work to do: recursion, strings, a switch, sections with tags, and a label passed as a parameter so that a routine can jump out of its caller. It says nothing about the parts they did not need that day. For those, the interpreter has only the manual’s short examples and programs written by the same agent that wrote the interpreter.

record.title: The manual stopped at line 40.
record.dek: Dartmouth BASIC, typed in from its first instruction manual of May 1964, and the one program a later BASIC would not run.
record.abstract: A note about Dartmouth BASIC, with the language running in the page. The first instruction manual, from May 1964, explains the language in a few pages and prints three example programs with their results; they are typed in here beside the pages they came from, and print the same figures. The interpreter running them was written in Rust with a coding agent and checked against later BASICs, which it matched. The manual’s own second example then stopped at line 40: in 1964 a square root was taken of the absolute value, and the later BASICs it had been checked against call that an error.
record.lineage: 1964 MANUAL → LATER BASICS → AGENT PORT → 1964 MANUAL

body.label: 01 / MAY 1964
body.text: BASIC’s first instruction manual is a typescript from the Dartmouth College Computation Center, dated May 1964 and marked First Draft. Its preface says the college was building a system that “will enable 20 or more people to use the computer at the same time”, and lists what the language for it had to do. The first requirement: “It should be very easy to learn.” Then, as evidence, and “without any explanation”, it prints a whole program. Three lines, to work out seven plus eight, divided by three.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: That program, with the line numbers the manual gives it on page 4. It is running in your browser, not replayed. Change the sum and run it again.

links.label: Open the full study — every program, and the pages

body.label: 02 / FOURTEEN WORDS
body.text: A Dartmouth BASIC program is a list of numbered instructions. The computer starts at the lowest number and works upwards, so the numbers are the order, whatever order the lines were typed in. The manual suggests leaving gaps, such as counting in tens, “so that further instructions may be inserted if the need arises.” Each instruction is one operation and what it applies to, and there are not many: “The last instruction in any BASIC program is ‘END’. There are only 13 other operations.” LET puts a value in a variable. PRINT shows it. FOR and NEXT repeat the lines between them. IF … THEN and GO TO decide which line comes next. READ takes numbers from DATA lines, and DEF gives a formula a name. A variable is “any single letter, or a letter followed by one digit.”

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.label: 03 / THE PAGE PRINTS ITS OWN ANSWERS
body.text: The reprint Dartmouth hosts, which is the beginners’ part, ends with three example programs and, under each, what it printed and how long it took. Program number 1 averages the logarithms of the numbers 1 to 100 and prints 1.5797, in three seconds. I typed all three in from the scan. They are a test nobody had to write, because the expected output is on the page.
Program number 1, from page 21. The 1964 page prints 1.5797, and so does this. Switch off AS IN 1964 and a later BASIC prints the same number to nine figures.

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 04 / WHAT IS NOT THERE
body.text: What the beginners’ part leaves out says as much as what it has. There is no way to ask the person at the teletype a question: a program’s numbers come from its DATA lines, and to try other numbers you change the program. There are no variables for words, only for numbers. Powers are written with an arrow, X↑2, because “on a tele-type typewriter it is impossible to print superscripts”. The manual treats changing the program as the normal way to use it. Under program number 3 it says, “We can find the root of a different function by changing a single instruction”, prints the new line 30, and prints the new result.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 3, from page 23. Run it, then do what the manual does: replace line 30 with 30 DEF FNF(Z) = EXP(X) -2 and run it again. The page prints .837585, then .693176. The new line is typed here as it is printed, with an X where the first one had a Z. It still works, because the program only ever asks for FNF(X).

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 05 / HOW IT RUNS HERE
body.text: This is not Dartmouth’s compiler. It is an interpreter written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. I had started it in Python: a tokenizer and a parser, which never ran a program. I asked a coding agent to move it to Rust and finish it. Neither of us began from the 1964 manual.

body.label: 06 / CHECKED AGAINST LATER BASICS
body.text: How would I know it was right? The agent wrote tests, and they passed. Then it ran 103 listings from David Ahl’s BASIC Computer Games of 1978, which nobody involved had written, and every one loads and runs without changes, as the coding-horror collection has them; that collection was normalised for Vintage BASIC, so they are not the printed book line for line. Then it ran test programs through PC-BASIC, an independent emulation of Microsoft’s GW-BASIC. Twenty-two of them print the same on standard output in both, byte for byte once PC-BASIC’s line endings and closing prompt are set aside, and the comparison found one real mistake. Error messages were not compared. Everything agreed. All of it was BASIC from fourteen years or more after the manual.

body.label: 07 / LINE 40
body.text: Then I asked for pages of the 1964 manual, for this note, and the example programs came with them. Programs 1 and 3 gave the page’s figures. Program 2 solves quadratic equations, and on its third set of numbers it stopped: Illegal function call: SQR, in line 40. Line 40 takes a square root before the program has looked at whether the number is negative. Page 5 says why that was fine in 1964: “SQR(A) stands for √A, where the square-root is always taken of the absolute value of A.” The games and the second interpreter come from later BASICs, where, in the two I could run, the square root of a negative number is an error. They agreed with each other, and my interpreter agreed with them. The oldest page disagreed with all of it.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 2, as later BASICs run it. Press RUN: it stops at line 40. Switch on AS IN 1964 and run it again, and the last result reads IMAGINARY PART= 1.41421, as the page does. It goes back for more numbers until there are none, and then, as page 15 says the computer does when READ runs out of data, it stops.

Source, tutorial and the scanned pages

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This is not Dartmouth’s 1964 BASIC. It is an interpreter written sixty-two years later. In 1964 mode it follows the manual on square roots, powers, printing and the end of the data, and Thomas Kurtz’s later account on INT, RND and a leading minus sign, which the beginners’ part does not cover. Taking Kurtz’s account as a description of May 1964 is a reading.

How numbers are printed in 1964 mode, six figures and a point after a whole number, is copied from the results on pages 21 to 23. The beginners’ part does not state the rule, and I have not seen Part II.
In 1964 mode it still accepts everything the later BASICs added. It does not refuse INPUT or a variable called NAME$.

Three examples agreeing is three examples, and agreeing in their figures: the page’s layout, its TIME: lines, and its READ PART where the program says REAL PART, are not reproduced. The rule for square roots turned up because one program happened to need it. Other differences may be waiting for a program that needs them.
The checks were run by the coding agent and reported to me. It also miscounted its own tests twice, saying 120 and then 122 when there were 88, and corrected itself when it ran them again.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently. It found that 1964 mode differed from Kurtz’s account on INT, RND and a leading minus, that RANDOMIZE could change numbers the playground had already shown, and that the games were described as unmodified. These are put right, and its review, with what was done about each point, is in the repository.
body.principle: Sources that agree with each other are evidence about those sources.

body.text: Which BASIC is the reference for BASIC?
body.detail: The interpreter now has a switch: later BASIC unless asked, Dartmouth’s 1964 arithmetic and printing on request. That is a decision, not a discovery. Every check I had was a later BASIC agreeing with a later BASIC, and the manual was on Dartmouth’s website the whole time.
