record.title: In 1965, the computer learned to say I.
record.dek: A computer you talked to at a typewriter, rebuilt from RAND’s papers by a coding agent and replayed against the pages it typed. A year in, it began to say I, for the reason chat assistants do.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding JOSS, the conversational computing system J. C. Shaw wrote for RAND’s JOHNNIAC, from its scanned papers with a coding agent. You typed a line at a typewriter in green, and JOSS answered in black. In 1964 it said “Zero divisor.” By 1965 it said “I have a zero divisor.”, and Shaw gives the reason: personal pronouns were introduced “to reinforce the model”, because the timeliness of its remarks gave “a feeling of interacting with a person”. The papers print pages typed at the console, mistakes included. Typed in again, line by line, the reconstruction answers as the page does on all 767 lines the pages show JOSS typing. Five of them come out right only when JOSS’s own logarithm, exponential and power routines are followed from a listing of the program: its logarithm cuts off where it should round. Most of the words JOSS used are not in the papers: they were decoded from a listing of the program. The console runs in the browser, at a typewriter.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTING AIDE
body.text: JOSS ran on the JOHNNIAC at RAND from 1963. You sat at an electric typewriter with a two-colour ribbon and typed a line in green; JOSS did what it said, or kept it as a step of a program, and answered in black. J. C. Shaw, who wrote it, wanted the user to “interact with JOSS as with a computing aide”. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the JOSS of 1964 and 1965 from RAND’s scanned papers, and to hold it to one test: type the sessions printed in those papers again, and get the same page.

references.label: Shaw, JOSS: Experience with an Experimental Computing Service, P-3149, May 1965

body.label: 02 / GO
body.text: The session that mattered most is figure 2 of Shaw’s 1965 paper. A user sets out to solve a quadratic equation and gets nine things wrong, one after another. The first two are typing slips, put right by typing the line again. Then the program runs, and seven times it stops. A value is missing. A divisor is zero. The argument of a square root is negative. The form for the answers does not exist, then is given too few values, then has no room for them, then has blanks that touch. Each time JOSS says what is wrong and stops where it is. The user puts that one thing right and types Go. The program is never started again from the top. A parser and an evaluator do not get you this. The task has to be kept, broken off in the middle of a step, while the user changes the program underneath it.

body.label: 03 / FORTY MESSAGES, FOURTEEN IN PRINT
body.text: Shaw wrote that JOSS “simply selects from a stock of forty ‘canned’ messages”. Figure 2 alone shows fourteen of them, and the papers between them not many more. The rest were not lost. A listing of the program survives, headed in his hand “JOSS 666” and “JCS 1-9-65”, and it holds each message as octal numbers, five characters to a word. The agent decoded them with the listing’s own table of characters. There are forty.

body.label: 04 / TWO JOSSES
body.text: The first replays would not settle, because the pages disagree with each other. A film made in March 1964 has JOSS say “Zero divisor.” The paper of May 1965 has “I have a zero divisor.” Shaw explains it: “After a year’s experience with neutral, impersonal messages, we introduced personal pronouns and some informal diction.” And why: “This was done not facetiously, but rather to reinforce the model.” The model was a person. JOSS, he says on the same page, cannot carry on a real conversation and picks from forty canned messages, “But the timeliness and appropriateness of its remarks give a feeling of interacting with a person.” So in 1965 the computer began to say I, to feel like someone you were talking to. Every chat assistant makes the same choice now. The wording was not all that changed. In the pages of 1965 every answer typed without a form sits one column further to the right than in 1964. And the JOSS of the film types one fiftieth as 2·10*(-2), where by 1965 a number that small is typed as .02. So the reconstruction has a year. A session from one does not replay on the other.

body.label: 05 / WHAT THE REPLAY FOUND IN THE FILM
body.text: The film’s scenario was printed as a report, with the typewriter’s real output pasted in as figures. Replayed as printed, it goes wrong halfway: a listing in the report shows none of the first program’s steps, though nothing typed before it removes them. Something like a Delete all was cut from the scenario. The report also has a comma that the listing of the same step does not have, a space where there should be a multiplication dot, and an answer labelled without the space the user typed. With those four put right, and a decimal point the scan has lost from a form restored, each marked, it replays.

body.label: 06 / FIVE LINES
body.text: The five transcripts have 385 lines typed by the user and 767 typed by JOSS that the pages show, not counting the blank lines of pages a typist had copied. All 767 come out the same: 689 column for column against the typewriter’s own output, and the rest against pages a typist had copied, where only the characters can be compared. Five of them took more than a modern library, and they are all the same kind of thing. The page has log 2 as .69314718, three times, and the correctly rounded figure ends in a 1. It has one long expression ending in 357 where the reconstruction gets 356. And in a table of a hundred exponentials, the row for 72 ends in a 7. JOSS rounded to nine digits and then to the form, and a correct exponential, rounded that way, gives an 8. Each is one unit in the last digit, of a logarithm, an exponential, or a power worked out through both. With a correctly rounded library, all five came out one unit away. So the agent followed JOSS’s own routines from the listing of January 1965, card by card. Its logarithm, for a result below 1, multiplies out nine digits and does not round them: log 2 is .69314718056, and cut off it is .69314718. Its exponential and its powers, followed the same way, give the 7 in the row for 72 and the 357. All five come out as printed.

body.label: 07 / CHECK IT
body.text: Among Shaw’s working papers there is a handwritten page headed F1, dated 11-19-64. F1 is the logarithm routine in the listing. The page works through its range reduction and ends: “Check it. Looks like coefficient between 1 and √2 gets doubled several times.” That is three months after the paper with log 2 in it. It is not the same fault. The doubling the note describes brings the number into range and works as written; the cutting off comes a few cards later.

The console runs in the browser, at a typewriter: your lines in green and JOSS’s in black, ten characters a second, and a gong when it hands the typewriter back. It is compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Each of the five original sessions can be replayed there and compared with its page.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The pages were read by the same coding agent that wrote the interpreter, with sub-agents doing the measuring. No person has checked the transcriptions against the scans by eye; a second model, OpenAI’s Codex, spot-checked twenty places independently. The pages are in the repository so that somebody can.

The column rules were set from these pages, so their matching is partly the reconstruction being fitted to them. The digits were not fitted: they come out of the arithmetic, which for logarithms, exponentials and powers follows JOSS’s own routines. Those routines are a reading of the listing, checked against a small emulator built from the same reading, not a run of the original program.

Matching five sessions says nothing about what they do not exercise. Stop and Cancel, most of the forty messages, and what happens when a step is deleted from under a loop are built from the listing and Shaw’s notes, and no page shows them.
The sine, cosine and arg here are a modern library’s, rounded to nine digits. JOSS’s own routines for them are in the listing and have not yet been followed.
The messages were decoded by machine from a scan of a printed listing. Each was checked against the capitals printed beside it, which have no small letters and no ≤.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository independently. Besides the spot check, it found that large powers could come out as zero, that Form would not take an expression, and that the listing answers arg(0,0) where the reconstruction had made a message up; these follow the listing now. Its review, and what was done about each point, is in the repository.
Where no page of 1964 shows a message, the 1964 setting uses the words of 1965. How much storage each step, value and level of a task takes is an estimate.
This is the JOSS of the JOHNNIAC. The later JOSS on the PDP-6 is a larger language and is not here. Nor are the punched cards, the sign-on, or the other seven users.
body.principle: A manual tells you what a system was meant to do. A page it typed tells you what it did, mistakes included.

body.text: How much of a conversation survives on paper?
body.detail: The pages keep what was typed, by whom, and in which column. They do not keep the gong that rang when JOSS handed the typewriter back, the half second it took to fetch your work from the drum, or what it was like to be told “Eh?” by a machine in 1965. A reconstruction that matches the page has matched the part that was written down.

record.title: Its manual printed a trace. So I could check.
record.dek: The first artificial intelligence programs held what they knew as symbols linked into lists. Their language, IPL-V, was written for a machine its 1964 manual describes. A coding agent rebuilt that machine and held it to the runs the manual prints.
record.abstract: Computers were built to calculate; IPL was built to hold symbols, in lists a program makes, changes and gives back as it runs. This is a note about building the IPL computer, the machine the IPL-V manual of 1964 describes, with a coding agent. The manual prints one run of its own system in full: the address each card was loaded at, and a trace of every instruction with a count of interpretation cycles. The reconstruction loads that program at the same addresses, and all 46 lines of the trace agree in level, instruction, test cell and count. The count settled how cycles were tallied, which the text leaves loose, and with it the effort figures of a 1963 version of the Logic Theorist, which runs with no change to its deck and finds the same proofs by the same search. Transcribing the manual’s own programs found two things wrong with the reconstruction. The machine runs in the browser.

body.label: 01 / SYMBOLS, NOT NUMBERS
body.text: The computers of the 1950s were built to calculate, and the IPL-V manual begins there: “We now recognize that the digital computer is a device for manipulating symbols of any kind, in any way. Its genesis, however, lies in the desk calculator.” Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw and Herbert Simon wanted programs that worked on symbols, proving theorems and playing chess, and IPL was built for them around a different way of holding data: the list. A list is a chain of cells. Each holds a symbol and the address of the next, the last holds 0, and the list’s name is the address of its first cell. A symbol on a list can name another list, which makes a list structure. Putting a symbol in or taking one out is a change of links, and the manual says why that mattered: “These operations change the structure of the data unit, not just its content. It is this ability that contrasts rather strongly with standard ways or organizing data on the computer.” The price is that storage loses its order. “New words are taken from the gradually diminishing block of unused space”, and “some scheme must be incorporated to make all of this space available again”. IPL’s scheme is one list of every cell not in use, available space, which programs take cells from and give them back to.

references.label: IPL-V Manual, Introduction to the First Edition, pages ix, xvi and xviii (scan)

body.label: 02 / A MACHINE NOBODY HAD
body.text: IPL-V was made between 1957 and 1964 at the RAND Corporation and the Carnegie Institute of Technology, by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, Herbert Simon, Fred Tonge and others, for programs that solve problems by search and rules of thumb. Its manual is frank that there was no such computer: “No computer currently available can process the IPL language directly”. What it describes is an IPL computer: cells that each hold one word, P Q SYMB LINK; one list of every cell not in use; a push-down list under every storage cell; and a cycle that interprets lists of instructions punched one to a card. I asked a coding agent to build that machine as a machine, with storage an array of cells, so that a program uses space, gives it back and runs out of it much as it did then; the exceptions are listed in the repository.

references.label: Information Processing Language-V Manual, second edition, 1964 (scan)

body.label: 03 / ONE RUN, PRINTED IN FULL
body.text: Part One of the manual takes one small program, which removes the repeated symbols from a list, “all the way through to assembly and execution on the computer”, and prints both. Fig. 1 is the assembly listing, with the address every card went to. Fig. 2 is a trace of every instruction the program executes, with the test cell, the communication cell and a count of interpretation cycles. The reconstruction loads the program at the same addresses, from cell 64, and ends its listing with the same line: NUMBER OF CELLS ON AVAILABLE SPACE=21858. All 46 lines of the trace agree in level, instruction address, test cell, instruction and count.

body.label: 04 / WHAT THE COUNT SAYS
body.text: The text defines the count loosely: the interpreter tallies one into H3 “every time an ADVANCE occurs”. The column in Fig. 2 is exact. It goes up by one at an instruction and by two at one that executes a basic process, and the first instruction is the fifth cycle. The agent read the rule off the column. It matters beyond the figure, because the Logic Theorist reports its effort as this count. Counted this way, its effort comes to between 98.3 and 98.7 per cent of the figures printed in 1963, on every theorem. Jeff Shrager’s reconstruction, which runs the same deck and counts differently, reports about two thirds.

body.label: 05 / A THEOREM IS A LIST STRUCTURE
body.text: The Logic Theorist holds what it reasons about in the same way. Stefferud’s memorandum of 1963 says so on page 5: “Expressions, variables, and connectives are represented by IPL-V data list structures. An expression is recursively defined as a single variable or a list of subexpressions with a connective in its head.” Stopped at the routine that prints an expression, just before it prints theorem *2.01, (P implies not P) implies not P, the reconstruction’s storage holds exactly that shape: a head of two cells naming a description list and the expression; on the description list the attribute Q15, its tree form, and Q7, the name, whose value is the text *2.01; and the expression, with I0, implies, in its head and a sublist for each side. When it comes to prove *2.01, the description list has three more attributes: Q2 = 4, the number of levels; Q3 = 1, the number of distinct variables; and Q4 = 3, the number of places a variable appears. The memorandum calls Q2 “an active attribute” (page 51): asked for its value, it looks on the description list, and if there is none, it counts and assigns the count there. In the deck those are J10 and J11, the processes that find and assign a value on any description list. The numbers save work: “Only problems with identical values for Q2, Q3, and Q4 are put through a full match test” (page 33).

body.label: 06 / THE LOGIC THEORIST OF 1963
body.text: Einar Stefferud’s IPL-V version of the Logic Theorist of Newell, Shaw and Simon was printed in a RAND memorandum in 1963, with its output. Rupert Lane and Jeff Shrager transcribed it, David Moews corrected the transcription and transcribed the output, and Shrager’s Executable Archaeology already runs it. On this reconstruction it runs with no change to the deck. Of the 24 theorems from Principia Mathematica it was given, it proves the same 23 and gives up on the same one, *2.15, at its effort limit, each by the same search: the same number of subproblems and of substitutions for every theorem. The 533 lines of its printout agree with the transcribed pages apart from the effort figures, the core addresses it prints for rejected subproblems, and three lines where the 1963 printout itself differs from this run: DFF. for DEF., probably a slip in the printing, and two missing commas, whose cause is not known. The transcription of those lines is right.

body.label: 07 / THE MANUAL WRITES ITS OWN PROCESSES
body.text: Part One teaches by programs, and the agent transcribed every one printed in full and ran it. Twice the manual writes one of the machine’s own basic processes in IPL. Its J101, which generates every cell of a list structure, gave a cell the reconstruction’s built-in J101 did not: after the head of each list, the head’s own word, pushed down by the mark that says the list has been visited. Part Two says the same, and the reconstruction had missed it. A step-by-step trace of a recursive search, Fig. 3, showed a second thing: a basic process reached through a LINK is part of the step that leads to it. Both are put right, the manual’s J101 and the built-in one now agree, and all 27 steps that Fig. 3 lists match.

body.label: 08 / A MISTAKE PRINTED ON PURPOSE
body.text: One routine, R62, is printed with a wrong Q code, and the reader is asked to find it. Run as printed, it does not do what the error suggests, which is to go round for ever. It stops and answers W1. The wrong instruction sends it into the push-down list of the working cell W1, and the copy it finds there is a word of zeros, because W1 was empty. A word of zeros is how this machine marks the end of a list, so the search ends there. Put a symbol in W1 first and it does go round for ever.
The machine runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with every program from Part One of the manual among its decks. Step one and watch storage change.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: Figs. 1 to 3 are three runs of one system the manual does not name, on three small programs. Agreeing with them shows the reconstruction does what that system did on these programs.

The last 1.5 per cent of the Logic Theorist’s effort is not explained. Some basic processes may have been IPL routines in the system of 1963, costing more cycles than a primitive; the counts do not show which.
The Logic Theorist deck is Lane and Shrager’s transcription with Moews’s corrections, and this is not the first reconstruction to run it: Moews’s interpreter and Shrager’s did so first.

A system of the period does not settle the effort figures either. Moews runs the deck under the IPL-V of an IBM 7094 emulator, after four changes, and there effort is between 98 and 120 per cent of the 1963 figures, varying from theorem to theorem. Those figures are as Moews reports them; they were not reproduced here.
The list F1 makes is cell 148 in Fig. 2 and cell 145 here. What the system of 1964 had done with three more cells, the manual does not say.

Where the manual leaves a choice to each machine’s write-up, such as the compressed and binary card forms, the formats of J162 and the console, the reconstruction makes one, and the repository lists each.

The reconstruction, the transcriptions of Part One and these comparisons were made by one coding agent in one session, from scans read by that agent. Each figure has a page number so that it can be checked by eye.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently. It found that print lines took no storage, that one compatibility change lost a card’s first column, that integer zero had no sign, and a missing blank in negative exponents; all are put right, and none changes the Logic Theorist’s run. Its review, and what was done about each point, is in the repository.
body.principle: A manual that prints its own run can be held to it, line by line.

body.text: How much of a system from the early 1960s can be recovered exactly from a manual that printed one run of it?
body.detail: Fig. 2 fixed the load addresses, the order of interpretation and the count of cycles. It could not fix what the program it traces never does: auxiliary storage, the error traps, or the cost of each basic process in a particular system. For those there is only the text, and programs like the Logic Theorist whose printed output depends on them.

record.title: A 1954 manual asked for trouble reports.
record.dek: One of the first systems that let you type ordinary algebra into a computer, rebuilt from its manual by a coding agent and held to that manual’s own rules.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding the algebraic system J. H. Laning Jr. and N. Zierler wrote for MIT’s Whirlwind I, from the manual they published in January 1954, with a coding agent. You typed equations on a Flexowriter and the answers came back typewritten. The manual ends by admitting that “exhaustive tests have not been made” and asking for reports of any trouble. Run under its own rules, the system reads a/b/c as ac over b, and it says so on purpose. A zero has two signs, and the manual’s own loops step round it. Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s 1976 example program in the language stops with an alarm on its last number, and under the restrictions of January 1954 it could not have run at all. The manual’s exponent examples, run in order, stop with an alarm. None of these is a bug: each follows from the manual’s rules, plus choices the reconstruction lists. The system runs in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTER WITHIN A COMPUTER
body.text: In 1952 J. H. Laning Jr. of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory wrote a program that let Whirlwind I take mathematics typed as mathematics. With N. Zierler he made it a usable system by May 1953. You typed equations on a Flexowriter, which punched them on paper tape; the tape was translated into Whirlwind’s own instructions and run; and the answers came back typewritten. Their manual, Engineering Memorandum E-364, puts it in one line: “The effect of our program is to create a computer within a computer …” In 1954 John Backus came to MIT with two colleagues to see it run. Knuth and Trabb Pardo, in 1976, wrote that the manual “ought to be reprinted some day because their language went so far beyond what had been implemented before”. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the system from that manual, and to run the manual’s programs under the manual’s own rules.

body.label: 02 / EXHAUSTIVE TESTS HAVE NOT BEEN MADE
body.text: The manual ends with a section called Temporary Rules and Restrictions. An SR or CR instruction “may not refer to an equation that makes use of a subroutine”, and “The x|N is not yet in operation.” Then: “All other portions of the program are believed to be operating satisfactorily but exhaustive tests have not been made. Information relative to any troubles encountered in the use of this program would be appreciated by the authors.” The Whirlwind progress report for the first three months of 1954 says that all the routines in the manual had been tested and worked, with the exception of the x|N routine, and that a report on the program’s inner workings had been started by Zierler, who had since moved to Project Lincoln. I have not found that report, and at the summer school that year it was said that there were no annotated copies of the conversion routine. So the manual is the specification. Everything here that it does not say is listed as this reconstruction’s choice.

references.label: Project Whirlwind Summary Report No. 37, first quarter 1954

body.label: 03 / A PERFECTLY REASONABLE EXPRESSION
body.text: Multiplication is writing things side by side, so 2ay is 2 times a times y, and even a space is a multiplication sign when it falls between two digits: 23 is twenty-three and 2 3 is six. Division follows a rule of its own. Plus and minus separate terms, and inside a term a slash sends everything after it to the other side of the fraction, until the next slash. So cd/a(b + c) is cd over a(b + c), which is what a mathematician means, and “a/b/c is properly interpreted as the product ac divided by b”, which is not what FORTRAN or most people would make of it. The manual means it: the rule is set out on purpose, and the reconstruction follows it. In 1976 Laning wrote: “The notion of operator precedence as a formal concept did not occur to me at the time; I lived in fear that someone would write a perfectly reasonable algebraic expression that my system would not analyze correctly.”

body.label: 04 / TWO ZEROS
body.text: Numbers are kept in “the 24, 6 number system”: 24 binary digits and an exponent, about seven decimal places, nothing larger than 2⁶³ − 2³⁹. Zero comes with a sign. CP jumps if the last quantity computed was negative, and on a zero, says the manual, “the CP may or may not behave like an SP since 0 may appear as +0 or −0.” Its own loops step round this: to go round ten times they test n − 9.5, never n − 10. The reconstruction gives a zero a sign: a zero typed as 0 is +0, and the difference of two equal numbers is −0, as a one’s-complement adder would make it. That rule is my inference, not something the manual or any listing says. It makes the ambiguity definite: n − 5 with n equal to 5 is typed −.00000000+00, and CP jumps.

body.label: 05 / KNUTH’S PROGRAM STOPS ON ITS LAST NUMBER
body.text: In 1976 Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote one small algorithm, TPK, in each early language they described, Laning and Zierler’s among them. It reads eleven numbers with v|N, copies them into a|0 to a|10, and works back down with i = i − 1, printing a function of each. The manual allows a letter as an index, rounded to the nearest whole number, with conditions: “Negative values of n are not permitted in this connection, nor are values between zero and one half inclusive, with the exception that the value zero is permissible if assigned by the specific equation n = 0,.” On the last time round, i is zero, and it got there by i = i − 1. Run on the reconstruction, the program types ten lines and then stops: ALARM EQUATION 2 PRECEDED BY 109. Under the restrictions of January 1954 it could not have run at all, because it begins with v|N, and “The x|N is not yet in operation.” TPK was written as an illustration twenty-two years later and was never run on Whirlwind. This says only what the manual’s rules make of it. With every zero made +0 it runs to the end, and its last line is 6, but that is a what-if, not the manual: the page-13 rule forbids a computed zero index whatever its sign, and making every zero +0 lets it through because the zero it computes is then +0, the sign a zero set by n = 0, has.

body.label: 06 / THE INNOCUOUS CHANGE
body.text: The system solved differential equations by itself. Write dy/dt as D y = …, and the stretch of program from the first D equation to the last is gone through four times for each step, by “the method of Gill - a variation of the 4th order Runge-Kutta technique”. The manual gives two equations whose answers are sin(t − 2) and cos(t − 2) − 1, and the reconstruction gets .84103733 and −.45941162 at t = 3, against .84147098 and −.45969769: what a step of one half should cost. Then it warns. Put y|2 + 1 into a helper, a = y|2 + 1, just before the first D equation, and write D y|1 = a: the change “would appear to be innocuous”. It is not, because the second, third and fourth passes start at the first D equation and never recompute a. Run that way, the reconstruction gets .93750000 at t = 3, and by t = 10 it is wrong in the first digit. Its checker now warns about it, quoting the page.

body.label: 07 / WHAT ELSE THE RULES TURNED UP
body.text: The manual gives a = 5², b = (a − 2)⁻² and c = (ab³)⁻⁵ as examples of exponents. Run in that order, they stop: (ab³)⁵ is about 10⁻³⁴, too small for the 24, 6 system, so in this reconstruction it becomes zero and c divides by it. The alarm comes either way: 1/(1.4 · 10⁻³⁴) is about 7 · 10³³, itself far beyond 2⁶³ − 2³⁹. The MIT summer school notes of 1954 give their own, shorter version of the manual’s differential-equation program, whose equation 1 is the first D equation and which has no e = 9.7 − t, CP 3, e = −e, CP 2 or SP 1. It also has no PRINT, and lacks the commas the rules require on its last two lines: as printed it would not be accepted, and with the commas put back it types nothing. And the manual prints .05 as +.50000000−01, which the nearest 24-bit number to .05, .0500000007…, gives only if the eight digits are cut off rather than rounded. So the reconstruction cuts them off.

body.label: 08 / IT RAN THE FIRST TIME
body.text: None of this is trouble of the kind the authors asked about. record.abstract: A note about rebuilding the algebraic system J. H. Laning Jr. and N. Zierler wrote for MIT’s Whirlwind I, from the manual they published in January 1954, with a coding agent. You typed equations on a Flexowriter and the answers came back typewritten. The manual ends by admitting that “exhaustive tests have not been made” and asking for information about “any troubles encountered in the use of this program”. Its three complete programs run on the reconstruction, and their answers check against mathematics. Its rules mean what they say: a/b/c is ac over b, and a zero has two signs, which its own loops step round. The troubles worth reporting are elsewhere. The manual’s decimal for its largest number is wrong in the fifth place. The 1954 summer school’s version of its differential-equation program would not have been accepted. And Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s 1976 example in the language reaches, on its last number, an index the manual does not permit. The system runs in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTER WITHIN A COMPUTER
body.text: In 1952 J. H. Laning Jr. of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory wrote a program that let Whirlwind I take mathematics typed as mathematics, and with N. Zierler made it a usable system by May 1953. Equations typed on a Flexowriter were punched on paper tape, translated into Whirlwind’s own instructions, and the answers typed back. “The effect of our program is to create a computer within a computer …” In 1954 John Backus came to MIT with two colleagues to see it run. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the system from its manual, Engineering Memorandum E-364, and to run the manual’s programs under the manual’s own rules.

body.label: 02 / EXHAUSTIVE TESTS HAVE NOT BEEN MADE
body.text: The manual ends with Temporary Rules and Restrictions, among them “The x|N is not yet in operation.” Then: “All other portions of the program are believed to be operating satisfactorily but exhaustive tests have not been made. Information relative to any troubles encountered in the use of this program would be appreciated by the authors.” A progress report for the first quarter of 1954 says every routine had been tested and worked except the x|N routine. Zierler’s report on the program’s inner workings I have not found, and that summer it was said that “there are no annotated copies of the conversion routine”. So the manual is the specification, and what it does not say is this reconstruction’s choice.

references.label: Project Whirlwind Summary Report No. 37, first quarter 1954

body.label: 03 / A PERFECTLY REASONABLE EXPRESSION
body.text: Multiplication is writing things side by side: 2ay is 2 times a times y, and a space between two digits is a multiplication sign, so 2 3 is six. Inside a term a slash sends everything after it to the other side of the fraction, until the next slash. So cd/a(b + c) is cd over a(b + c), and “a/b/c is properly interpreted as the product ac divided by b”, not a over bc, as FORTRAN would have it. In 1976 Laning wrote: “The notion of operator precedence as a formal concept did not occur to me at the time; I lived in fear that someone would write a perfectly reasonable algebraic expression that my system would not analyze correctly.”

body.label: 04 / TWO ZEROS
body.text: Numbers have 24 binary digits and an exponent, about seven decimal places, and zero has a sign. CP jumps if the last quantity computed was negative, and on a zero “the CP may or may not behave like an SP since 0 may appear as +0 or −0.” The manual’s loops step round this: to go round ten times they test n − 9.5, never n − 10. The reconstruction has to decide, and my inference is a one’s-complement adder’s: a zero typed as 0 is +0, and the difference of two equal numbers is −0. So n − 5 with n equal to 5 is typed −.00000000+00, and CP jumps.

body.label: 05 / KNUTH’S PROGRAM STOPS ON ITS LAST NUMBER
body.text: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s 1976 example in the language, TPK, reads eleven numbers with v|N, copies them to a|0 to a|10, and works back down with i = i − 1. Page 13 allows a letter as an index, but: “Negative values of n are not permitted in this connection, nor are values between zero and one half inclusive, with the exception that the value zero is permissible if assigned by the specific equation n = 0,.” The last time round, i is zero, and it got there by i = i − 1. The reconstruction tells the two zeros apart by sign, so it stops: ten lines, then ALARM EQUATION 2 PRECEDED BY 109. The stop rests on page 13 and on my inference that a computed zero is −0. Make every zero +0 and they cannot be told apart, so TPK runs to the end: a what-if the manual would not allow. Its checker now points at i = i − 1 before anything runs. And under the rules of January 1954 TPK could not have run at all, because it begins with v|N.

body.label: 06 / THE INNOCUOUS CHANGE
body.text: Write dy/dt as D y = …, and the stretch from the first D equation to the last is gone through four times a step, by “the method of Gill - a variation of the 4th order Runge-Kutta technique”. The manual’s example has the answers sin(t − 2) and cos(t − 2) − 1, and the reconstruction is within about .004 of them at every t it prints: what a step of one half costs. Then the manual warns. Move y|2 + 1 into a helper, a = y|2 + 1, just before the first D equation, and the change “would appear to be innocuous”. It is not, because the later passes start at the first D equation and never recompute a. At t = 10, y|1 is 2.58 where sin 8 is .99. The checker warns about it, quoting the page.

body.label: 07 / A PROGRAM THAT WOULD NOT HAVE RUN
body.text: The MIT summer school notes of 1954 give their own, shorter version of the manual’s differential-equation program. As printed, its last two lines lack the commas the rules require, so the translator would not have accepted it, and it has no PRINT: with the commas put back, it integrates from t = 2 to past t = 10 and types nothing. The manual has a slip of its own, on page 6. Its largest number, 2⁶³ − 2³⁹, is “(or, roughly, 9.2233995 · 10¹⁸)”. It is 9.2233715 · 10¹⁸, wrong in the fifth decimal place. And the manual prints .05 as +.50000000−01, which the nearest 24-bit number to .05 gives only if the digits are cut off rather than rounded, so the reconstruction cuts them off.

body.label: 08 / IT RAN THE FIRST TIME
body.text: These are the troubles the authors asked for, seventy years late: a slip in the manual, one in a copy of it, and the rest its rules doing what they say. The system itself did real work. Laning recalled a three-dimensional lead-pursuit problem, coded with its sceptical owners “in a 2-1/2 hour coding session, at least half of which was spent in defining notation”, which “ran successfully the first time”: 79 statements, with seven uses of the differential-equation feature. The summer school heard that “with a single exception, all programs coded in the Laning-Zierler system have been completed successfully on their first run”. The price was speed: “a reduction of computing speed of the order of magnitude of ten to one from an efficient computer program”, as C. W. Adams put it in May 1954, and six to eight times the Laboratory’s usual interpretive system, as the summer school did.

The system runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the manual’s programs among its tapes. Type a tape, feed it, and the printer types the answers, as slowly as ten characters a second if you like. The translation shows each equation’s block of orders, and the same tape can be fed with each kind of zero side by side.

record.title: A scribe wrote 15 where his working says 14
record.dek: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus shows its working, about 1550 BCE. Transcribed by a coding agent and checked exactly, 845 of 956 lines agree with the working above them. Most of the rest is a notation the editions read differently, or is already known.
record.abstract: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus writes out its working, so its figures can be worked again. This is a note about a program, rhind, that checks each figure the notation can hold, as an exact fraction, against what the working above it gives, under interpretive choices it lists; and, separately, writes working the scribe’s way, by doubling, halving, two-thirds and the papyrus’s own table. It ran over a transcription of the papyrus from two editions, Chace (1929) and Peet (1923), made by a coding agent and its sub-agents. It checks 956 lines: 845 agree with the working and 111 do not. Of the 113 diagnostic records on those lines, 75 differ only in the sign for “part”, a notation Chace says need not be an error; 4 are ticks; 34 are figures, most of them pointed out by Chace or Peet. In Problem 27 the scribe wrote 15 where four times 3 2̅ is 14, as Peet notes. A second model reviewed the reconstruction independently, found no misread digit at the 72 places it checked, and found the first census and several of the checker’s rules unsound; this note gives the numbers after those were fixed. No person has checked the transcription, and nothing here is claimed as new. The papyrus can be checked page by page in the browser.
record.lineage: PAPYRUS → EDITIONS → AGENT → TRANSCRIPTION → RHIND → REVIEW

body.label: 01 / FIFTEEN FOR FOURTEEN
body.text: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied by the scribe Ahmose about 1550 BCE, by his own account from an older original. It opens with a table of 2 divided by each odd number from 3 to 101, and goes on to problems: loaves shared among men, quantities and their parts, granaries, fields and pyramids. The working is written out, in columns of doublings with a tick against the rows to be added, so its figures can be worked again. In Problem 27 a quantity and its fifth make 21. The scribe finds 3 2̅ and multiplies it by 5, and his row for 4 has 15, where four times 3 2̅ is 14. Peet marks it (sic); Chace prints 15 without comment. The answer the scribe gives in words, 17 2̅, is 3 2̅ and 14. I asked a coding agent to transcribe the working from two editions and to build a program, rhind, that checks every figure the notation can hold against the working above it. This is not a calculator for Egyptian fractions. It is a reading of one document: what the scribe wrote, what his working gives, and where they part.

references.label: rhind, the program and the transcription

body.label: 02 / A CHECK AND A GENERATOR
body.text: The papyrus writes fractions only as parts of one, with two-thirds the one exception: 5̅, the sign for “part” over 5, is a fifth. It divides by multiplying: to divide, the scribe doubles the divisor until the rows can be picked to make the dividend, and to double an odd part he looks it up in the table at the head of the papyrus. rhind does two separate things. It checks: each figure the scribe wrote is compared, as an exact fraction, with what the working above it gives. That is exact arithmetic under the interpretive choices rhind decisions lists, not a trace of the scribe’s operations, so a disagreement can come from the figure, the transcription or one of those choices. And it works: where a page asks for a multiplication or a division, it writes the working the scribe’s way, by doubling, halving, two-thirds and the table. A transcription never corrects the scribe: where the papyrus has 15, the file has 15.

body.label: 03 / 956 LINES OF WORKING
body.text: These are counts against this project’s transcription, under the rules in rhind decisions. rhind checks 956 lines of working across 91 problem sections and the two tables: 845 agree with the working, 111 do not. Those 111 lines give 113 diagnostic records, since one written figure can give two. They are of three kinds. In 75 the figure differs from the working only by the sign for “part”: 30 where 3̅0̅ is meant, or the reverse. In 4 the total written is right for other rows than those ticked. In 34 a figure differs in more than its part sign.

body.label: 04 / THE SIGN FOR “PART”
body.text: The first kind is not a count of errors. Chace (vol. II, p. xi) says the part sign is often left off where the context makes the fraction clear, and that its omission need not be an error; Peet (p. 38) counts wrong dots among the scribe’s errors and corrects them silently. The editions disagree about what these are, and rhind reports them apart, as notation.

body.label: 05 / THE 34 FIGURES
body.text: Most of the 34 are known: 2 ÷ 79 (2̅3̅3̅ and 4̅1̅6̅ for 2̅3̅7̅ and 3̅1̅6̅), No. 27 (four times 3 2̅ written 15), No. 31 (a total of 99 for 97), No. 43 (4̅5̅ for 1̅8̅0̅), No. 58 (1 4̅ for 1 2̅ 4̅), No. 63 (113 3̅ for 133 3̅ in a list totalled 700), No. 79 (2301 for 2401), and the 9̅-for-1̅4̅ sequence of Nos. 10 to 14, all pointed out by Chace or Peet. For each record, rhind errata lists the explanations that fit, not the cause: one hieratic number sign for another, the multiplier one sign away from the one written, one figure of a list, and others; of all 113, none of these fits 13. The transcribers’ notes quote an edition commenting at 97 of the 113, but that is a keyword search of the notes, not a census of what Chace and Peet say, and the 16 it misses are not “unnoted”.

body.label: 06 / SIXTY FOR EIGHTY
body.text: “One sign for another” is inferred from the decimal places of the numbers, not from the shapes of the hieratic signs. Among the candidates rhind emits, the pair that recurs is 60 for 80: 6̅6̅ for 8̅6̅ in 2 ÷ 43, 63 for 83 in 2 ÷ 83 and 1̅6̅6̅ for 1̅8̅6̅ in 2 ÷ 93, five places. Chace saw this: his note to 2 ÷ 43 names all five. No other pair is emitted more than twice.

The red answer at the head of the entry for 2 ÷ 59 has 2̅2̅6̅; the working under it has 2̅3̅6̅, and 4 × 59 is 236. Chace prints 226 in the answer and 236 in the working; Peet prints 236 in both, without remark on this page. The transcriber read 226 on Chace’s plate before rhind could run, and the review read it again. This is a discrepancy between the editions, and a question for the British Museum photograph. It is not shown to be an error of the scribe’s.

body.label: 08 / THE ROUTES
body.text: rhind routes asks whether the scribe sets out a column the way rhind’s generator would. The problems have 139 columns of two rows or more. 128 can be read in full, and 65 of those begin with a row for 1, say what they multiply and tick at least one row; only those 65 are compared, by their multipliers and ticks. Doubling alone gives the same multipliers and ticks in 40. Three conventions, each visible in the papyrus, bring it to 47: the tens done by a row for 10, 3̅ taken straight from the first row, and a division read as halving. The targets are often taken from the scribe’s own ticks, so this describes the subset, and does not validate the procedure. The columns that differ may differ because of the transcription or the model as well as the scribe’s choice.

body.label: 09 / THE TABLE OF 2 ÷ n
body.text: Why does the papyrus write 2 ÷ 13 as 8̅ 5̅2̅ 1̅0̅4̅, when 7̅ 9̅1̅ has fewer parts? rhind 2/n runs candidate rules for every odd n from 5 to 101 against the 49 entries, with at most four parts and none past 1000. The largest part that fits, again and again, gives 4 of 49. Fewest parts gives 25 or 29, depending on how ties are broken. Writing 2/n as m̅ + (2m − n)/mn, with 2m − n made of up to three divisors of m, gives 32, and 34 if the smallest last part is preferred. The scores depend on the bounds: with parts up to 10,000, the first divisor rule falls from 32 to 25. The targets take 2 ÷ 43, 59 and 93 as the working, not the answers, gives them. No rule here gives 2 ÷ 13 or 2 ÷ 95. Agreement describes a rule; it does not show the scribe used it. Rules of these kinds have been proposed for a long time, and none here is claimed to be any one scholar’s, or new.

body.label: 10 / AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW
body.text: A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the first release independently. It checked 72 places in the transcription against the scans of both editions, wrote probe pages to make the checker fail, recomputed the 2 ÷ n scores with a program of its own, and read the code. It found no misread digit, and confirmed 2 ÷ 59 and the five 60-for-80 places. It also found the first census unsound. That release called the part sign the commonest slip; split the figures into those the editions point out and those they do not, by what was only a keyword search; and concluded, from a test of whether an error was carried into the total, that the scribe worked from the right figure and wrote another. That test was wrong. Fixed, it applies at 12 places, 11 of them a part sign, and says nothing general about how the scribe worked. Several of the checker’s rules put errors on correct figures or let wrong ones through. Every finding was checked and acted on, and the numbers in this note are after those changes.

references.label: The independent review, and what was done about each finding

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The papyrus itself was not read. Two editions were, Chace’s and Peet’s, from page images. The transcription was made by a coding agent and its sub-agents, and reviewed at 72 places by a second model. No person has checked it against the pages.

Every count here is against this transcription, under the interpretive choices rhind decisions lists, not against the papyrus. A disagreement can come from the figure, the transcription or one of those choices.
The 75 part-sign records are a notation the editions read differently, not errors, and are not a rate of anything.
There is no count here of figures the editions do not point out. The first release gave one; it came from a keyword search of the transcribers’ notes, and is withdrawn.
The explanations rhind lists are ways a figure could have come to differ, not records of what happened. “One sign for another” is inferred from decimal places, not from the shapes of the signs.
2 ÷ 59 is a discrepancy between the editions and a question for the British Museum photograph, not a discovery and not shown to be the scribe’s error.
The routes describe 65 eligible columns of 139 and do not validate the procedure; the 2 ÷ n scores depend on the bounds chosen.

The papyrus has been edited and studied for 150 years: Eisenlohr, Peet, Chace, Gillings, Robins and Shute, and much since. Annette Imhausen’s Ägyptische Algorithmen (2003) reads the problems as algorithms, the idea this project runs with. It was not read, so nothing here says how close it is. The rules for the 2 ÷ n table have a literature of their own, and the rules here have not been checked against it. Nothing here is claimed as new until it has been checked against that literature and the photographs.
What does not fit the notation is kept as the scribe’s words in quotes and not computed: the hundred-hekat notation of Problems 68 to 86, ditto marks, drawings, and some columns set side by side.
body.principle: Running the working shows where the figures and the working part. It does not show who made the difference: the scribe, the editors, the transcriber, or the rules of the check.

body.text: Where a copy’s figures and its working part, how much of the difference is on the papyrus?
body.detail: rhind can say exactly where this transcription’s figures and its working disagree, and list the explanations that fit. It cannot say whether a difference is the scribe’s, the editions’ or the transcriber’s, nor whether a dropped part sign was an error at all; the editions themselves disagree about that. Only the photographs, read by someone who reads hieratic, can settle the places where they differ.

record.title: A handwritten program from 1958 runs again, to the last binary digit.
record.dek: Charles Hamblin’s GEORGE, a stack language for the English Electric DEUCE: rebuilt from its manual with a coding agent, then his own translator transcribed from 22 coding sheets and run on a simulated DEUCE, until the two agreed word for word.
record.abstract: A working note about rebuilding GEORGE, the General Order Generator that Charles Hamblin wrote for the English Electric DEUCE in 1957–58, from the three documents that survive: the programming manual, 52 pages of flow diagrams and 22 coding sheets. GEORGE programs are reverse Polish, with no addresses, run on a running accumulator of twelve cells. An interpreter built from the manual runs the manual’s programs, and Example 3 punches a quarter of what Simpson’s rule gives, because its coefficients are for the wrong step. Then the coding sheets, transcribed, were run as a deck of cards on a simulated DEUCE. Hamblin’s own translator runs the manual’s programs, and tracing his routines one instruction at a time brought the interpreter to the same 32-digit words as his code, for every one of 5,000 random programs. On the way it found four places where a sheet contradicts its flow diagram, and arithmetic in this version that is not what the manual says: an addition that drops a binary digit, and a multiplication that can lose the sign.
record.lineage: TYPESCRIPT · FLOW DIAGRAMS · CODING SHEETS → SCAN → AGENT → INTERPRETER · SIMULATED DEUCE

body.label: 01 / THREE DOCUMENTS
body.text: GEORGE was written by Charles Hamblin at the New South Wales University of Technology in 1957 and 1958, for its English Electric DEUCE. The manual opens: “GEORGE, or the General Order Generator, is a program for DEUCE permitting mathematical problems to be presented to the machine in a simple “addressless” instruction language, here called “G-code”.” Three documents survive, all on David Green’s DEUCE archive, scanned from the originals and supplied by Robin Vowels: the programming and operation manual, 23 typed pages; the flow diagrams, 52 handwritten pages; and the coding sheets, 22 handwritten pages of DEUCE instructions. The archive says the last two are “the only extant copy” and “correspond to the penultimate version of GEORGE IA”. I asked a coding agent to build the language from the manual, and then to read the other two against it.

references.label: David Green’s DEUCE archive, section GEORGE

body.label: 02 / TWELVE CELLS
body.text: A G-program is written in reverse Polish and names no addresses. The manual asks the reader to picture a pseudo-machine with a “running accumulator”: “a set of storage locations (known as “cells”) arranged in a linear order and operated on the “last-in-first-out” principle.” A number or a variable goes into the first empty cell; an operator works on the last cell or the last two. So a b + leaves the sum where a was. “The accumulator is limited to 12 cells. This is more than enough for all normal calculations”. Beside it are a link list of six for subroutines and repetitions, and a store of 32 plain variables, 1,024 with one suffix and 4,096 with two. Numbers are floating point with a 22-digit binary mantissa. The interpreter obeys a program a symbol at a time, as GEORGE II did, and the playground shows the twelve cells after every symbol.

body.label: 03 / EXAMPLE 3 IS OUT BY A FACTOR OF FOUR
body.text: Example 3 of the manual integrates exp(−x²/2) / (1 + exp(−ax)) from 1 to 5 by Simpson’s rule with 16 intervals, for five values of a read from cards. The argument is worked out as j 4 ÷ 1 +, so the step is a quarter. Simpson’s rule then weights the ordinates by a twelfth: 1/12, 4/12, 2/12 and so on. The manual’s Simpson vector holds 1/48, 4/48, 2/48, and its program for preparing the vector begins 1, 48 ÷. Run as printed, every result is a quarter of what Simpson’s rule gives: 0.0497078 for a = 0, where Simpson’s rule worked in double precision gives 0.198831. Everything else in the program is right. 1/48 would be the weight for a step of a sixteenth, which suggests the example was changed from another range at some point. That is a guess.

body.label: 04 / NUMERALS RUN TOGETHER
body.text: A number is written one digit to a symbol, and two numerals side by side are one number. The manual says so: “When two numbers must be written consecutively they should be separated by a comma (special symbol, omitted in translation)”. It is easy to forget when writing. 3, 4 14 ↓ looks like a call of subroutine 14 with 3 and 4 in the accumulator. It calls subroutine 414, taken modulo 32, which is 30. The interpreter does what the machine would, and its language server warns when numerals run together.

body.label: 05 / WHAT THE FLOW DIAGRAMS SETTLED
body.text: The manual leaves open how a repetition counts and what truth is. The flow diagrams are DEUCE instruction listings, not boxes and arrows, and they answer both. On page 26, a b rep (x) sets x to a and stores the count b − a in the link list with no test on the way in; the count is first looked at by ], on pages 23 and 27. So the body of a repetition is always obeyed at least once. When a is greater than b, the 16-digit count wraps round, to about 65,536 − (a − b) passes. On page 22, = and > leave a word with only the sign digit set for truth, which reads as −1, and zero for falsehood, and a conditional skip tests only the sign digit. ~ complements every digit of the word, exponent and all, so ~ of truth is just under a half. It still acts correctly in a skip. All of this was later confirmed by running Hamblin’s own code (07).

body.label: 06 / WHAT THE CODING SHEETS HOLD
body.text: The flow diagram for sin and cos, page 38, shows a polynomial taken from a track but not its coefficients. The coding sheets were transcribed minor cycle by minor cycle, about 1,830 written rows, with the 20 doubtful cells marked. Sheet 21, DL8, track 15/13, holds five constants written as base-32 digits at minor cycles 1, 3, 5, 7 and 13. At 30 binary places they are −1.2337005, +0.2536693, −0.0208627, +0.00091768 and −0.0000238. They are close to the Taylor coefficients of cos(πx/2), but not equal to them, in the way of a polynomial fitted to the whole interval; with them, 1 plus the polynomial in x² is within 3.0·10⁻⁸ of cos(πx/2) from 0 to 1. Beside them, on track 15/12, is 2/π, which turns the argument into quarter periods. Tracing the routine on the simulator (07) confirmed the order in which they are used.

body.label: 07 / HAMBLIN’S OWN TRANSLATOR, RUNNING
body.text: A DEUCE was simulated from English Electric’s programming manual and course notes, and the 22 transcribed coding sheets were fed to it as a deck of 193 cards, as an operator would have, followed by each G-program and its data. This version took its program as 8-bit codes, four to a card row, not the decimal pairs the manual describes; the read routine says so. Four places on the sheets, each clear on the scan, contradict their flow diagrams: divide falls into the multiply routine, R| and P| do nothing, any number below about a quarter punches zeros without end, and wait reads the wrong track. For the last, the flow diagram carries Hamblin’s own correction, written over the old value; the sheet still has the old one. With the flow diagrams’ versions, applied at run time, Hamblin’s translator runs all 16 of the manual’s programs. sin and cos needed the DEUCE Logical Design Manual as well: his routine reads the multiplier’s store while it is still multiplying.

body.label: 08 / TO THE LAST BINARY DIGIT
body.text: At first the interpreter and Hamblin’s code disagreed in the sixth figure of Example 3. Tracing his addition register by register showed why: when it shifts the smaller number into line, it drops that number’s lowest binary digit and doubles another, and then rounds half up. The same method was used on multiplication, division, the punch’s decimal conversion, every function, and the reading of numerals and data cards, and each was written into the interpreter as his code does it, then checked word for word on random inputs: 200,324 sums and differences, 122,576 products, 112,819 quotients, 160,056 punched cards, 60,000 arguments for each function, 200,145 numerals, 180,105 data cards, all the same. Random programs with arithmetic, functions, suffixes, repetitions, skips, logic and subroutines now punch the same both ways, 5,000 of 5,000. It also brought out what the manual does not say. Indexing numbers go through the same fetch-integer routine as rem’s divisor, right only within the range the manual allows. 0 ÷ 0 is 0. Copying from an empty accumulator gives 0. 0 sin is −2⁻²⁵. The punch nearly always takes an exact half down. And some of it is plainly wrong: 0.609211 times −0.820734, which is −0.50000018, is punched as +0.5, the sign lost in standardising; 2, 5 max is −5.

The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the manual’s programs as examples. Every run is traced, so the twelve cells can be stepped through a symbol at a time.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The two routes share the program reader and the symbol codes. Their agreement cannot check those. The interpreter now copies Hamblin’s arithmetic, so the agreement of the two is no longer independent evidence about the arithmetic: it says the model is faithful to his code, not that his code was right. An independent model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository and checked samples of the transcription against the scans; its findings and what was done about them are in the repository.

Running Hamblin’s code needed choices the sheets cannot show. A binary digit, P31, has no column on the form, and for one class of words its value rests only on the program running. One doubtful cell is filled from the flow diagram. The three corrections are applied at run time, not written into the transcription.

All of the reading, of the manual, the flow diagrams and the coding sheets, was done by coding agents. No person has yet checked it against the pages. The transcription of the coding sheets marks 20 lines as doubtful.
The flow diagrams and coding sheets are the penultimate version of GEORGE IA. Nothing describes GEORGE II, and margin notes mention variants 1B and 1C.
The interpreter follows the manual, not Hamblin’s code, in two places: max, and the zero that a single shot gives after the square root of a negative number (his code gives 0.5).
The simulator is built from manuals, not from a DEUCE. Where they do not say, for instance the reader’s timing between its minimum and maximum, it chooses, and the choices are written down.
That Example 3 changed its range at some point is a guess. The documents do not say how the 1/48 came about, or whether anyone ran the example as printed.
body.principle: A manual describes a language. Only the program says what the machine did, and the program has to be run to say it.

body.text: When a run of handwritten code disagrees with its manual, which one was GEORGE?
body.detail: A disagreement has four places to look: the transcription, the simulator, the reading of DEUCE, and the 1958 program itself. Most of the disagreements found so far were traced to one of the first three and put right. A few, max and the lost sign in multiplication among them, are the program as written, the version before the last, which Hamblin may well have corrected himself.

record.title: The first ALGOL 60 system’s run-time is missing. Its 1964 printout is not.
record.dek: ALGOL 60 rebuilt from its Report, and its first implementation, Dijkstra and Zonneveld’s for the Electrologica X1, rebuilt from that system’s documents, then checked against what the X1 printed in 1964: 80 of 82 numbers to the last digit.
record.abstract: A note about building an ALGOL 60 interpreter from the 1962 Revised Report with a coding agent, and then a second mode that runs programs as the first ALGOL 60 system ran them: the one Dijkstra and Zonneveld wrote for the Electrologica X1 in Amsterdam, which went into operation in 1960. The X1’s compiler survives and has been run again; the run-time routines its programs called were printed by the Mathematical Centre, but no copy has been found. So the second mode was built from what the system’s documents say those routines did, and checked two ways: against the real compiler on a simulator, and against output the X1 printed in 1964. Of the 82 numbers of its first run, it reproduces 80. The other two are last digits that sit just above a decimal tie. Both modes run in the browser, side by side.

body.label: 01 / MAN OR BOY
body.text: ALGOL 60 is defined by a report of seventeen pages, the Revised Report of 1962. What makes it hard to implement is not the syntax but call by name: a parameter is not a value but a piece of the caller’s program, worked out again every time it is used. In 1964 Donald Knuth wrote to the Algol Bulletin with a ten-line test that would “separate the man-compilers from the boy-compilers”. He had no man-compiler himself, worked it by hand, and guessed −121, “probably wrong”. The answer compilers found is −67. I asked a coding agent to build an interpreter from the Report alone, with call by name done the way the Report’s copy rule describes it. It gives −67.

references.label: Revised Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60, 1962
Knuth, “Man or boy?”, Algol Bulletin 17, July 1964

body.label: 02 / THE FIRST IMPLEMENTATION
body.text: A report can be implemented many ways. The first implementation of ALGOL 60 was written by Edsger Dijkstra and Jaap Zonneveld at the Mathematical Centre in Amsterdam, for the Electrologica X1, and went into operation in the summer of 1960. Its compiler survives: Kruseman Aretz, who looked after the system in the 1960s, published the full text of a 1964 version in 2003, with an equivalent in Pascal, and Serge Vakulenko has since run that again on a simulator of the X1. The other half of the system is missing. The run-time routines that compiled programs called for arithmetic, for statements, procedure calls and printing were printed by the Mathematical Centre as a series of its own, and Kruseman Aretz typed them in again to rerun the system, but no copy has been found. So I asked the agent for a second mode, --x1, that runs a program the way the X1 did, as far as the system’s own documents say: the system as its 1962 manual describes it, not the first version of 1960.

body.label: 03 / THE MANUAL’S RULES WERE NOT THE COMPILER’S CHECKS
body.text: The X1’s user manual of 1962 lists 23 “special properties”: rules a program had to keep, such as declaring simple variables before procedures and specifying every parameter. The first version of --x1 refused programs that broke them. Then the real compiler, run on Vakulenko’s simulator, compiled a procedure declared before a variable, and Knuth’s program as printed, with five parameters unspecified, and both ran: −67. Most of the manual’s rules were advice to programmers, not checks the compiler made, though not all: it stops on a label that is a number, as the manual says it will. --x1 now warns about the rules the compiler did not check, and says that what followed on the X1 is not known.

body.label: 04 / WHERE THE X1 PARTS FROM THE REPORT
body.text: Some of the X1’s properties, and the way it stored numbers, change what a program means. In a for statement with a step, the X1 worked the step out once each time round, and the first time before assigning the starting value; the Report works it out twice each time round, after. Parameters called by value were evaluated in the order of their specifications, not the order written. Only the first nine characters of a name counted. An integer procedure could return 1.5. A real kept a 40-bit mantissa in store, so x := 1/3 followed by x − 1/3 gives about 1.5⏨−13, not 0. One example program, x1-probes, prints a line for each of these, six in all, and every line differs between the two modes.

body.label: 05 / A REAL IS NEVER ZERO
body.text: An extract of the X1 user manual, printed in an appendix of Kruseman Aretz’s comparison of the X1 and X8 systems, describes the arithmetic of the lost run-time routines. On the X1 a real number is never 0: zero as a real is the least positive number the machine has, and “the relation ‘a = 0’ can never have the value true for variable a of type real”. So 1/0 is not an error. A real too large to store becomes the largest one there is, and an integer result too large for 26 bits quietly becomes a real. --x1 does all of this, each rule with the sentence it comes from.

body.label: 06 / AGAINST THE REAL COMPILER
body.text: Vakulenko’s simulator runs the real 1964 compiler, but with run-time routines he reconstructed himself, as --x1’s are. So a program run there is evidence about the X1 only where the compiler decides the answer. The agent wrote 39 probe programs, each asking one question, and ran them on both. Of the 14 the compiler decides, such as the order in which f(1) − f(2) × f(3) calls f, all agree, and so do the 7 decided by both halves. Of the 18 the run-time decides, 7 differ. One is a jump the manual leaves undefined. In the other six the X1 manual’s words are on the side of --x1: x1sim’s abs returns a real where the manual says it keeps the type of its argument, and its sqrt refuses a negative number where the manual says it takes the absolute value.

references.label: Vakulenko, the X1 ALGOL compiler and simulator

body.label: 07 / WHAT THE X1 PRINTED IN 1964
body.text: Two reconstructions agreeing is not the X1. What would settle the run-time is the X1’s own output, and some survives. Zonneveld’s thesis of 1964, Automatic Numerical Integration, prints his program for the motion of the five outer planets with what the X1 printed for it, four runs on three pages. --x1 had been checked against a version of that program on the simulator all along: the one in Kruseman Aretz’s report, which types its output where the thesis’s punches it, with the same layout. The first run fills page 103 and has 82 numbers, besides the tolerance and the times. --x1 prints 80 of them digit for digit. The other two differ in the last digit, 6.641455425 against 6.641455426 and 16.281370896 against 16.281370897, and both values lie a hair above a decimal tie, less than one unit of the 40-bit mantissa, where the answer turns on how precisely the X1 converted binary to decimal, which is not known. Making stores truncate instead of round would explain the first, but two other input values the X1 printed back exactly would then come out one lower; so stores round, as the manual says.

references.label: Zonneveld, Automatic Numerical Integration, MC Tract 8, 1964, pp. 102–107

body.label: 08 / WHAT THE PAGE CORRECTED
body.text: The page also corrected the reconstruction. --x1 had put the sign of a fixed-point number beside its first digit; the X1 put it in the first column, + 3.429474152. It had printed the X1’s smallest real as .3094⏨−616; Dijkstra’s ALGOL course says such a number is typed as “the integer 0 or ‘inf’”, and page 106 shows the mass of Pluto, set to zero, as a plus sign and a 0. And where the documents are silent, the designer can be. --x1 rounds a real that is exactly halfway between two integers away from zero. Dijkstra’s course says that for an integer x, x := 7/2 “is undefined: x can just as well become 3 as 4”. The X1 promised nothing, so the choice is recorded as --x1’s own.

references.label: Dijkstra, Cursus programmeren in ALGOL 60, 2nd edition, 1962

body.text: Both modes run in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, each program twice, side by side, with the lines that differ marked. For the outer planets a third column holds the X1’s page of 1964.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: --x1 is not the X1. The compiler’s decisions were checked against the real compiler; the run-time’s are rebuilt from what documents say, and documents describe, they do not execute.

The 1964 page is one program. It exercises real arithmetic, procedures and printing, not switches, own variables or deep recursion. Agreement on 80 of its numbers says nothing about what it does not use.
The two last digits are explained, not reproduced. The explanation, a conversion of unknown precision, fits both, but another rule might too.
Everything here was read and built by a coding agent over two days, including the transcription of the 1964 page from the scan’s text layer. The page is linked so that it can be checked by eye.

The original run-time routines were printed by the Mathematical Centre, but I have not found them. Gauthier van den Hove’s 2019 thesis has a chapter on how the X1 executed ALGOL 60 programs; it is held back until 2027, and was not read. It may answer what this cannot.
Nothing here is claimed as new. Kruseman Aretz recovered and described the compiler, and Vakulenko made it run again; this project builds on both.
body.principle: A reconstruction checked only against another reconstruction has been checked for consistency. A page the machine printed is a different kind of witness.

body.text: How much of a lost run-time can be rebuilt from what its documents say, and how would you know?
body.detail: For the X1 the answer so far is: enough to reproduce 80 of 82 printed numbers, with the other two at the limit of what the documents fix. Two more of Zonneveld’s programs, with their X1 output, are in a 1963 report of the Mathematical Centre, and are the next test. The run-time’s own text, if it surfaces, would be the last.
