record.title: A scribe wrote 15 where his working says 14
record.dek: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus shows its working, about 1550 BCE. Transcribed by a coding agent and checked exactly, 845 of 956 lines agree with the working above them. Most of the rest is a notation the editions read differently, or is already known.
record.abstract: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus writes out its working, so its figures can be worked again. This is a note about a program, rhind, that checks each figure the notation can hold, as an exact fraction, against what the working above it gives, under interpretive choices it lists; and, separately, writes working the scribe’s way, by doubling, halving, two-thirds and the papyrus’s own table. It ran over a transcription of the papyrus from two editions, Chace (1929) and Peet (1923), made by a coding agent and its sub-agents. It checks 956 lines: 845 agree with the working and 111 do not. Of the 113 diagnostic records on those lines, 75 differ only in the sign for “part”, a notation Chace says need not be an error; 4 are ticks; 34 are figures, most of them pointed out by Chace or Peet. In Problem 27 the scribe wrote 15 where four times 3 2̅ is 14, as Peet notes. A second model reviewed the reconstruction independently, found no misread digit at the 72 places it checked, and found the first census and several of the checker’s rules unsound; this note gives the numbers after those were fixed. No person has checked the transcription, and nothing here is claimed as new. The papyrus can be checked page by page in the browser.
record.lineage: PAPYRUS → EDITIONS → AGENT → TRANSCRIPTION → RHIND → REVIEW

body.label: 01 / FIFTEEN FOR FOURTEEN
body.text: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied by the scribe Ahmose about 1550 BCE, by his own account from an older original. It opens with a table of 2 divided by each odd number from 3 to 101, and goes on to problems: loaves shared among men, quantities and their parts, granaries, fields and pyramids. The working is written out, in columns of doublings with a tick against the rows to be added, so its figures can be worked again. In Problem 27 a quantity and its fifth make 21. The scribe finds 3 2̅ and multiplies it by 5, and his row for 4 has 15, where four times 3 2̅ is 14. Peet marks it (sic); Chace prints 15 without comment. The answer the scribe gives in words, 17 2̅, is 3 2̅ and 14. I asked a coding agent to transcribe the working from two editions and to build a program, rhind, that checks every figure the notation can hold against the working above it. This is not a calculator for Egyptian fractions. It is a reading of one document: what the scribe wrote, what his working gives, and where they part.

references.label: rhind, the program and the transcription

body.label: 02 / A CHECK AND A GENERATOR
body.text: The papyrus writes fractions only as parts of one, with two-thirds the one exception: 5̅, the sign for “part” over 5, is a fifth. It divides by multiplying: to divide, the scribe doubles the divisor until the rows can be picked to make the dividend, and to double an odd part he looks it up in the table at the head of the papyrus. rhind does two separate things. It checks: each figure the scribe wrote is compared, as an exact fraction, with what the working above it gives. That is exact arithmetic under the interpretive choices rhind decisions lists, not a trace of the scribe’s operations, so a disagreement can come from the figure, the transcription or one of those choices. And it works: where a page asks for a multiplication or a division, it writes the working the scribe’s way, by doubling, halving, two-thirds and the table. A transcription never corrects the scribe: where the papyrus has 15, the file has 15.

body.label: 03 / 956 LINES OF WORKING
body.text: These are counts against this project’s transcription, under the rules in rhind decisions. rhind checks 956 lines of working across 91 problem sections and the two tables: 845 agree with the working, 111 do not. Those 111 lines give 113 diagnostic records, since one written figure can give two. They are of three kinds. In 75 the figure differs from the working only by the sign for “part”: 30 where 3̅0̅ is meant, or the reverse. In 4 the total written is right for other rows than those ticked. In 34 a figure differs in more than its part sign.

body.label: 04 / THE SIGN FOR “PART”
body.text: The first kind is not a count of errors. Chace (vol. II, p. xi) says the part sign is often left off where the context makes the fraction clear, and that its omission need not be an error; Peet (p. 38) counts wrong dots among the scribe’s errors and corrects them silently. The editions disagree about what these are, and rhind reports them apart, as notation.

body.label: 05 / THE 34 FIGURES
body.text: Most of the 34 are known: 2 ÷ 79 (2̅3̅3̅ and 4̅1̅6̅ for 2̅3̅7̅ and 3̅1̅6̅), No. 27 (four times 3 2̅ written 15), No. 31 (a total of 99 for 97), No. 43 (4̅5̅ for 1̅8̅0̅), No. 58 (1 4̅ for 1 2̅ 4̅), No. 63 (113 3̅ for 133 3̅ in a list totalled 700), No. 79 (2301 for 2401), and the 9̅-for-1̅4̅ sequence of Nos. 10 to 14, all pointed out by Chace or Peet. For each record, rhind errata lists the explanations that fit, not the cause: one hieratic number sign for another, the multiplier one sign away from the one written, one figure of a list, and others; of all 113, none of these fits 13. The transcribers’ notes quote an edition commenting at 97 of the 113, but that is a keyword search of the notes, not a census of what Chace and Peet say, and the 16 it misses are not “unnoted”.

body.label: 06 / SIXTY FOR EIGHTY
body.text: “One sign for another” is inferred from the decimal places of the numbers, not from the shapes of the hieratic signs. Among the candidates rhind emits, the pair that recurs is 60 for 80: 6̅6̅ for 8̅6̅ in 2 ÷ 43, 63 for 83 in 2 ÷ 83 and 1̅6̅6̅ for 1̅8̅6̅ in 2 ÷ 93, five places. Chace saw this: his note to 2 ÷ 43 names all five. No other pair is emitted more than twice.

The red answer at the head of the entry for 2 ÷ 59 has 2̅2̅6̅; the working under it has 2̅3̅6̅, and 4 × 59 is 236. Chace prints 226 in the answer and 236 in the working; Peet prints 236 in both, without remark on this page. The transcriber read 226 on Chace’s plate before rhind could run, and the review read it again. This is a discrepancy between the editions, and a question for the British Museum photograph. It is not shown to be an error of the scribe’s.

body.label: 08 / THE ROUTES
body.text: rhind routes asks whether the scribe sets out a column the way rhind’s generator would. The problems have 139 columns of two rows or more. 128 can be read in full, and 65 of those begin with a row for 1, say what they multiply and tick at least one row; only those 65 are compared, by their multipliers and ticks. Doubling alone gives the same multipliers and ticks in 40. Three conventions, each visible in the papyrus, bring it to 47: the tens done by a row for 10, 3̅ taken straight from the first row, and a division read as halving. The targets are often taken from the scribe’s own ticks, so this describes the subset, and does not validate the procedure. The columns that differ may differ because of the transcription or the model as well as the scribe’s choice.

body.label: 09 / THE TABLE OF 2 ÷ n
body.text: Why does the papyrus write 2 ÷ 13 as 8̅ 5̅2̅ 1̅0̅4̅, when 7̅ 9̅1̅ has fewer parts? rhind 2/n runs candidate rules for every odd n from 5 to 101 against the 49 entries, with at most four parts and none past 1000. The largest part that fits, again and again, gives 4 of 49. Fewest parts gives 25 or 29, depending on how ties are broken. Writing 2/n as m̅ + (2m − n)/mn, with 2m − n made of up to three divisors of m, gives 32, and 34 if the smallest last part is preferred. The scores depend on the bounds: with parts up to 10,000, the first divisor rule falls from 32 to 25. The targets take 2 ÷ 43, 59 and 93 as the working, not the answers, gives them. No rule here gives 2 ÷ 13 or 2 ÷ 95. Agreement describes a rule; it does not show the scribe used it. Rules of these kinds have been proposed for a long time, and none here is claimed to be any one scholar’s, or new.

body.label: 10 / AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW
body.text: A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the first release independently. It checked 72 places in the transcription against the scans of both editions, wrote probe pages to make the checker fail, recomputed the 2 ÷ n scores with a program of its own, and read the code. It found no misread digit, and confirmed 2 ÷ 59 and the five 60-for-80 places. It also found the first census unsound. That release called the part sign the commonest slip; split the figures into those the editions point out and those they do not, by what was only a keyword search; and concluded, from a test of whether an error was carried into the total, that the scribe worked from the right figure and wrote another. That test was wrong. Fixed, it applies at 12 places, 11 of them a part sign, and says nothing general about how the scribe worked. Several of the checker’s rules put errors on correct figures or let wrong ones through. Every finding was checked and acted on, and the numbers in this note are after those changes.

references.label: The independent review, and what was done about each finding

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The papyrus itself was not read. Two editions were, Chace’s and Peet’s, from page images. The transcription was made by a coding agent and its sub-agents, and reviewed at 72 places by a second model. No person has checked it against the pages.

Every count here is against this transcription, under the interpretive choices rhind decisions lists, not against the papyrus. A disagreement can come from the figure, the transcription or one of those choices.
The 75 part-sign records are a notation the editions read differently, not errors, and are not a rate of anything.
There is no count here of figures the editions do not point out. The first release gave one; it came from a keyword search of the transcribers’ notes, and is withdrawn.
The explanations rhind lists are ways a figure could have come to differ, not records of what happened. “One sign for another” is inferred from decimal places, not from the shapes of the signs.
2 ÷ 59 is a discrepancy between the editions and a question for the British Museum photograph, not a discovery and not shown to be the scribe’s error.
The routes describe 65 eligible columns of 139 and do not validate the procedure; the 2 ÷ n scores depend on the bounds chosen.

The papyrus has been edited and studied for 150 years: Eisenlohr, Peet, Chace, Gillings, Robins and Shute, and much since. Annette Imhausen’s Ägyptische Algorithmen (2003) reads the problems as algorithms, the idea this project runs with. It was not read, so nothing here says how close it is. The rules for the 2 ÷ n table have a literature of their own, and the rules here have not been checked against it. Nothing here is claimed as new until it has been checked against that literature and the photographs.
What does not fit the notation is kept as the scribe’s words in quotes and not computed: the hundred-hekat notation of Problems 68 to 86, ditto marks, drawings, and some columns set side by side.
body.principle: Running the working shows where the figures and the working part. It does not show who made the difference: the scribe, the editors, the transcriber, or the rules of the check.

body.text: Where a copy’s figures and its working part, how much of the difference is on the papyrus?
body.detail: rhind can say exactly where this transcription’s figures and its working disagree, and list the explanations that fit. It cannot say whether a difference is the scribe’s, the editions’ or the transcriber’s, nor whether a dropped part sign was an error at all; the editions themselves disagree about that. Only the photographs, read by someone who reads hieratic, can settle the places where they differ.

body.label: 11 / WHAT THE WORKING HAS BECOME
body.text: Nothing in this note is a new fact about the papyrus. What has changed is the form its working is in. The 956 lines are now a structured, executable object: each row a multiplier and a product, each tick a choice of rows, each total a sum, and every figure worked again, exactly, from the rows above it. A step of the working is no longer only something to read and remark on; it can be challenged. Change a figure or a tick, as the steps under Problem 27 do, and the check says at once what follows and what no longer holds. The same check runs over every page, so a question about one figure becomes a question asked of all of them, under rules that are written down, answered with a count, and asked again when a rule or a reading changes, as it was after the independent review. The editions point out the scribe’s slips where they meet them, and most of the 34 figures are theirs. What this adds is a way to test the intermediate steps systematically, every one the notation can hold, and anyone can do it in the browser.

record.title: The Nine Chapters writes 18/52 as the board leaves it
record.dek: Chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, set out in counting rods and worked as the text says. Of 39 statements of the text the board reaches, 38 agree. Its answers are written over one denominator each, and not always in lowest terms.
record.abstract: Chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (九章算術, 方程) solves what we would call simultaneous linear equations on a counting board: columns of rods, worked against each other until one figure is left over another. This is a note about a program, jiuzhang, that sets out each problem of the chapter, and the boards its commentators work, as the text sets them, works them a step at a time as the text says, and compares what the text states, where the notation can hold it, with what the board gives. It ran over a transcription of the Sibu congkan reprint of the Weiboxie edition, made from the scans by a coding agent and its sub-agents. On 26 pages it checks 39 statements the board reaches: 38 agree, and the one that does not is Problem 6, whose signs in this edition give −8 and −3 where the answer is 8 and 3. That is not a census of every number in the text. The text writes its eleven fractional answers over one denominator each, and not always in lowest terms: Problem 2 is 1 18/52, not 1 9/26, and 52 is the 法 as the board leaves it. Of three readings of the last step, the 法 and the 實s divided by what they share writes all 11 as the text does; that describes how the answers are written, not where a reduction was made. Dai Zhen’s 145 算 is given by two rules of counting, his 99 only by one proposed after both were known; none of 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations makes Liu Hui’s passage on 77 算 work as printed. A second model reviewed the reconstruction independently, found no mistranscription, and found the checker could give a false ✓; this note gives the results after that was fixed. A literature check by a second model found that several of these results are already known: Problem 6’s signs were corrected by Li Huang, and Chemla and Guo (2004) print his correction; Hart (2011) discusses how the denominators follow the board, for Problem 14’s 33/111 and the determinant; and Liu Hui’s 77 passage has been emended by Chemla and Guo and worked through to 77 by Guo Shuchun (2020), where this project ran only the unemended text. No person has checked the transcription, and nothing here is claimed as new. Every page can be run on the board in the browser.
record.lineage: TEXT → SCANS → AGENT → TRANSCRIPTION → JIUZHANG → BOARD → REVIEW

body.label: 01 / EIGHTEEN FIFTY-SECONDS
body.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art is a Chinese book of problems and procedures, put together under the Han from older material, with a commentary by Liu Hui (263), notes by Li Chunfeng (656) and, in the 1770s, Dai Zhen’s collation notes. Chapter 8, 方程 (fangcheng), is on what we would call simultaneous linear equations. Its procedure is done on a counting board: the conditions are set out as columns of rods, right to left, and worked against each other until one figure is left over another, the 法 (divisor) over the 實. In Problem 2, two kinds of grain, the text’s answer for a bundle of the top grade is 1 斗 and 18/52: 一斗五十二分斗之十八. Not 9/26. Worked as the text says, the board leaves its 法 at 52. I asked a coding agent to transcribe the chapter from the scans and to build a program, jiuzhang, that does what each line of the text says to the board and compares what the text states, where the notation can hold it, with what the board gives. This is not a solver for linear equations. It is a reading of one chapter: what the text says to do, what doing it gives, and where they part.

references.label: jiuzhang, the program and the transcription

body.label: 02 / A BOARD AND WHAT IS DONE TO IT
body.text: A page in jiuzhang’s notation is a board and what is done to it, one operation to a line, in the order the text gives them. Set right 3 2 1 39 sets the first column, the 實 last. Multiply middle by the head of right is the text’s 徧乘; Take right from middle until the head is gone is its 直除. Negative quantities are black rods, positive red, and the rule of signs (正負術) is the signed arithmetic jiuzhang does without being told. jiuzhang does three things. It runs a page: each operation on the board, as transcribed. It checks what the source states: a column a commentator says the board now holds, an answer as the text writes it, a set of rates, a count of operations (算). Some figures the notation cannot hold, rates read crosswise and arithmetic in fractions off the board, and those are kept as the source’s words, unchecked. And it reads in the alternative: where a clause of a commentary can be read more than one way, the page gives every reading, and jiuzhang readings runs every combination. A transcription never corrects the text. Where the text’s signs give the wrong answer, the page has the text’s signs.

body.label: 03 / 39 STATEMENTS
body.text: These are results against this project’s transcription, under the choices jiuzhang decisions lists. jiuzhang verify runs 26 pages: the 18 problems and 8 pages of commentary. They make 39 checked statements, a column a commentator gives, an answer, a set of rates or a count: 38 agree with the board and 1 does not. Five more are not reached: they come after a step that cannot be done. A statement can hold several figures, and some figures the sources give are quoted and not checked, so this is not a census of every number in the text.

body.label: 04 / HOW THE ANSWERS ARE WRITTEN
body.text: Eleven answers have fractions. The text writes them over one denominator, and not always in lowest terms: Problem 2 is 1 斗 and 18/52, not 9/26; Problem 14 is 33/111, not 11/37. Which reading of the last step writes them so? Every 實 over the 法 as the board leaves it writes 7 of the 11 as the text does. Each answer in its lowest terms writes 9. The 法 and all the 實s divided by what they share (約) writes all 11. So the answers are written over one denominator for each problem, and it is not the board’s 法 as it stands (Problem 1’s board leaves 36, the text writes quarters; Problem 16’s 976, the text 122), and not each fraction in its own lowest terms (52 and 111 survive). The 約 reading gives the same denominators as reducing each answer and then writing them all over the least of their common denominators: the table shows how the answers are written, not where in the working a reduction was made. That the denominators reflect the board is known: Hart (2011, pp. 173–174) discusses Problem 14’s 33/111, not 11/37, and its relation to the determinant. The count across all eleven answers was not found in the literature searched, which does not make it new. In Problem 2 the denominator the text writes, 52, is the 法 as the board leaves it. Problem 13’s answer is the extreme case: the depth of the well, 721, is the 法 itself, given as a rate (舉率以言之), and Liu Hui’s 法得七百二十一實七十六 is the board’s left column, checked.

body.label: 05 / PROBLEM 6
body.text: In this edition, the Weiboxie text, Problem 6’s procedure sets its 實 as 正 in both columns: 益實六斗正 … 益實一斗正. Run as printed, the board gives −8 and −3 where the answer is 8 and 3. This is the one statement of the 39 that does not agree. The other text consulted has 負 in both places, and with 負 the board gives the answer. The scan was read twice. This is known: Li Huang (李潢, 九章算術細草圖說, juan 8) says both 正 should be 負 (正正皆當作負), and Chemla and Guo (2004, p. 632, n. 51) print 負, credit him, and record 正 in other witnesses too, so it is not peculiar to this edition. The board finds the same thing by another road: it cannot get 8 and 3 from the signs as printed.

body.label: 06 / DAI ZHEN’S 145 AND 99
body.text: In his collation notes, Dai Zhen says that Problem 18 by the plain method, cross-multiplying each pair of columns (互乘) and then finding the prices from the bottom up, takes “145 算, counting multiplications, takings and divisions together” (兼乘減除言之), and that a shorter way, working from a column whose head is one, takes 99. He does not say what one 算 is beyond that, so jiuzhang rules tries several conventions and prefers none. Plain counts each multiplication, taking and division of one figure, less the heads that cross-multiplying makes equal: 145 for the plain method, 101 for the shorter way. Worked also saves everything multiplied or divided by one: 140 and 98. Readoff is plain with a division by one read off, not worked: 145 and 99. Plain is the nearest to his words, but leaving out the heads’ takings as well as their multiplications is this project’s convention, not his; worked extends his economies, which are about multiplying, to dividing, which he does not mention. Readoff was proposed by the independent review after both numbers were known. It gives both, and is reported as a rule fitted after the fact, not as Dai Zhen’s. A reading of his 145 as a count of single-figure operations was not found in the literature the check could read; two of the likeliest places, Shen, Crossley and Lun and Guo Shuchun’s 彙校, could not be opened.

body.label: 07 / THE BOARD’S WORKSPACE
body.text: By the text’s own 徧乘 and 直除, Problem 18 counts 158 算 under each of the three rules, with at most 160 rods and an 11-place figure on the recorded boards. Those are the boards as recorded after each step. The working of the last step is not on them: finding the 荅 by the text’s method forms a product of 16 places, and cross-multiplying forms products the board never shows, so these are not the workspace a reckoner needed. Under the repeated rule, which counts a taking done several times over as that many takings of single figures, the text’s method on Problem 18 comes to 180,403 operations, 180,330 of them takings, or 89,773 takings of a whole column.

body.label: 08 / LIU HUI’S 77
body.text: In his commentary to Problem 18, Liu Hui works it “by the old method, made short” (以舊術爲之…今欲要約), clause by clause, and says it takes 77 算. Dai Zhen calls the passage corrupt (訛舛不可通). The page gives each clause in every reading this project could find: the columns as written, and, for the clause 及減第三行, which as written takes the 3rd column from itself, other columns or nothing; and each 減 or 去 done once, until the head is gone, as far as it goes, in turn, or crosswise. That is 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations, not 100,000,000 interpretations. 229,906 of them can be done to the end. None leaves the 4th column giving the price of 黍, as the passage says it should. So none of these readings of the passage as printed works; that does not show that no reading does, and Liu Hui’s 77 is not tested here. The passage has been emended and worked by others. Chemla and Guo (2004, pp. 652–655) repair its opening, 及減第三行 among other words, and restore 六 for 空, crediting Dai Dunyuan; Guo Shuchun (2020) works the emended passage through and tallies 77, counting each placing of rods, each operation on a whole column and each division of a 實 by a 法 as one 算. Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) and Zhu Yiwen (2025) read 算 as counting rods. The census here ran the text as printed, not these emendations: it says only that the unemended passage does not work under the readings offered, which is what Dai Zhen said. Among what the menu leaves out: 頭位 as anything but the first figure of the column worked on; the columns set one at a time, as 先置第三行 … 次置第二行 … 次置右行 says, with copies kept; other repairs of 及減第三行; mutual subtraction ending in either column. The independent review tried a wider search of its own, heads of either column and other orders, and found no working reading either. His new method, 124 算, which Guo (2020) also works through, was given the same treatment and stops, under every reading offered, by the passage’s fourth clause. Its last part, where the columns are set afresh, checks: the 3rd less the 4th leaves 麻 1, 菽 4, 荅 −3, 實 4, as he says, and as Guo (2020) explains.

body.label: 09 / AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW
body.text: A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository at commit 8532977 independently. It checked every answer, the Problem 6 signs, the commentary figures, the 77 passage and the four stated counts against the scans, and found no mistranscription. It reproduced the answers table, the counts and the censuses with programs of its own. And it wrote probe pages that made the checker fail. A board with contradictory conditions was solved and its answer ticked; an answer could be checked against a board that had since changed; an answer with the wrong number of figures got no mark; an answer written in a form no reading gives got ✓; and the fractions of the last step could overflow without saying so. Each was confirmed here and fixed: a contradictory board is not solved, an answer belongs to the board it was found on, wrong arity and unwritten forms are ✗, and the fractions are checked. It also found the claims wider than the program: figures it called checked that are only quoted, the workspace measured on recorded boards, the census of the 77 passage narrower than its size, and Dai Zhen’s words defining no one rule. Those were reworded, and the census now counts as done to the end only what it ran. The results in this note are after those changes.

references.label: The independent review, and what was done about each finding

body.label: 10 / READING THE TEXT
body.text: The text read is the Sibu congkan photographic reprint of the Weiboxie edition, with Liu Hui’s commentary, Li Chunfeng’s notes and Dai Zhen’s collation notes, from Wikimedia Commons, read from the page images. Wikisource’s transcription of the same pages is marked unproofread, and was used only to find places: it drops 直 (in 直除, and 直 “worth”) throughout, drops 兔 throughout Problem 17, and has 八之 for 入之 and 損妓之 for 損益之. A second, punctuated text of the main text, from another edition, is a third witness.

body.label: 11 / EARLIER WORK
body.text: The literature on chapter 8 is large, and this project did not read it. A second model, OpenAI’s Codex with web search, looked for each result in what it could reach: parts of Li Huang, Chemla and Guo, Hart, Guo Shuchun’s revised translation and Zhu Yiwen. It could not open Shen, Crossley and Lun, or Guo’s 彙校. Problem 6’s 正 for 負 is known, from Li Huang to Chemla and Guo. That the denominators reflect the board is partly known, from Hart; the count across all eleven answers was not found. Dai Zhen’s 145 as a count of single-figure operations was not found. Liu Hui’s 77 passage has been emended by Chemla and Guo and worked through to 77 by Guo (2020), and his 124 worked through by Guo; the census here ran only the text as printed. Liu Hui’s rates 7:4:3:5:6 are in Guo (2020) and in Chemla and Guo. “Not found” means not found in what could be read, never that a result is new.

body.text: jiuzhang runs in the browser, compiled unchanged from the same Rust source as the command-line version, and draws the board in three dimensions: each figure in rods, the units upright and the tens lying (一縱十橫), five as one rod across, red for 正 and black for 負, the columns right to left. Step through a page, or play it: a rod that stays stays put, a new one is dropped into place, and the rods taken off the board are knocked off the felt. Beside it, the page in an editor whose colours, problems and hover come from jiuzhang’s language server, running in the page too.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The transcription was made by a coding agent and its sub-agents, from the scans, and checked against them at the answers, the signs of Problem 6, the commentary figures, the 77 passage and the four counts by a second model. No person has checked it.
The 39 statements are what the notation can hold. Some figures the sources give are quoted and not checked, so 38 of 39 is not a census of every number in the text.

Every result here is against that transcription, under the choices jiuzhang decisions lists: that the rule of signs is signed arithmetic, how 徧乘 and 直除 are read, what “head” means, the three readings of the last step, that no rule of counting is preferred, that the readings offered for a corrupt passage are the transcriber’s, and the units.

That 約 writes all 11 answers as the text does describes how they are written. It gives the same denominators as reducing each answer and writing them over their least common denominator, so it does not show where in the working a reduction was made, or how the answers were found.

Problem 6 is a difference between this edition’s signs and the answer, and it is not a finding of this project: Li Huang corrected the signs, and Chemla and Guo (2004) print his correction and record 正 in other witnesses.
Dai Zhen’s words define no one rule of counting. Plain gives his 145 and not his 99; readoff gives both, but was proposed after both were known, and is not shown to be his.
The rods and places are those of the recorded boards, not the workspace a reckoner needed: the last step works a product of 16 places off the board.

None of 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations makes Liu Hui’s 77 passage work as printed, and the review’s wider search found none either. That is not a finding of this project: Dai Zhen called the passage corrupt, Chemla and Guo (2004) emend it, and Guo (2020) works the emended passage to 77. Those emendations were not run here, and his 77 is not tested.

Chapter 8 and its commentaries have been edited, translated and studied at length: Qian Baocong’s and Guo Shuchun’s critical editions; Shen Kangshen, Crossley and Lun (1999); Chemla and Guo Shuchun (2004); Hart (2011); Guo’s revised translation (2020); and Zhu Yiwen on the rods (2010, 2025). This project did not read them. The literature check was a second model’s search, which read parts of some and could not open others; what it did not find may still be there. Nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: Running the procedure shows where the text and the board part. It does not show whether the difference is the text’s, the edition’s, the transcriber’s, or the reading’s.

body.text: Does the emended passage, run on the board, take 77 算 and leave the price of 黍?
body.detail: Chemla and Guo (2004) emend Liu Hui’s passage, and Guo Shuchun (2020) works it through and tallies 77, counting each placing of rods, each operation on a whole column and each division as one 算. jiuzhang has run only the text as printed, where none of the readings offered works. Run as a page, under Guo’s way of counting, the emended passage can be checked step by step against both his tally and the price of 黍; that is the next page to write.

body.label: 12 / WHAT THE CHAPTER HAS BECOME
body.text: Nothing in this note is a new fact about the Nine Chapters: Problem 6’s signs were corrected by Li Huang, the link between the denominators and the board is in Hart, and Liu Hui’s 77 has been worked by Guo Shuchun. What has changed is the form the chapter is in. Its eighteen procedures, and the boards its commentators describe, are now a structured, executable object: each line an operation on a board of rods, done as the text says, with the board after it, and every statement the board reaches checked against it. A step is no longer only something to read; it can be challenged. Change a sign, or the way an answer is written, as the steps in the second section do, and the run says at once what follows and what no longer holds. The same check runs over every page, under choices that are written down, so a question about one answer becomes a question asked of all eleven, answered with a count, and asked again when a choice changes, as it was after the independent review. A reading of a corrupt passage becomes something that can be run, and the published emendation of Liu Hui’s is the next to run. What this adds is a way to test the chapter’s intermediate steps systematically, and anyone can do it in the browser.

record.title: A handwritten program from 1958 runs again, to the last binary digit.
record.dek: Charles Hamblin’s GEORGE, a stack language for the English Electric DEUCE: rebuilt from its manual with a coding agent, then his own translator transcribed from 22 coding sheets and run on a simulated DEUCE, until the two agreed word for word.
record.abstract: A working note about rebuilding GEORGE, the General Order Generator that Charles Hamblin wrote for the English Electric DEUCE in 1957–58, from the three documents that survive: the programming manual, 52 pages of flow diagrams and 22 coding sheets. GEORGE programs are reverse Polish, with no addresses, run on a running accumulator of twelve cells. An interpreter built from the manual runs the manual’s programs, and Example 3 punches a quarter of what Simpson’s rule gives, because its coefficients are for the wrong step. Then the coding sheets, transcribed, were run as a deck of cards on a simulated DEUCE. Hamblin’s own translator runs the manual’s programs, and tracing his routines one instruction at a time brought the interpreter to the same 32-digit words as his code: of 5,000 random programs, 4,993 run the same both ways in every respect, and the other 7 differ on purpose, where the manual says something his code does not do. On the way it found four places where a sheet contradicts its flow diagram, and arithmetic in this version that is not what the manual says: an addition that drops a binary digit, and a multiplication that can lose the sign.
record.lineage: TYPESCRIPT · FLOW DIAGRAMS · CODING SHEETS → SCAN → AGENT → INTERPRETER · SIMULATED DEUCE

body.label: 01 / THREE DOCUMENTS
body.text: GEORGE was written by Charles Hamblin at the New South Wales University of Technology in 1957 and 1958, for its English Electric DEUCE. The manual opens: “GEORGE, or the General Order Generator, is a program for DEUCE permitting mathematical problems to be presented to the machine in a simple “addressless” instruction language, here called “G-code”.” Three documents survive, all on David Green’s DEUCE archive, scanned from the originals and supplied by Robin Vowels: the programming and operation manual, 23 typed pages; the flow diagrams, 52 handwritten pages; and the coding sheets, 22 handwritten pages of DEUCE instructions. The archive says the last two are “the only extant copy” and “correspond to the penultimate version of GEORGE IA”. I asked a coding agent to build the language from the manual, and then to read the other two against it.

references.label: David Green’s DEUCE archive, section GEORGE

body.label: 02 / TWELVE CELLS
body.text: A G-program is written in reverse Polish and names no addresses. The manual asks the reader to picture a pseudo-machine with a “running accumulator”: “a set of storage locations (known as “cells”) arranged in a linear order and operated on the “last-in-first-out” principle.” A number or a variable goes into the first empty cell; an operator works on the last cell or the last two. So a b + leaves the sum where a was. “The accumulator is limited to 12 cells. This is more than enough for all normal calculations”. Beside it are a link list of six for subroutines and repetitions, and a store of 32 plain variables, 1,024 with one suffix and 4,096 with two. Numbers are floating point with a 22-digit binary mantissa. The interpreter obeys a program a symbol at a time, as GEORGE II did, and the playground shows the twelve cells after every symbol.

body.label: 03 / EXAMPLE 3 IS OUT BY A FACTOR OF FOUR
body.text: Example 3 of the manual integrates exp(−x²/2) / (1 + exp(−ax)) from 1 to 5 by Simpson’s rule with 16 intervals, for five values of a read from cards. The argument is worked out as j 4 ÷ 1 +, so the step is a quarter. Simpson’s rule then weights the ordinates by a twelfth: 1/12, 4/12, 2/12 and so on. The manual’s Simpson vector holds 1/48, 4/48, 2/48, and its program for preparing the vector begins 1, 48 ÷. Run as printed, every result is a quarter of what Simpson’s rule gives: 0.0497078 for a = 0, where Simpson’s rule worked in double precision gives 0.198831. Everything else in the program is right. 1/48 would be the weight for a step of a sixteenth, which suggests the example was changed from another range at some point. That is a guess.

body.label: 04 / NUMERALS RUN TOGETHER
body.text: A number is written one digit to a symbol, and two numerals side by side are one number. The manual says so: “When two numbers must be written consecutively they should be separated by a comma (special symbol, omitted in translation)”. It is easy to forget when writing. 3, 4 14 ↓ looks like a call of subroutine 14 with 3 and 4 in the accumulator. It calls subroutine 414, taken modulo 32, which is 30. The interpreter does what the machine would, and its language server warns when numerals run together.

body.label: 05 / WHAT THE FLOW DIAGRAMS SETTLED
body.text: The manual leaves open how a repetition counts and what truth is. The flow diagrams are DEUCE instruction listings, not boxes and arrows, and they answer both. On page 26, a b rep (x) sets x to a and stores the count b − a in the link list with no test on the way in; the count is first looked at by ], on pages 23 and 27. So the body of a repetition is always obeyed at least once. When a is greater than b, the 16-digit count wraps round, to about 65,536 − (a − b) passes. On page 22, = and > leave a word with only the sign digit set for truth, which reads as −1, and zero for falsehood, and a conditional skip tests only the sign digit. ~ complements every digit of the word, exponent and all, so ~ of truth is just under a half. It still acts correctly in a skip. All of this was later confirmed by running Hamblin’s own code (07).

body.label: 06 / WHAT THE CODING SHEETS HOLD
body.text: The flow diagram for sin and cos, page 38, shows a polynomial taken from a track but not its coefficients. The coding sheets were transcribed minor cycle by minor cycle, about 1,830 written rows, with the 20 doubtful cells marked. Sheet 21, DL8, track 15/13, holds five constants written as base-32 digits at minor cycles 1, 3, 5, 7 and 13. At 30 binary places they are −1.2337005, +0.2536693, −0.0208627, +0.00091768 and −0.0000238. They are close to the Taylor coefficients of cos(πx/2), but not equal to them, in the way of a polynomial fitted to the whole interval; with them, 1 plus the polynomial in x² is within 3.0·10⁻⁸ of cos(πx/2) from 0 to 1. Beside them, on track 15/12, is 2/π, which turns the argument into quarter periods. Tracing the routine on the simulator (07) confirmed the order in which they are used.

body.label: 07 / HAMBLIN’S OWN TRANSLATOR, RUNNING
body.text: A DEUCE was simulated from English Electric’s programming manual and course notes, and the 22 transcribed coding sheets were fed to it as a deck of 193 cards, as an operator would have, followed by each G-program and its data. This version took its program as 8-bit codes, four to a card row, not the decimal pairs the manual describes; the read routine says so. Four places on the sheets, each clear on the scan, contradict their flow diagrams: divide falls into the multiply routine, R| and P| do nothing, any number below about a quarter punches zeros without end, and wait reads the wrong track. For the last, the flow diagram carries Hamblin’s own correction, written over the old value; the sheet still has the old one. With the flow diagrams’ versions, applied at run time, Hamblin’s translator runs all 16 of the manual’s programs. sin and cos needed the DEUCE Logical Design Manual as well: his routine reads the multiplier’s store while it is still multiplying.

body.label: 08 / TO THE LAST BINARY DIGIT
body.text: At first the interpreter and Hamblin’s code disagreed in the sixth figure of Example 3. Tracing his addition register by register showed why: when it shifts the smaller number into line, it drops that number’s lowest binary digit and doubles another, and then rounds half up. The DEUCE Logical Design Manual describes that shift (p. 58). The same method was used on multiplication, division, the punch’s decimal conversion, every function, the reading of numerals and data cards, the step of a repetition and the single shot after an overflow, and each was written into the interpreter as his code does it, then checked word for word on random inputs: 200,324 sums and differences, 122,576 products, 112,819 quotients, 160,056 punched cards, 60,000 arguments for each function, 200,145 numerals, 180,105 data cards. Random programs with arithmetic, functions, suffixes, repetitions, skips, logic and subroutines are compared on everything they punch and on the stop they end with: of 5,000, 4,993 are the same both ways, and the other 7 are 0 ÷ 0, which the manual’s stop table says stops and Hamblin’s code passes as 0. It also brought out what the manual does not say. Indexing numbers go through the same fetch-integer routine as rem’s divisor, right only within the range the manual allows. Copying from an empty accumulator gives 0. 0 sin is −2⁻²⁵. The punch nearly always takes an exact half down. A repetition variable set to a small fraction in the loop sends the machine astray. And some of it is plainly wrong: 0.609211 times −0.820734, which is −0.50000018, is punched as +0.5, the sign lost in standardising; 2, 5 max is −5.

The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the manual’s programs as examples. Every run is traced, so the twelve cells can be stepped through a symbol at a time.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: Word for word means agreement with the sheets as simulated, with four corrections and one reconstructed cell. Much of what the arithmetic rests on is documented in English Electric’s manuals; the divider’s working, the reader’s timing and one class of P31 digits are chosen or inferred. The two routes share the program reader and the symbol codes. Their agreement cannot check those. The interpreter now copies Hamblin’s arithmetic, so the agreement of the two is no longer independent evidence about the arithmetic: it says the model is faithful to his code, not that his code was right. An independent model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository and checked samples of the transcription against the scans; its findings and what was done about them are in the repository.

Running Hamblin’s code needed choices the sheets cannot show. A binary digit, P31, has no column on the form, and for one class of words its value rests only on the program running. One doubtful cell is filled from the flow diagram. The three corrections are applied at run time, not written into the transcription.

All of the reading, of the manual, the flow diagrams and the coding sheets, was done by coding agents. No person has yet checked it against the pages. The transcription of the coding sheets marks 20 lines as doubtful.
The flow diagrams and coding sheets are the penultimate version of GEORGE IA. Nothing describes GEORGE II, and margin notes mention variants 1B and 1C.

Where the manual says something specific, the interpreter follows it and not Hamblin’s code: max, the single shot after the square root of a negative number, 0 ÷ 0, rem by a whole divisor of 2¹⁵ or more, and > on a zero word with an exponent. Everywhere the manual is silent, it follows his code.
The simulator is built from manuals, not from a DEUCE. Where they do not say, for instance the reader’s timing between its minimum and maximum, it chooses, and the choices are written down.
That Example 3 changed its range at some point is a guess. The documents do not say how the 1/48 came about, or whether anyone ran the example as printed.
body.principle: A manual describes a language. Only the program says what the machine did, and the program has to be run to say it.

body.text: When a run of handwritten code disagrees with its manual, which one was GEORGE?
body.detail: A disagreement has four places to look: the transcription, the simulator, the reading of DEUCE, and the 1958 program itself. Most of the disagreements found so far were traced to one of the first three and put right. A few, max and the lost sign in multiplication among them, are the program as written, the version before the last, which Hamblin may well have corrected himself.

record.title: The Nine Chapters writes 18/52 as the board leaves it
record.dek: Chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, set out in counting rods and worked as the text says. Of 39 statements of the text the board reaches, 38 agree. Its answers are written over one denominator each, and not always in lowest terms.
record.abstract: Chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (九章算術, 方程) solves what we would call simultaneous linear equations on a counting board: columns of rods, worked against each other until one figure is left over another. This is a note about a program, jiuzhang, that sets out each problem of the chapter, and the boards its commentators work, as the text sets them, works them a step at a time as the text says, and compares what the text states, where the notation can hold it, with what the board gives. It ran over a transcription of the Sibu congkan reprint of the Weiboxie edition, made from the scans by a coding agent and its sub-agents. On 26 pages it checks 39 statements the board reaches: 38 agree, and the one that does not is Problem 6, whose signs in this edition give −8 and −3 where the answer is 8 and 3. That is not a census of every number in the text. The text writes its eleven fractional answers over one denominator each, and not always in lowest terms: Problem 2 is 1 18/52, not 1 9/26, and 52 is the 法 as the board leaves it. Of three readings of the last step, the 法 and the 實s divided by what they share writes all 11 as the text does; that describes how the answers are written, not where a reduction was made. Dai Zhen’s 145 算 is given by two rules of counting, his 99 only by one proposed after both were known. Liu Hui’s passage on 77 算 does not work as printed under any of 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations, as Dai Zhen said; the two published reconstructions of it do. Guo Shuchun’s emended text, which reads 算 as operations, runs to the prices, and his own rule accounts for 67 of the 77, leaving 10 for placing rods. Roger Hart’s, which reads 算 as rods, agrees with the board at every one of his fifteen counts, and keeps within 77 rods only if each step is worked a position at a time from the bottom. Each gives 77 only on its own path, so the number does not choose between them. A second model reviewed the reconstruction independently, found no mistranscription, and found the checker could give a false ✓; this note gives the results after that was fixed. A literature check by a second model found that several of these results are already known: Problem 6’s signs were corrected by Li Huang, and Chemla and Guo (2004) print his correction; Hart (2011) discusses how the denominators follow the board, for Problem 14’s 33/111 and the determinant; and Liu Hui’s 77 passage has been emended by Chemla and Guo and worked through to 77 by Guo Shuchun (2020), and reconstructed in rods by Hart (2012); this project ran their reconstructions, it did not make them. No person has checked the transcription, and nothing here is claimed as new. Every page can be run on the board in the browser.

body.label: 01 / EIGHTEEN FIFTY-SECONDS
body.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art is a Chinese book of problems and procedures, put together under the Han from older material, with a commentary by Liu Hui (263), notes by Li Chunfeng (656) and, in the 1770s, Dai Zhen’s collation notes. Chapter 8, 方程 (fangcheng), is on what we would call simultaneous linear equations. Its procedure is done on a counting board: the conditions are set out as columns of rods, right to left, and worked against each other until one figure is left over another, the 法 (divisor) over the 實. In Problem 2, two kinds of grain, the text’s answer for a bundle of the top grade is 1 斗 and 18/52: 一斗五十二分斗之十八. Not 9/26. Worked as the text says, the board leaves its 法 at 52. I asked a coding agent to transcribe the chapter from the scans and to build a program, jiuzhang, that does what each line of the text says to the board and compares what the text states, where the notation can hold it, with what the board gives. This is not a solver for linear equations. It is a reading of one chapter: what the text says to do, what doing it gives, and where they part.

references.label: jiuzhang, the program and the transcription

body.label: 02 / A BOARD AND WHAT IS DONE TO IT
body.text: A page in jiuzhang’s notation is a board and what is done to it, one operation to a line, in the order the text gives them. Set right 3 2 1 39 sets the first column, the 實 last. Multiply middle by the head of right is the text’s 徧乘; Take right from middle until the head is gone is its 直除. Negative quantities are black rods, positive red, and the rule of signs (正負術) is the signed arithmetic jiuzhang does without being told. jiuzhang does three things. It runs a page: each operation on the board, as transcribed. It checks what the source states: a column a commentator says the board now holds, an answer as the text writes it, a set of rates, a count of operations (算). Some figures the notation cannot hold, rates read crosswise and arithmetic in fractions off the board, and those are kept as the source’s words, unchecked. And it reads in the alternative: where a clause of a commentary can be read more than one way, the page gives every reading, and jiuzhang readings runs every combination. A transcription never corrects the text. Where the text’s signs give the wrong answer, the page has the text’s signs.

body.label: 03 / 39 STATEMENTS
body.text: These are results against this project’s transcription, under the choices jiuzhang decisions lists. jiuzhang verify runs 26 pages: the 18 problems and 8 pages of commentary. They make 39 checked statements, a column a commentator gives, an answer, a set of rates or a count: 38 agree with the board and 1 does not. Five more are not reached: they come after a step that cannot be done. A statement can hold several figures, and some figures the sources give are quoted and not checked, so this is not a census of every number in the text. Two more pages are modern reconstructions of Liu Hui’s 77, not the text (09); their 18 statements all agree, and are counted apart.

body.label: 04 / HOW THE ANSWERS ARE WRITTEN
body.text: Eleven answers have fractions. The text writes them over one denominator, and not always in lowest terms: Problem 2 is 1 斗 and 18/52, not 9/26; Problem 14 is 33/111, not 11/37. Which reading of the last step writes them so? Every 實 over the 法 as the board leaves it writes 7 of the 11 as the text does. Each answer in its lowest terms writes 9. The 法 and all the 實s divided by what they share (約) writes all 11. So the answers are written over one denominator for each problem, and it is not the board’s 法 as it stands (Problem 1’s board leaves 36, the text writes quarters; Problem 16’s 976, the text 122), and not each fraction in its own lowest terms (52 and 111 survive). The 約 reading gives the same denominators as reducing each answer and then writing them all over the least of their common denominators: the table shows how the answers are written, not where in the working a reduction was made. That the denominators reflect the board is known: Hart (2011, pp. 173–174) discusses Problem 14’s 33/111, not 11/37, and its relation to the determinant. The count across all eleven answers was not found in the literature searched, which does not make it new. In Problem 2 the denominator the text writes, 52, is the 法 as the board leaves it. Problem 13’s answer is the extreme case: the depth of the well, 721, is the 法 itself, given as a rate (舉率以言之), and Liu Hui’s 法得七百二十一實七十六 is the board’s left column, checked.

body.label: 05 / PROBLEM 6
body.text: In this edition, the Weiboxie text, Problem 6’s procedure sets its 實 as 正 in both columns: 益實六斗正 … 益實一斗正. Run as printed, the board gives −8 and −3 where the answer is 8 and 3. This is the one statement of the 39 that does not agree. The other text consulted has 負 in both places, and with 負 the board gives the answer. The scan was read twice. This is known: Li Huang (李潢, 九章算術細草圖說, juan 8) says both 正 should be 負 (正正皆當作負), and Chemla and Guo (2004, p. 632, n. 51) print 負, credit him, and record 正 in other witnesses too, so it is not peculiar to this edition. The board finds the same thing by another road: it cannot get 8 and 3 from the signs as printed.

body.label: 06 / DAI ZHEN’S 145 AND 99
body.text: In his collation notes, Dai Zhen says that Problem 18 by the plain method, cross-multiplying each pair of columns (互乘) and then finding the prices from the bottom up, takes “145 算, counting multiplications, takings and divisions together” (兼乘減除言之), and that a shorter way, working from a column whose head is one, takes 99. He does not say what one 算 is beyond that, so jiuzhang rules tries several conventions and prefers none. Plain counts each multiplication, taking and division of one figure, less the heads that cross-multiplying makes equal: 145 for the plain method, 101 for the shorter way. Worked also saves everything multiplied or divided by one: 140 and 98. Readoff is plain with a division by one read off, not worked: 145 and 99. Plain is the nearest to his words, but leaving out the heads’ takings as well as their multiplications is this project’s convention, not his; worked extends his economies, which are about multiplying, to dividing, which he does not mention. Readoff was proposed by the independent review after both numbers were known. It gives both, and is reported as a rule fitted after the fact, not as Dai Zhen’s. A reading of his 145 as a count of single-figure operations was not found in the literature the check could read; two of the likeliest places, Shen, Crossley and Lun and Guo Shuchun’s 彙校, could not be opened.

body.label: 07 / THE BOARD’S WORKSPACE
body.text: By the text’s own 徧乘 and 直除, Problem 18 counts 158 算 under each of the three rules, with at most 160 rods and an 11-place figure on the recorded boards. Those are the boards as recorded after each step. The working of the last step is not on them: finding the 荅 by the text’s method forms a product of 16 places, and cross-multiplying forms products the board never shows, so these are not the workspace a reckoner needed. Under the repeated rule, which counts a taking done several times over as that many takings of single figures, the text’s method on Problem 18 comes to 180,403 operations, 180,330 of them takings, or 89,773 takings of a whole column.

body.label: 08 / LIU HUI’S 77
body.text: In his commentary to Problem 18, Liu Hui works it “by the old method, made short” (以舊術爲之…今欲要約), clause by clause, and says it takes 77 算. Dai Zhen calls the passage corrupt (訛舛不可通). The page gives each clause in every reading this project could find: the columns as written, and, for the clause 及減第三行, which as written takes the 3rd column from itself, other columns or nothing; and each 減 or 去 done once, until the head is gone, as far as it goes, in turn, or crosswise. That is 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations, not 100,000,000 interpretations. 229,906 of them can be done to the end. None leaves the 4th column giving the price of 黍, as the passage says it should. So none of these readings of the passage as printed works; that does not show that no reading does, and Liu Hui’s 77 is not tested here. The passage has been emended and worked by others. Chemla and Guo (2004, pp. 652–655) repair its opening, 及減第三行 among other words, and restore 六 for 空, crediting Dai Dunyuan; Guo Shuchun (2020) works the emended passage through and tallies 77, counting each placing of rods, each operation on a whole column and each division of a 實 by a 法 as one 算. Hart (2012), Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) and Zhu Yiwen (2025) read 算 as counting rods. The census here ran the text as printed: it says only that the unemended passage does not work under the readings offered, which is what Dai Zhen said. The published reconstructions are run in the next section. Among what the menu leaves out: 頭位 as anything but the first figure of the column worked on; the columns set one at a time, as 先置第三行 … 次置第二行 … 次置右行 says, with copies kept; other repairs of 及減第三行; mutual subtraction ending in either column. The independent review tried a wider search of its own, heads of either column and other orders, and found no working reading either. His new method, 124 算, which Guo (2020) also works through, was given the same treatment and stops, under every reading offered, by the passage’s fourth clause. Its last part, where the columns are set afresh, checks: the 3rd less the 4th leaves 麻 1, 菽 4, 荅 −3, 實 4, as he says, and as Guo (2020) explains.

body.label: 09 / TWO PUBLISHED READINGS OF THE 77, RUN
body.text: Two published reconstructions of Liu Hui’s old method read 算 differently. Both were transcribed as pages and run, from a second model’s extraction of the sources, which marks what it read and what it reconstructed; the pages assert only what the sources state. Guo Shuchun (2020), with Chemla and Guo (2004), emends the passage and reads 算 as operations: his note 40 counts as one each placing of rods, each multiplication or division of a whole column, each taking of one column from another, and each division of a 實 by a 法. His emended text runs on the board to the end. Both halvings (餘可半) go exactly, the 黍 comes out at six, and all five prices check. Under his rule, without the placings, the working is 67 operations; his 77 leaves 10 for placing rods, which the board does not model, and his figure 8-7, which would show how he assigns them, could not be read. Roger Hart (2012) reads 算 as rods. He works the old method on a board where columns are set as they are needed, and counts the rods after each step: never more than 77. Every one of the fifteen counts he reports agrees with the board, counted by jiuzhang’s rule of rods (a digit to five is that many rods, six to nine one for five and the rest), which was written before his paper was read; his path, too, ends with the 黍 at six. jiuzhang rods then asks how many rods a step needs while it is being worked, not only when it is done. Hart’s 77 holds if each column is worked a position at a time, straight to its new figures, from the bottom, or in the best order for each step. Worked from the top, his twelfth step briefly needs 78; worked a column at a time, setting down a product and then taking from it, 86. So his reconstruction keeps to 77 rods under an assumption about how a step is worked that neither the text nor he states. And each reading gives 77 only on its own path: Guo’s working holds up to 116 rods, since all five columns are set at the start, and Hart’s comes to 59 operations and 5 placings under Guo’s rule. The number 77 does not choose between them. That Hart’s bound depends on the order of working was not found in what could be read, which does not make it new; the reconstructions of Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) and Zhu Yiwen (2025), who also read 算 as rods, could not be read.

references.label: The source extraction for both pages, marking what was read and what reconstructed

body.label: 10 / AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW
body.text: A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository at commit 8532977 independently. It checked every answer, the Problem 6 signs, the commentary figures, the 77 passage and the four stated counts against the scans, and found no mistranscription. It reproduced the answers table, the counts and the censuses with programs of its own. And it wrote probe pages that made the checker fail. A board with contradictory conditions was solved and its answer ticked; an answer could be checked against a board that had since changed; an answer with the wrong number of figures got no mark; an answer written in a form no reading gives got ✓; and the fractions of the last step could overflow without saying so. Each was confirmed here and fixed: a contradictory board is not solved, an answer belongs to the board it was found on, wrong arity and unwritten forms are ✗, and the fractions are checked. It also found the claims wider than the program: figures it called checked that are only quoted, the workspace measured on recorded boards, the census of the 77 passage narrower than its size, and Dai Zhen’s words defining no one rule. Those were reworded, and the census now counts as done to the end only what it ran. The results in this note are after those changes.

references.label: The independent review, and what was done about each finding

body.label: 11 / READING THE TEXT
body.text: The text read is the Sibu congkan photographic reprint of the Weiboxie edition, with Liu Hui’s commentary, Li Chunfeng’s notes and Dai Zhen’s collation notes, from Wikimedia Commons, read from the page images. Wikisource’s transcription of the same pages is marked unproofread, and was used only to find places: it drops 直 (in 直除, and 直 “worth”) throughout, drops 兔 throughout Problem 17, and has 八之 for 入之 and 損妓之 for 損益之. A second, punctuated text of the main text, from another edition, is a third witness.

body.label: 12 / EARLIER WORK
body.text: The literature on chapter 8 is large, and this project did not read it. A second model, OpenAI’s Codex with web search, looked for each result in what it could reach: parts of Li Huang, Chemla and Guo, Hart, Guo Shuchun’s revised translation and Zhu Yiwen. It could not open Shen, Crossley and Lun, or Guo’s 彙校. Problem 6’s 正 for 負 is known, from Li Huang to Chemla and Guo. That the denominators reflect the board is partly known, from Hart; the count across all eleven answers was not found. Dai Zhen’s 145 as a count of single-figure operations was not found. Liu Hui’s 77 passage has been emended by Chemla and Guo and worked through to 77 by Guo (2020), reading 算 as operations, and by Hart (2012), reading it as rods; his 124 has been worked through by Guo. Both reconstructions of the 77 are run here (09); what running them adds, Guo’s 67 and 10, the agreement of Hart’s fifteen counts, and that his bound depends on the order a step is worked, was not found. Liu Hui’s rates 7:4:3:5:6 are in Guo (2020) and in Chemla and Guo. “Not found” means not found in what could be read, never that a result is new.

references.label: The literature check, with its sources

body.text: jiuzhang runs in the browser, compiled unchanged from the same Rust source as the command-line version, and draws the board in three dimensions: each figure in rods, the units upright and the tens lying (一縱十橫), five as one rod across, red for 正 and black for 負, the columns right to left. Step through a page, or play it: a rod that stays stays put, a new one is dropped into place, and the rods taken off the board are knocked off the felt. Beside it, the page in an editor whose colours, problems and hover come from jiuzhang’s language server, running in the page too.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: The transcription was made by a coding agent and its sub-agents, from the scans, and checked against them at the answers, the signs of Problem 6, the commentary figures, the 77 passage and the four counts by a second model. No person has checked it.
The 39 statements are what the notation can hold. Some figures the sources give are quoted and not checked, so 38 of 39 is not a census of every number in the text.

Every result here is against that transcription, under the choices jiuzhang decisions lists: that the rule of signs is signed arithmetic, how 徧乘 and 直除 are read, what “head” means, the three readings of the last step, that no rule of counting is preferred, that the readings offered for a corrupt passage are the transcriber’s, and the units.

That 約 writes all 11 answers as the text does describes how they are written. It gives the same denominators as reducing each answer and writing them over their least common denominator, so it does not show where in the working a reduction was made, or how the answers were found.

Problem 6 is a difference between this edition’s signs and the answer, and it is not a finding of this project: Li Huang corrected the signs, and Chemla and Guo (2004) print his correction and record 正 in other witnesses.
Dai Zhen’s words define no one rule of counting. Plain gives his 145 and not his 99; readoff gives both, but was proposed after both were known, and is not shown to be his.
The rods and places are those of the recorded boards, not the workspace a reckoner needed: the last step works a product of 16 places off the board.

None of 100,000,000 combinations of a small menu of operations makes Liu Hui’s 77 passage work as printed, and the review’s wider search found none either. That is not a finding of this project: Dai Zhen called the passage corrupt, Chemla and Guo (2004) emend it, and Guo (2020) works the emended passage to 77. Guo’s and Hart’s reconstructions were run from a second model’s extraction of their books and papers, not read by this project. Guo’s 10 placings are not modelled, and his figure 8-7 was not read. The rods a step needs while it is worked assume a reckoner sets each position straight to its new figure; neither the text nor Hart says how a step was worked. Which reading of 算 Liu Hui meant is not decided here.

Chapter 8 and its commentaries have been edited, translated and studied at length: Qian Baocong’s and Guo Shuchun’s critical editions; Shen Kangshen, Crossley and Lun (1999); Chemla and Guo Shuchun (2004); Hart (2011); Guo’s revised translation (2020); and Zhu Yiwen on the rods (2010, 2025). This project did not read them. The literature check was a second model’s search, which read parts of some and could not open others; what it did not find may still be there. Nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: Running the procedure shows where the text and the board part. It does not show whether the difference is the text’s, the edition’s, the transcriber’s, or the reading’s.

body.text: Does Liu Hui’s 124, for his new method, choose between the two readings of 算?
body.detail: 77 does not: each reading reaches it only on its own path. Liu Hui gives a second number, 124 算 for his new method, which as printed stops, under every reading offered, by its fourth clause. Guo Shuchun (2020, nn. 41–82) works it through. Run as a page, his working can be counted under his rule and in rods, by each order of working; if only one reading gives 124, the second number decides what the first could not. That is the next page to write.

body.label: 13 / WHAT THE CHAPTER HAS BECOME
body.text: Nothing in this note is a new fact about the Nine Chapters: Problem 6’s signs were corrected by Li Huang, the link between the denominators and the board is in Hart, and Liu Hui’s 77 has been worked by Guo Shuchun and by Roger Hart. What has changed is the form the chapter is in. Its eighteen procedures, and the boards its commentators describe, are now a structured, executable object: each line an operation on a board of rods, done as the text says, with the board after it, and every statement the board reaches checked against it. A step is no longer only something to read; it can be challenged. Change a sign, or the way an answer is written, as the steps in the second section do, and the run says at once what follows and what no longer holds. The same check runs over every page, under choices that are written down, so a question about one answer becomes a question asked of all eleven, answered with a count, and asked again when a choice changes, as it was after the independent review. A reading of a corrupt passage becomes something that can be run. Two published reconstructions of Liu Hui’s 77, made by hand from the same passage, were each set down as a page and run: the run confirmed each on its own terms, measured what each leaves unstated, and showed that the number they share cannot decide between them. What this adds is a way to test the chapter’s intermediate steps systematically, and anyone can do it in the browser.

record.title: Liu Hui’s 124 is the most rods the board holds
record.dek: In 263 Liu Hui said his new method for the last problem of the Nine Chapters’ chapter 8 takes 124 算. Run on the one published working of it, no count of operations gives 124. It is the most counting rods the board ever holds, just before the text clears a column away.
record.abstract: Liu Hui closes two workings of the last problem of chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters with a number: the old method, made short, takes 77 算, and his new method 124. 算 can mean an operation or a counting rod, and both readings are published. An earlier note ran two reconstructions of the 77, one for each reading, and found that each reaches 77 only on its own path, so the 77 cannot decide. This note runs the 124. Guo Shuchun’s working of the new method (2020), transcribed as a page, runs on the board, and all seven figures the text and his notes state agree. Counted as operations it cannot be 124: under Guo’s own rule, as his tally of the 77 applies it, the part that finds the rates is already 228, and no other rule gives 124. Counted as rods, with the rule that confirmed all fifteen of Hart’s counts for the 77, the board holds 116 rods when the five columns are set and at most 124 after, exactly. Up to that peak, every operation is fixed by the text, and the peak falls just before the text says 訖廢去第三行, take the third column away. The same question asked of the old method gives 100, not 77, on Guo’s working: a rods reading of the 77 needs another path, such as Hart’s. That 124 means rods is already the reading of Hart (2012) and of Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016), whose full text could not be read and may contain this count; Hudeček (2008) prints this board. A second model’s search did not find the peak stated in what it could read. No person has checked the transcription.
record.lineage: TEXT → GUO 2020 → SOURCE EXTRACTION → PAGE → JIUZHANG → RODS

body.label: 01 / TWO NUMBERS
body.text: Problem 18 of chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters asks the prices of five grains from five conditions: five columns of six figures on a counting board. Liu Hui, in his commentary of 263, works it twice. Of the old method, made short, he says 如此凡用七十七算: this way uses 77 算 in all. Of his new method he says 如此則凡用一百二十四算也: 124. 算 is a calculation, or a counting rod (筭), and both readings are published. Chemla and Guo (2004) and Guo Shuchun (2020) count operations: Guo’s note 40 makes one 算 each placing of rods, each multiplication or division of a whole column, each taking of one column from another, and each division of a 實 by a 法, and his working of the 77 adds up to 77. Hart (2012) and Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) count rods: the most the board holds. Hart’s working of the old method never holds more than 77. The earlier note on chapter 8 ran both workings of the 77 on jiuzhang’s board. Each reached 77, but only on its own path: Guo’s needs 116 rods, and Hart’s is 59 operations and 5 placings. The 77 cannot choose. This note asks the same of the 124.

references.label: The earlier note: the Nine Chapters writes 18/52 as the board leaves it

body.label: 02 / THE NEW METHOD, AS GUO WORKS IT
body.text: As printed, the passage of the new method stops by its fourth clause under every reading the project offered: Dai Zhen called it corrupt too. Guo Shuchun works it through (九章筭術譯注, 2020, notes 41–62), and a second model, OpenAI’s Codex, read his notes and wrote out the operations, marking what it read and what it worked out: the figure that would show each board, 8-8, was not in the transcription it could read, so how many times each column is taken is calculated from the figures, not read. That working was set down as a page in jiuzhang’s notation. It runs to the end. The seven figures the text and Guo’s notes state all agree with the board: 菽 5 against 荅 3, 荅 6 against 黍 5, 麥 3 against 菽 4, 麻 4 against 麥 7, and the figures before two of the reductions, −310 and 186, and −10 and 5. Its last board is, column for column, the one the extraction worked out by hand. One sign differs: at note 61, adding as the page says gives 3 and −4 where Guo’s note has −3 and 4, the same rate.

body.label: 03 / AS OPERATIONS, IT CANNOT BE 124
body.text: Guo gives no tally for the 124: his note 82 states the total only. His rule, applied as his tally of the 77 applies it, counts a column taken from another seven times as seven takings. The new method takes the third column from the first 35 times, to clear its 實 of 140 by 4 at a time, from the second 32 times and from the fourth 28. Counted so, the part of the method that finds the rates, before the last part, is already 228. jiuzhang’s other rules of counting do no better: counting each figure multiplied, taken or divided gives 199; counting every figure, by one or not, 123, and the last part’s first taking alone adds 6; counting each operation on a whole column gives 35, far short. On this working, no way of counting operations that the project could find gives 124.

body.label: 04 / AS RODS, IT IS 124 EXACTLY
body.text: A figure in rods takes as many rods as its digits do: one to five rods for one to five, one rod across for five and the rest for six to nine, none for zero, and none for the sign, which is the colour. Counted so, all fifteen of Hart’s counts for the 77 agree with jiuzhang’s board. The new method sets all five columns: 116 rods. Then, for its first six operations, the text leaves nothing to choose. 先以第四行減第三行: the fourth from the third, once. 次以第三行去右行及第二行第四行下位: the third clears the 實 of the right, the second and the fourth, 35, 32 and 28 times. 又以減右行下位不足減乃止: the third from the left as far as it goes, 23 times, with the printed 右 read as 左, as Guo reads it, since the right’s 實 is already gone. 次以左行減第三行下位: the left from the third, once. The board now holds 124 rods: 23, 21, 27, 27 and 26 in its five columns. 次以第三行去左行下位: the third clears the left’s 實, 3 times; the left changes, and the board still holds 124. Then the text says 訖廢去第三行: that done, take the third column away. Its 27 rods go, and the board never holds as many again. The last part, the columns set afresh, needs about half as many.

body.label: 05 / HOW A STEP IS WORKED
body.text: Those counts are of the board after each step. While a column is being worked it passes through other figures, and jiuzhang rods measures the board within a step too. Worked a position at a time, each figure set straight to its new value from the bottom up, or in the best order for the step, or a whole column at once, the new method keeps to 124. Worked from the top down, it needs 130 at one step. Hart’s 77 behaves the same way: 77 from the bottom up or in the best order, 78 from the top. Both of Liu Hui’s numbers, read as rods, hold under one way of working and not under another, and neither the text nor the reconstructions say which way a reckoner worked.

body.label: 06 / THE OLD METHOD, ASKED THE SAME
body.text: If 算 is rods, the 77 should be the most rods on the old method’s board. Guo’s working of it sets all five columns at the start, 116 rods. The text sets them one at a time (先置第三行 … 次置第二行 … 次置右行), so the same working was run with each column set only when an operation first uses it. It peaks at 100, not 77. So, read as rods, the 77 needs a different path from Guo’s emended working: Hart’s, which sets the columns as they are needed and is built to keep within 77, is one. The 124 needs no such path. On the only published working of the new method, it is what the board holds.

body.label: 07 / WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN
body.text: That the 124 counts rods is not a new reading. Hart (2012, note 34) reads both 77 and 124 as rods, though he works only the old method. Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) argue that 算 here means counting rods, and say they begin from the new method to settle the meaning; their full text is behind a login and could not be read, so they may well have counted this peak, perhaps on this board. Zhu Yiwen (2025) calls the totals 77 rods and 124 rods, citing them. Hudeček (2008, p. 206) prints this board’s figures, and his note 71 records failed attempts to reach 124 by counting operations. Chemla and Guo (2004) and Guo (2020) read 124 as calculation steps. A second model’s search, which read parts of most of these, did not find the peak itself, 124 rods on Guo’s working at the step before 訖廢去第三行, stated in anything it could read. One difference is open: Zhu (2010, p. 82) counts 110 rods to set out the problem, where this rule counts 116.
