body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: It is one working. Guo’s is the only published working of the new method the project could read; another working could peak elsewhere. Up to the peak the text fixes the operations, so any working that follows the text there, with all five columns set, reaches 124 at that step, but nothing here shows that no working exceeds it later.

It is not shown what Liu Hui meant. A board total near 124 could arise by chance: in the first steps it runs between 104 and 124. What makes it more than a number near another is that it is exact, that it is the most the board holds, that it falls where the text itself clears a column away, and that no count of operations gives 124. That is evidence for a reading, not proof of one.

Guo’s working was read by a second model from an OCR transcription of his book; his figure 8-8 was not seen, and how many times each column is taken was worked out, not read. No person has checked it against the printed page.

The rule of rods is the one Hart’s counts follow, and it confirms all fifteen of them; Zhu (2010) counts 110 for setting out the problem, where it counts 116, and the reason is not known. The counts are of figures on the board: rods held in the hand, or set aside for a product, are not counted.
Wei and Guo (2016) may already state this. Their paper could not be read beyond its opening. Nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: A number in a text can be tested by running what the text says; it cannot be proved by the run.

body.text: Do Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) count 124 rods on this board?
body.detail: Their paper, 《九章算术》方程章“麻麦”问刘徽注中“算”字新释及方程“旧术”新校, 自然科学史研究 35(1), pp. 10–17, argues that 算 here is counting rods and begins from the new method. Its body is on CNKI behind a login. If it counts the board on the same working, the peak is theirs and this note is a confirmation by machine; if it counts another way, the two can be run side by side.

body.label: 08 / WHAT THE SECOND NUMBER DID
body.text: The 77 could not decide between the readings: each reading has a path that reaches it. The 124 can, on the evidence there is. On the one published working of the new method, with every operation up to the peak fixed by the text, a count of operations misses it by a hundred, and a count of rods lands on it, at the step before the text takes a column away. The test came from running the text as written, on a board that confirmed another scholar’s fifteen counts before it was asked this question. What was hard by hand, counting the rods on five columns of three-figure numbers after every step, under every way of working a step, is a command. The interpretation was already published. What the run adds is a measurement that supports it, and that anyone can repeat in the browser.

record.title: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s TPK, run: none of their three programs is accepted as printed
record.dek: In 1976 Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote one program, TPK, in about twenty early languages. Run on reconstructions built from each system’s own sources, their Böhm, Laning–Zierler and ALGOL 60 programs are each refused as printed. Six systems they did not cover give six other answers.
record.abstract: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s survey of early programming languages (1976) compares them by writing one fixed algorithm, TPK, in each, as “fairly close replicas” of what each language’s author would have written. This collection has executable reconstructions of nine early systems, each built from its own primary sources and independently of their paper. Three are languages they wrote TPK in, and each of those programs is refused as printed: Böhm’s, because it names a group S and a variable X, the letters his compiler keeps for itself, so compiled by his method it prints nothing; Laning and Zierler’s, because it reads its input with v|N, which the manual says “is not yet in operation”, and uses a computed zero as an index; ALGOL 60’s, because its procedure heading puts the specification before the value part, against the Report, and because the surviving X1 compiler, run on a simulator, stops on its label and compiles the heading’s parameter as a value array. Knuth had already corrected the heading in his errata (2014); the other findings were not found in a limited search. The six systems they did not cover give six kinds of answer: Turing’s ACE runs TPK only after correcting two of Turing’s own tables; GEORGE, IPL-V and JOSS accept it by their manuals; whether the first Dartmouth BASIC could run it cannot be settled from what survives; and the defining document of CPL cannot express it. Where they run, every value is right at the system’s precision but one, GEORGE’s 79.7062, traced to Hamblin’s add routine. On the two machine-level systems, output costs more than the arithmetic.
record.lineage: 1976 SURVEY → PRIMARY SOURCES → NINE RECONSTRUCTIONS → TPK, RUN

body.label: 01 / ONE FIXED ALGORITHM
body.text: In The Early Development of Programming Languages (Stanford, 1976), Donald Knuth and Luis Trabb Pardo compare about twenty early languages by writing one program, TPK, in each. Read eleven numbers. Then, from the last to the first, print each one’s position i and f(aᵢ) = √|aᵢ| + 5aᵢ³, or TOO LARGE if that exceeds 400. They say plainly what the programs are: written in the style of each language’s author, “not truly authentic excerpts from the historical record, but … fairly close replicas” (p. 3). For weaker languages they give rules: integers only means integer input and an integer square root; no text means 999 for TOO LARGE; no user functions means f written out. This collection has executable reconstructions of nine early systems, each built from its own manuals and papers, without reference to their paper. Three are languages they wrote TPK in. That makes a test possible that they could not make: would each printed program have been accepted by the system it was written for?

body.label: 02 / ALGOL 60: THE REPORT, AND THE FIRST COMPILER
body.text: Their reference version is “in a dialect of Algol 60”. Against the Revised Report it fails twice. Its procedure heading, real procedure f(t); real t; value t;, gives the specification before the value part, and section 5.4.1 puts the value part first. And read and write are not in the Report, which has no input or output. The first ALGOL 60 system, Dijkstra and Zonneveld’s for the Electrologica X1, has a compiler that survives and can be run on a simulator. Given the program with only read and write changed to the X1’s, the compiler stops at once with stop 0–25: TPK: begin is a labelled program, and property 1 of the system’s manual says a program is an unlabelled block. Given the heading as printed in a program of its own, it accepts it without comment, but compiles t as a value array, with the operations RVA and VAP where value t; real t; gives TRAD. The simulator’s run-time then stops with “too many dimensions for value array”; what the X1’s own run-time did is not known, because its routines have not been found. With the label dropped and the value part first, the compiler’s program gives all eleven values to the 13 digits the simulator prints. The X1 findings come from the real compiler, not from the reconstruction.

references.label: The X1 probes and their results, compare/README.md

body.label: 03 / BÖHM: TWO LETTERS HIS COMPILER KEEPS
body.text: Corrado Böhm’s thesis (1951) defines a language and a compiler for it, written in the language itself. Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s TPK for it is right as algebra: read as formulas, it gives all 22 values, 999 for i = 10 down to 5 and then 322, 136, 41, 6 and 0. But it names a group S and a variable X, and chapter 6 of the thesis uses those two letters for the polynomials its compiler builds. Compiled by Böhm’s own method, the program’s S and X collide with the compiler’s, and the machine stops after 142 steps having printed nothing. The same program with S and X renamed K and Z agrees all three ways: as algebra, through a reference translation, and through Böhm’s compiler on the machine.

body.label: 04 / LANING AND ZIERLER: AN INPUT NOT YET IN OPERATION
body.text: Their Laning and Zierler program (pp. 56–57) reads its eleven numbers with v|N. The manual of January 1954 lists that among its temporary restrictions: it “is not yet in operation” (E-364, p. 21). It also counts i down by i = i − 1 and uses it as an index when it reaches zero, and page 13 permits a zero index only “if assigned by the specific equation n = 0”. Under the rules of January 1954 the translator stops at the first line. Run without that restriction it types ten lines and then an alarm at the computed zero, though that alarm rests on this reconstruction’s model of zero, not on the manual. Whether Whirlwind itself would have failed is not known.

body.label: 05 / WHAT WAS ALREADY KNOWN
body.text: A search in November 2026 covered Knuth’s errata, reviews of the paper and its reprints, histories of each language, Rosetta Code, Wikipedia’s talk pages and Hacker News. The heading was found: Knuth’s errata for Selected Papers on Computer Languages (2003), which reprints the paper, change “real t; value t;” to “value t; real t;” in an entry dated 12 February 2014, listed as a typographical correction. Wikipedia’s article on TPK still prints the old order. The same errata (22 September 2022) correct a different line of the Laning and Zierler program, so that 999 is printed for y > 400 and not for y ≥ 400, if the zero the test produces is +0; on Whirlwind a zero may or may not take the jump (E-364, p. 8). They leave v|N and the count down to zero as they were. Sestoft’s translation of Böhm’s thesis notes that the letters are used in the translation of polynomials (appendix A.1), but the search found no one connecting that to TPK. Nothing was found on the X1 refusing the label or compiling the heading as a value array, on v|N, or on the zero index. The search was limited, and the 1977 and 1980 reprints and most of van den Hove’s 2019 thesis on the X1 system could not be read.

references.label: Knuth, errata for Selected Papers on Computer Languages

body.label: 06 / SIX SYSTEMS THEY DID NOT COVER
body.text: Their survey stops in 1957, and machine codes are outside it. The collection’s other six systems therefore have no printed TPK, and the programs for them are new: each written from that system’s own sources, in its author’s style, following Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s rules, and checked against its manual. They were written with a reconstruction to test them on, which Knuth and Trabb Pardo did not have, so that they run is no evidence that they were better read. What is of interest is what each system forced, and whether its own documents would accept the result. The six give six different kinds of answer.

body.label: 07 / TURING’S ACE: ONLY AFTER CORRECTING TURING
body.text: The ACE of Turing’s 1945 report is a design, not a machine, and TPK on it is an instruction table. Its arithmetic is whole numbers, so by Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s rules the input is 0 to 10, the square root is an integer one, here by taking away 1, 3, 5 … and counting, and TOO LARGE is 999. The report has no square root, no input conversion and no way to step an index down, and the program needs two of the subsidiary tables Turing printed: INDEXIN, to fetch aᵢ, and DISCRIM, to choose a way on. As printed, INDEXIN gives wrong cards, and DISCRIM answers “no” to the word that both of TPK’s tests produce, so the square root never ends. With the two corrections the reconstruction already lists, it runs, in 24.4 seconds of the design’s time, three quarters of the computing spent converting to decimal.

body.label: 08 / GEORGE, IPL-V AND JOSS: ACCEPTED BY THEIR MANUALS
body.text: Three of the six accept TPK as their manuals describe them. GEORGE, Hamblin’s reverse Polish scheme for the DEUCE (1957), has no text, so TOO LARGE is 999 and the output is 22 cards; its repetition only counts up, so i is 10 − j; and t³ is dup dup × ×, because its power goes through a logarithm and stops on a negative base. It runs both in the interpreter and on Hamblin’s own coding sheets in a simulated DEUCE. IPL-V (1961) has no arrays and no square root: the eleven numbers are a list, reversed by J64, and the square root is a routine by Newton’s method, which takes two thirds of the run’s 2,757 interpretation cycles. TOO LARGE is two data terms, because a data term holds five characters. JOSS (1964–65) has no user functions before JOSS-II, so f is written out; Demand asks for each number; and text and a number share a line only through a form. Each is a judgement from the manuals. For IPL-V it rests on every process used being older than the 1964 additions, and the JOSS reconstruction is the only JOSS that runs.

body.label: 09 / BASIC AND CPL: WHAT SURVIVES CANNOT DECIDE
body.text: For the first Dartmouth BASIC the question cannot be settled. The instruction manual of May 1964 survives only as Part I. Arrays, DIM and probably REM are left to Part II. Page 4 counts the operations: nine in Part I and four more in Part II. The October 1964 manual lists fifteen statements, five of them, GOSUB, RETURN, DIM, STOP and REM, not in Part I, so one of those five was not yet in the first system. Which one cannot be identified, so whether TPK could be written in May 1964 is unknown. The program also has to write the cube as T*T*T, because the manual says A↑B “is actually interpreted as |A|^B”. For CPL the defining document cannot express TPK at all: the 1966 Reference Manual’s section on input and output was “postponed”, and the appendix that would define square root and absolute value was never finished. The program uses the Elementary Programming Manual and its supplement for the trial Cambridge system instead.

body.label: 10 / THE VALUES, AND ONE THAT IS NOT
body.text: On Knuth’s input, 1 (.5) 2 (.25) 3.5 (1) 5.5, every value printed by every system that runs is the true value at that system’s precision, with two exceptions. The X1’s 40-bit numbers end …005 at i = 4 where the true value ends …008: that is storage, not a fault. And GEORGE prints 79.7062 where the value, 79.70614, rounds to 79.7061. The interpreter and Hamblin’s own coding sheets on the simulated DEUCE both print it, and the reconstruction traces it to Hamblin’s add routine, which rounds a leftover 0.38 of a unit upward. It has not been checked against a real DEUCE. The integer systems, the ACE and Böhm, agree with each other and with the arithmetic.

body.label: 11 / THE COST, IN EACH SYSTEM’S OWN UNITS
body.text: The units do not convert into one another, so each is reported as its reconstruction counts it. Turing’s ACE: 48,246 instructions in 761,189 minor cycles of 32 µs, 24.4 seconds if cards go at 100 a minute, about three quarters of the computing spent converting to decimal. GEORGE on the simulated DEUCE: 33,477 instructions, 38.7 seconds, about 59% of it punching the 22 cards, after 57 seconds to load GEORGE. IPL-V: 2,757 interpretation cycles, the unit the Logic Theorist’s effort was measured in, 68% of them in the square root. CPL: 437 steps of the reconstruction’s abstract machine, a modern unit. On both machine-level systems, output costs more than the arithmetic; where a system lacked a primitive, the substitute dominated. All of these are from simulations, with the DEUCE’s reader and punch at the simulator’s mid-range timings.
Each program runs where it is described, on the same WebAssembly builds as the playgrounds. Change one and run it again, or open its playground.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: It does not show that Knuth and Trabb Pardo were careless. They said their programs were replicas. What is measured is the distance between a careful reading of each language in 1976 and what its own system enforced, and each time it comes from something a reader of the papers would not see: a compiler’s private letters, a routine not yet in operation, a rule about labels, code that depends on the order of a heading.

Only the X1 findings come from a surviving system. The Böhm, Laning and Zierler, and Report findings are the rules of their documents applied by a reconstruction, and the reconstructions are readings of those documents. Whether Whirlwind would have run the Laning and Zierler program is not known.

The six new programs are ours, and that they run says as much about the reconstructions they were tested on as about the languages. ‘Accepted by the manual’ is a judgement for IPL-V and JOSS, and BASIC’s answer depends on a part of a manual that is lost.
The costs are from simulators, not machines, and are not comparable with each other.
The search for earlier work was limited, by a coding agent. Nothing here is claimed as new beyond what that search did not find.
body.principle: A program printed as a replica can be tested by running it on what it replicates.

body.text: Did the 1977 or 1980 reprint of the paper change the ALGOL heading?
body.detail: The paper was reprinted in the Encyclopedia of Computer Science and Technology (1977) and in A History of Computing in the Twentieth Century (1980). Both are only lent by archive.org, and were not read. Knuth’s correction is dated 2014, against the 2003 reprint.

body.label: 12 / WHAT THE COMPARISON DID
body.text: In 1976 a common program let two readers compare twenty languages on paper. Run on systems rebuilt from their own sources, the same program asks something sharper of each language: not what it looks like, but whether its own rules let it through. Of their three programs that could be asked, none passes as printed, and one of the reasons, the heading, Knuth had already found. Of the six new ones, the answers range from accepted, to accepted only after correcting the designer, to a question that a lost Part II of a manual would settle. The reconstructions gained something too. Writing TPK in each exposed gaps of their own: the ALGOL interpreter accepted the misordered heading and, in X1 mode, the labelled program; the IPL-V loader read a floating-point digit from a column its manual leaves unused; and a JOSS listing was dated too late. Each is now fixed or recorded in its repository.

record.title: Liu Hui’s 124 is the most rods the board holds
record.dek: In 263 Liu Hui said his new method for the last problem of the Nine Chapters’ chapter 8 takes 124 算. Run on the one published working of it, no count of operations gives 124. It is the most counting rods the board ever holds, just before the text clears a column away.
record.abstract: Liu Hui closes two workings of the last problem of chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters with a number: the old method, made short, takes 77 算, and his new method 124. 算 can mean an operation or a counting rod, and both readings are published. An earlier note ran two reconstructions of the 77, one for each reading, and found that each reaches 77 only on its own path, so the 77 cannot decide. This note runs the 124. Guo Shuchun’s working of the new method (2020), transcribed as a page, runs on the board, and all seven figures the text and his notes state agree. Counted as operations it cannot be 124: under Guo’s own rule, as his tally of the 77 applies it, the part that finds the rates is already 228, and no other rule gives 124. Counted as rods, with the rule that confirmed all fifteen of Hart’s counts for the 77, the board holds 116 rods when the five columns are set and at most 124 after, exactly. Up to that peak, every operation is fixed by the text, and the peak falls just before the text says 訖廢去第三行, take the third column away. The same question asked of the old method gives 100, not 77, on Guo’s working: a rods reading of the 77 needs another path, such as Hart’s. That 124 means rods is already the reading of Hart (2012) and of Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016), whose full text could not be read and may contain this count; Hudeček (2008) prints this board. A second model’s search did not find the peak stated in what it could read. No person has checked the transcription.
record.lineage: TEXT → GUO 2020 → SOURCE EXTRACTION → PAGE → JIUZHANG → RODS

body.label: 01 / TWO NUMBERS
body.text: Problem 18 of chapter 8 of the Nine Chapters asks the prices of five grains from five conditions: five columns of six figures on a counting board. Liu Hui, in his commentary of 263, works it twice. Of the old method, made short, he says 如此凡用七十七算: this way uses 77 算 in all. Of his new method he says 如此則凡用一百二十四算也: 124. 算 is a calculation, or a counting rod (筭), and both readings are published. Chemla and Guo (2004) and Guo Shuchun (2020) count operations: Guo’s note 40 makes one 算 each placing of rods, each multiplication or division of a whole column, each taking of one column from another, and each division of a 實 by a 法, and his working of the 77 adds up to 77. Hart (2012) and Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) count rods: the most the board holds. Hart’s working of the old method never holds more than 77. The earlier note on chapter 8 ran both workings of the 77 on jiuzhang’s board. Each reached 77, but only on its own path: Guo’s needs 116 rods, and Hart’s is 59 operations and 5 placings. The 77 cannot choose. This note asks the same of the 124.

references.label: The earlier note: the Nine Chapters writes 18/52 as the board leaves it

body.label: 02 / THE NEW METHOD, AS GUO WORKS IT
body.text: As printed, the passage of the new method stops by its fourth clause under every reading the project offered: Dai Zhen called it corrupt too. Guo Shuchun works it through (九章筭術譯注, 2020, notes 41–62), and a second model, OpenAI’s Codex, read his notes and wrote out the operations, marking what it read and what it worked out: the figure that would show each board, 8-8, was not in the transcription it could read, so how many times each column is taken is calculated from the figures, not read. That working was set down as a page in jiuzhang’s notation. It runs to the end. The seven figures the text and Guo’s notes state all agree with the board: 菽 5 against 荅 3, 荅 6 against 黍 5, 麥 3 against 菽 4, 麻 4 against 麥 7, and the figures before two of the reductions, −310 and 186, and −10 and 5. Its last board is, column for column, the one the extraction worked out by hand. One sign differs: at note 61, adding as the page says gives 3 and −4 where Guo’s note has −3 and 4, the same rate.

body.label: 03 / AS OPERATIONS, IT CANNOT BE 124
body.text: Guo gives no tally for the 124: his note 82 states the total only. His rule, applied as his tally of the 77 applies it, counts a column taken from another seven times as seven takings. The new method takes the third column from the first 35 times, to clear its 實 of 140 by 4 at a time, from the second 32 times and from the fourth 28. Counted so, the part of the method that finds the rates, before the last part, is already 228. jiuzhang’s other rules of counting do no better: counting each figure multiplied, taken or divided gives 199; counting every figure, by one or not, 123, and the last part’s first taking alone adds 6; counting each operation on a whole column gives 35, far short. On this working, no way of counting operations that the project could find gives 124.

body.label: 04 / AS RODS, IT IS 124 EXACTLY
body.text: A figure in rods takes as many rods as its digits do: one to five rods for one to five, one rod across for five and the rest for six to nine, none for zero, and none for the sign, which is the colour. Counted so, all fifteen of Hart’s counts for the 77 agree with jiuzhang’s board. The new method sets all five columns: 116 rods. Then, for its first six operations, the text leaves nothing to choose. 先以第四行減第三行: the fourth from the third, once. 次以第三行去右行及第二行第四行下位: the third clears the 實 of the right, the second and the fourth, 35, 32 and 28 times. 又以減右行下位不足減乃止: the third from the left as far as it goes, 23 times, with the printed 右 read as 左, as Guo reads it, since the right’s 實 is already gone. 次以左行減第三行下位: the left from the third, once. The board now holds 124 rods: 23, 21, 27, 27 and 26 in its five columns. 次以第三行去左行下位: the third clears the left’s 實, 3 times; the left changes, and the board still holds 124. Then the text says 訖廢去第三行: that done, take the third column away. Its 27 rods go, and the board never holds as many again. The last part, the columns set afresh, needs about half as many.

body.label: 05 / HOW A STEP IS WORKED
body.text: Those counts are of the board after each step. While a column is being worked it passes through other figures, and jiuzhang rods measures the board within a step too. Worked a position at a time, each figure set straight to its new value from the bottom up, or in the best order for the step, or a whole column at once, the new method keeps to 124. Worked from the top down, it needs 130 at one step. Hart’s 77 behaves the same way: 77 from the bottom up or in the best order, 78 from the top. Both of Liu Hui’s numbers, read as rods, hold under one way of working and not under another, and neither the text nor the reconstructions say which way a reckoner worked. A reader then asked what happens if a repeated taking is done literally, one take at a time. At the step just before the peak, 次以第三行去左行下位, the third column is taken from the left three times, until the left’s 實 of 3 is gone. Taken singly on the whole column, the left column passes through −68 9 −278 237 15 1, 35 rods, and the board reaches 133. Taken singly a position at a time, each position passing through every figure its own takes give it, jiuzhang rods now searches every interleaving of the positions: the least is 125, one more than Liu Hui’s number. One figure taken three times at once, any one of the 麻, 菽 or 荅, brings it back to 124, and no other step needs more than 124 with its takes done singly. Hart’s 77 survives the same test. So if the 124 counts rods, it also says something about how the work was done: a multiple taken at once, at one position at least, not the column taken again and again.

body.label: 06 / THE OLD METHOD, ASKED THE SAME
body.text: If 算 is rods, the 77 should be the most rods on the old method’s board. Guo’s working of it sets all five columns at the start, 116 rods. The text sets them one at a time (先置第三行 … 次置第二行 … 次置右行), so the same working was run with each column set only when an operation first uses it. It peaks at 100, not 77. So, read as rods, the 77 needs a different path from Guo’s emended working: Hart’s, which sets the columns as they are needed and is built to keep within 77, is one. The 124 needs no such path. On the only published working of the new method, it is what the board holds.

body.label: 07 / WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN
body.text: That the 124 counts rods is not a new reading. Hart (2012, note 34) reads both 77 and 124 as rods, though he works only the old method. Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) argue that 算 here means counting rods, and say they begin from the new method to settle the meaning; their full text is behind a login and could not be read, so they may well have counted this peak, perhaps on this board. Zhu Yiwen (2025) calls the totals 77 rods and 124 rods, citing them. Hudeček (2008, p. 206) prints this board’s figures, and his note 71 records failed attempts to reach 124 by counting operations. Chemla and Guo (2004) and Guo (2020) read 124 as calculation steps. A second model’s search, which read parts of most of these, did not find the peak itself, 124 rods on Guo’s working at the step before 訖廢去第三行, stated in anything it could read. One difference is open: Zhu (2010, p. 82) counts 110 rods to set out the problem, where this rule counts 116.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: It is one working. Guo’s is the only published working of the new method the project could read; another working could peak elsewhere. Up to the peak the text fixes the operations, so any working that follows the text there, with all five columns set, reaches 124 at that step, but nothing here shows that no working exceeds it later.

It is not shown what Liu Hui meant. A board total near 124 could arise by chance: in the first steps it runs between 104 and 124. What makes it more than a number near another is that it is exact, that it is the most the board holds, that it falls where the text itself clears a column away, and that no count of operations gives 124. That is evidence for a reading, not proof of one.

Guo’s working was read by a second model from an OCR transcription of his book; his figure 8-8 was not seen, and how many times each column is taken was worked out, not read. No person has checked it against the printed page.

The rule of rods is the one Hart’s counts follow, and it confirms all fifteen of them; Zhu (2010, p. 82) gives 110 for setting out the problem, where it counts 116, but his digit rule (note 29) is the same one, and under it that board is 116 rods; his 110 matches the board’s 38 non-zero digits at the average of 2.9 rods a digit he gives in the next sentence, 110.2, which no other rule and no single misread coefficient does. That is an inference, since he does not show the count. The counts are of figures on the board: rods held in the hand, or set aside for a product, are not counted.

With every take done singly, the least the new method needs is 125, not 124; the 124 holds only if at least one figure at the step before the peak is taken three times at once. Whether a Han reckoner did that, the text does not say, and nothing here shows it.
Wei and Guo (2016) may already state this. Their paper could not be read beyond its opening. Nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: A number in a text can be tested by running what the text says; it cannot be proved by the run.

body.text: Do Wei Xuegang and Guo Shirong (2016) count 124 rods on this board?
body.detail: Their paper, 《九章算术》方程章“麻麦”问刘徽注中“算”字新释及方程“旧术”新校, 自然科学史研究 35(1), pp. 10–17, argues that 算 here is counting rods and begins from the new method. Its body is on CNKI behind a login. If it counts the board on the same working, the peak is theirs and this note is a confirmation by machine; if it counts another way, the two can be run side by side.

body.label: 08 / WHAT THE SECOND NUMBER DID
body.text: The 77 could not decide between the readings: each reading has a path that reaches it. The 124 can, on the evidence there is. On the one published working of the new method, with every operation up to the peak fixed by the text, a count of operations misses it by a hundred, and a count of rods lands on it, at the step before the text takes a column away. The test came from running the text as written, on a board that confirmed another scholar’s fifteen counts before it was asked this question. What was hard by hand, counting the rods on five columns of three-figure numbers after every step, under every way of working a step, is a command. The interpretation was already published. What the run adds is a measurement that supports it, and that anyone can repeat in the browser.

record.title: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s TPK, run: none of their three programs is accepted as printed
record.dek: In 1976 Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote one program, TPK, in about twenty early languages. Run on reconstructions built from each system’s own sources, their Böhm, Laning–Zierler and ALGOL 60 programs are each refused as printed. Six systems they did not cover give six other answers.
record.abstract: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s survey of early programming languages (1976) compares them by writing one fixed algorithm, TPK, in each, as “fairly close replicas” of what each language’s author would have written. This collection has executable reconstructions of nine early systems, each built from its own primary sources and independently of their paper. Three are languages they wrote TPK in, and each of those programs is refused as printed: Böhm’s, because it names a group S and a variable X, the letters his compiler keeps for itself, so compiled by his method it prints nothing; Laning and Zierler’s, because it reads its input with v|N, which the manual says “is not yet in operation”, and uses a computed zero as an index; ALGOL 60’s, because its procedure heading puts the specification before the value part, against the Report, and because the surviving X1 compiler, run on a simulator, stops on its label and compiles the heading’s parameter as a value array. Knuth had already corrected the heading in his errata (2014); the other findings were not found in a limited search. The six systems they did not cover give six kinds of answer: Turing’s ACE runs TPK only after correcting two of Turing’s own tables; GEORGE, IPL-V and JOSS accept it by their manuals; whether the first Dartmouth BASIC could run it cannot be settled from what survives; and the defining document of CPL cannot express it. Where they run, every value is right at the system’s precision but one, GEORGE’s 79.7062, traced to Hamblin’s add routine. On the two machine-level systems, output costs more than the arithmetic. A second input, with negative numbers, finds every program right in general but ours for JOSS, whose output form is too narrow, and shows that the X1 mode prints a stand-in’s digits for f(0).
record.lineage: 1976 SURVEY → PRIMARY SOURCES → NINE RECONSTRUCTIONS → TPK, RUN

body.label: 01 / ONE FIXED ALGORITHM
body.text: In The Early Development of Programming Languages (Stanford, 1976), Donald Knuth and Luis Trabb Pardo compare about twenty early languages by writing one program, TPK, in each. Read eleven numbers. Then, from the last to the first, print each one’s position i and f(aᵢ) = √|aᵢ| + 5aᵢ³, or TOO LARGE if that exceeds 400. They say plainly what the programs are: written in the style of each language’s author, “not truly authentic excerpts from the historical record, but … fairly close replicas” (p. 3). For weaker languages they give rules: integers only means integer input and an integer square root; no text means 999 for TOO LARGE; no user functions means f written out. This collection has executable reconstructions of nine early systems, each built from its own manuals and papers, without reference to their paper. Three are languages they wrote TPK in. That makes a test possible that they could not make: would each printed program have been accepted by the system it was written for?

body.label: 02 / ALGOL 60: THE REPORT, AND THE FIRST COMPILER
body.text: Their reference version is “in a dialect of Algol 60”. Against the Revised Report it fails twice. Its procedure heading, real procedure f(t); real t; value t;, gives the specification before the value part, and section 5.4.1 puts the value part first. And read and write are not in the Report, which has no input or output. The first ALGOL 60 system, Dijkstra and Zonneveld’s for the Electrologica X1, has a compiler that survives and can be run on a simulator. Given the program with only read and write changed to the X1’s, the compiler stops at once with stop 0–25: TPK: begin is a labelled program, and property 1 of the system’s manual says a program is an unlabelled block. Given the heading as printed in a program of its own, it accepts it without comment, but compiles t as a value array, with the operations RVA and VAP where value t; real t; gives TRAD. The simulator’s run-time then stops with “too many dimensions for value array”; what the X1’s own run-time did is not known, because its routines have not been found. With the label dropped and the value part first, the compiler’s program gives all eleven values to the 13 digits the simulator prints. The X1 findings come from the real compiler, not from the reconstruction.

references.label: The X1 probes and their results, compare/README.md

body.label: 03 / BÖHM: TWO LETTERS HIS COMPILER KEEPS
body.text: Corrado Böhm’s thesis (1951) defines a language and a compiler for it, written in the language itself. Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s TPK for it is right as algebra: read as formulas, it gives all 22 values, 999 for i = 10 down to 5 and then 322, 136, 41, 6 and 0. But it names a group S and a variable X, and chapter 6 of the thesis uses those two letters for the polynomials its compiler builds. Compiled by Böhm’s own method, the program’s S and X collide with the compiler’s, and the machine stops after 142 steps having printed nothing. The same program with S and X renamed K and Z agrees all three ways: as algebra, through a reference translation, and through Böhm’s compiler on the machine.

body.label: 04 / LANING AND ZIERLER: AN INPUT NOT YET IN OPERATION
body.text: Their Laning and Zierler program (pp. 56–57) reads its eleven numbers with v|N. The manual of January 1954 lists that among its temporary restrictions: it “is not yet in operation” (E-364, p. 21). It also counts i down by i = i − 1 and uses it as an index when it reaches zero, and page 13 permits a zero index only “if assigned by the specific equation n = 0”. Under the rules of January 1954 the translator stops at the first line. Run without that restriction it types ten lines and then an alarm at the computed zero, though that alarm rests on this reconstruction’s model of zero, not on the manual. Whether Whirlwind itself would have failed is not known.

body.label: 05 / WHAT WAS ALREADY KNOWN
body.text: A search in November 2026 covered Knuth’s errata, reviews of the paper and its reprints, histories of each language, Rosetta Code, Wikipedia’s talk pages and Hacker News. The heading was found: Knuth’s errata for Selected Papers on Computer Languages (2003), which reprints the paper, change “real t; value t;” to “value t; real t;” in an entry dated 12 February 2014, listed as a typographical correction. Wikipedia’s article on TPK still prints the old order. The same errata (22 September 2022) correct a different line of the Laning and Zierler program, so that 999 is printed for y > 400 and not for y ≥ 400, if the zero the test produces is +0; on Whirlwind a zero may or may not take the jump (E-364, p. 8). They leave v|N and the count down to zero as they were. Sestoft’s translation of Böhm’s thesis notes that the letters are used in the translation of polynomials (appendix A.1), but the search found no one connecting that to TPK. Nothing was found on the X1 refusing the label or compiling the heading as a value array, on v|N, or on the zero index. The search was limited, and the 1977 and 1980 reprints and most of van den Hove’s 2019 thesis on the X1 system could not be read.

references.label: Knuth, errata for Selected Papers on Computer Languages

body.label: 06 / SIX SYSTEMS THEY DID NOT COVER
body.text: Their survey stops in 1957, and machine codes are outside it. The collection’s other six systems therefore have no printed TPK, and the programs for them are new: each written from that system’s own sources, in its author’s style, following Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s rules, and checked against its manual. They were written with a reconstruction to test them on, which Knuth and Trabb Pardo did not have, so that they run is no evidence that they were better read. What is of interest is what each system forced, and whether its own documents would accept the result. The six give six different kinds of answer.

body.label: 07 / TURING’S ACE: ONLY AFTER CORRECTING TURING
body.text: The ACE of Turing’s 1945 report is a design, not a machine, and TPK on it is an instruction table. Its arithmetic is whole numbers, so by Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s rules the input is 0 to 10, the square root is an integer one, here by taking away 1, 3, 5 … and counting, and TOO LARGE is 999. The report has no square root, no input conversion and no way to step an index down, and the program needs two of the subsidiary tables Turing printed: INDEXIN, to fetch aᵢ, and DISCRIM, to choose a way on. As printed, INDEXIN gives wrong cards, and DISCRIM answers “no” to the word that both of TPK’s tests produce, so the square root never ends. With the two corrections the reconstruction already lists, it runs, in 24.4 seconds of the design’s time, three quarters of the computing spent converting to decimal.

body.label: 08 / GEORGE, IPL-V AND JOSS: ACCEPTED BY THEIR MANUALS
body.text: Three of the six accept TPK as their manuals describe them. GEORGE, Hamblin’s reverse Polish scheme for the DEUCE (1957), has no text, so TOO LARGE is 999 and the output is 22 cards; its repetition only counts up, so i is 10 − j; and t³ is dup dup × ×, because its power goes through a logarithm and stops on a negative base. It runs both in the interpreter and on Hamblin’s own coding sheets in a simulated DEUCE. IPL-V (1961) has no arrays and no square root: the eleven numbers are a list, reversed by J64, and the square root is a routine by Newton’s method, which takes two thirds of the run’s 2,757 interpretation cycles. TOO LARGE is two data terms, because a data term holds five characters. JOSS (1964–65) has no user functions before JOSS-II, so f is written out; Demand asks for each number; and text and a number share a line only through a form. Each is a judgement from the manuals. For IPL-V it rests on every process used being older than the 1964 additions, and the JOSS reconstruction is the only JOSS that runs.

body.label: 09 / BASIC AND CPL: WHAT SURVIVES CANNOT DECIDE
body.text: For the first Dartmouth BASIC the question cannot be settled. The instruction manual of May 1964 survives only as Part I. Arrays, DIM and probably REM are left to Part II. Page 4 counts the operations: nine in Part I and four more in Part II. The October 1964 manual lists fifteen statements, five of them, GOSUB, RETURN, DIM, STOP and REM, not in Part I, so one of those five was not yet in the first system. Which one cannot be identified, so whether TPK could be written in May 1964 is unknown. The program also has to write the cube as T*T*T, because the manual says A↑B “is actually interpreted as |A|^B”. For CPL the defining document cannot express TPK at all: the 1966 Reference Manual’s section on input and output was “postponed”, and the appendix that would define square root and absolute value was never finished. The program uses the Elementary Programming Manual and its supplement for the trial Cambridge system instead.

body.label: 10 / THE VALUES, AND ONE THAT IS NOT
body.text: On Knuth’s input, 1 (.5) 2 (.25) 3.5 (1) 5.5, every value printed by every system that runs is the true value at that system’s precision, with two exceptions. The X1’s 40-bit numbers end …005 at i = 4 where the true value ends …008: that is storage, not a fault. And GEORGE prints 79.7062 where the value, 79.70614, rounds to 79.7061. The interpreter and Hamblin’s own coding sheets on the simulated DEUCE both print it, and the reconstruction traces it to Hamblin’s add routine, which rounds a leftover 0.38 of a unit upward. It has not been checked against a real DEUCE. The integer systems, the ACE and Böhm, agree with each other and with the arithmetic.

body.label: 11 / THE COST, IN EACH SYSTEM’S OWN UNITS
body.text: The units do not convert into one another, so each is reported as its reconstruction counts it. Turing’s ACE: 48,246 instructions in 761,189 minor cycles of 32 µs, 24.4 seconds if cards go at 100 a minute, about three quarters of the computing spent converting to decimal. GEORGE on the simulated DEUCE: 33,477 instructions, 38.7 seconds, about 59% of it punching the 22 cards, after 57 seconds to load GEORGE. IPL-V: 2,757 interpretation cycles, the unit the Logic Theorist’s effort was measured in, 68% of them in the square root. CPL: 437 steps of the reconstruction’s abstract machine, a modern unit. On both machine-level systems, output costs more than the arithmetic; where a system lacked a primitive, the substitute dominated. All of these are from simulations, with the DEUCE’s reader and punch at the simulator’s mid-range timings.

body.label: 12 / A SECOND INPUT, WITH NEGATIVES
body.text: Knuth’s eleven numbers are all positive, so several of the adaptations above are never tested by them: BASIC’s cube, GEORGE’s, the integer square roots, and how each prints a negative result. The programs were run again on −1, −2.5, 0, 0.25, −4, 4.5, −9, 2, −0.5, 3.5, −5.5, and the integer systems on −1, −2, 0, 1, −4, 4, −9, 2, −3, 3, −5. ALGOL 60 by the Report, CPL, IPL-V, BASIC and the ACE give every value right: f(−5.5) = −829.5298, f(−9) = −3642, and on the ACE −623 and −3642 for −5 and −9. Laning and Zierler’s values are right to its 24-bit arithmetic, and it still stops at the zero index. GEORGE prints 0.0821066 where the value rounds to 0.0821068, and −76.5438 for −76.5439: each is one unit low in the last binary digit, from the add routine already traced for 79.7062. Böhm’s numbers are never negative, so the question does not arise. Two answers were not right. Our JOSS program stops at the first negative value with “I can’t express value in your form.”: form 2 holds y only from −99.999999 to 999.999999, and below 400 f can be any size. JOSS refuses rather than types a wrong number, and a field of dots, which types six figures and a power of ten, fits every value. And in X1 mode f(0) prints as 1.49166814624004e-154, not 0. The X1’s manual says a real variable never holds 0, only the least positive number, about 10⁻⁶¹⁶, so a result that is not 0 is right; but the reconstruction’s stand-in for that number is about 10⁻³⁰⁸, and its square root, 10⁻¹⁵⁴, prints the stand-in’s digits. The X1’s would be about .556⏨−308. Written with BASIC’s ↑, as T↑3, f(−5.5) would be TOO LARGE: 1964 BASIC takes the power of |T|.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: It does not show that Knuth and Trabb Pardo were careless. They said their programs were replicas. What is measured is the distance between a careful reading of each language in 1976 and what its own system enforced, and each time it comes from something a reader of the papers would not see: a compiler’s private letters, a routine not yet in operation, a rule about labels, code that depends on the order of a heading.

Only the X1 findings come from a surviving system. The Böhm, Laning and Zierler, and Report findings are the rules of their documents applied by a reconstruction, and the reconstructions are readings of those documents. Whether Whirlwind would have run the Laning and Zierler program is not known.

The six new programs are ours, and that they run says as much about the reconstructions they were tested on as about the languages. ‘Accepted by the manual’ is a judgement for IPL-V and JOSS, and BASIC’s answer depends on a part of a manual that is lost.
The costs are from simulators, not machines, and are not comparable with each other.
The search for earlier work was limited, by a coding agent. Nothing here is claimed as new beyond what that search did not find.
body.principle: A program printed as a replica can be tested by running it on what it replicates.

body.text: Did the 1977 or 1980 reprint of the paper change the ALGOL heading?
body.detail: The paper was reprinted in the Encyclopedia of Computer Science and Technology (1977) and in A History of Computing in the Twentieth Century (1980). Both are only lent by archive.org, and were not read. Knuth’s correction is dated 2014, against the 2003 reprint.

body.label: 13 / WHAT THE COMPARISON DID
body.text: In 1976 a common program let two readers compare twenty languages on paper. Run on systems rebuilt from their own sources, the same program asks something sharper of each language: not what it looks like, but whether its own rules let it through. Of their three programs that could be asked, none passes as printed, and one of the reasons, the heading, Knuth had already found. Of the six new ones, the answers range from accepted, to accepted only after correcting the designer, to a question that a lost Part II of a manual would settle. The reconstructions gained something too. Writing TPK in each exposed gaps of their own: the ALGOL interpreter accepted the misordered heading and, in X1 mode, the labelled program; the IPL-V loader read a floating-point digit from a column its manual leaves unused; and a JOSS listing was dated too late. Each is now fixed or recorded in its repository.

record.dek: Dartmouth BASIC, typed in from its first instruction manual of May 1964, and the one program a later BASIC would not run.
record.abstract: A note about Dartmouth BASIC, with the language running in the page. The first instruction manual, from May 1964, explains the language in a few pages and prints three example programs with their results; they are typed in here beside the pages they came from, and print the same figures. The interpreter running them was written in Rust with a coding agent and checked against later BASICs, which it matched. The manual’s own second example then stopped at line 40: in 1964 a square root was taken of the absolute value, and the later BASICs it had been checked against call that an error. A second manual, of October 1964, later supplied the rules for printing the first had left out, and twenty-six more programs.
record.lineage: 1964 MANUAL → LATER BASICS → AGENT PORT → 1964 MANUAL

body.label: 01 / MAY 1964
body.text: BASIC’s first instruction manual is a typescript from the Dartmouth College Computation Center, dated May 1964 and marked First Draft. Its preface says the college was building a system that “will enable 20 or more people to use the computer at the same time”, and lists what the language for it had to do. The first requirement: “It should be very easy to learn.” Then, as evidence, and “without any explanation”, it prints a whole program. Three lines, to work out seven plus eight, divided by three.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: That program, with the line numbers the manual gives it on page 4. It is running in your browser, not replayed. Change the sum and run it again.

links.label: Open the full study — every program, and the pages

body.label: 02 / FOURTEEN WORDS
body.text: A Dartmouth BASIC program is a list of numbered instructions. The computer starts at the lowest number and works upwards, so the numbers are the order, whatever order the lines were typed in. The manual suggests leaving gaps, such as counting in tens, “so that further instructions may be inserted if the need arises.” Each instruction is one operation and what it applies to, and there are not many: “The last instruction in any BASIC program is ‘END’. There are only 13 other operations.” LET puts a value in a variable. PRINT shows it. FOR and NEXT repeat the lines between them. IF … THEN and GO TO decide which line comes next. READ takes numbers from DATA lines, and DEF gives a formula a name. A variable is “any single letter, or a letter followed by one digit.”

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.label: 03 / THE PAGE PRINTS ITS OWN ANSWERS
body.text: The reprint Dartmouth hosts, which is the beginners’ part, ends with three example programs and, under each, what it printed and how long it took. Program number 1 averages the logarithms of the numbers 1 to 100 and prints 1.5797, in three seconds. I typed all three in from the scan. They are a test nobody had to write, because the expected output is on the page.
Program number 1, from page 21. The 1964 page prints 1.5797, and so does this. Switch off AS IN 1964 and a later BASIC prints the same number to nine figures.

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 04 / WHAT IS NOT THERE
body.text: What the beginners’ part leaves out says as much as what it has. There is no way to ask the person at the teletype a question: a program’s numbers come from its DATA lines, and to try other numbers you change the program. There are no variables for words, only for numbers. Powers are written with an arrow, X↑2, because “on a tele-type typewriter it is impossible to print superscripts”. The manual treats changing the program as the normal way to use it. Under program number 3 it says, “We can find the root of a different function by changing a single instruction”, prints the new line 30, and prints the new result.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 3, from page 23. Run it, then do what the manual does: replace line 30 with 30 DEF FNF(Z) = EXP(X) -2 and run it again. The page prints .837585, then .693176. The new line is typed here as it is printed, with an X where the first one had a Z. It still works, because the program only ever asks for FNF(X).

links.label: Open the full study

body.label: 05 / HOW IT RUNS HERE
body.text: This is not Dartmouth’s compiler. It is an interpreter written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. I had started it in Python: a tokenizer and a parser, which never ran a program. I asked a coding agent to move it to Rust and finish it. Neither of us began from the 1964 manual.

body.label: 06 / CHECKED AGAINST LATER BASICS
body.text: How would I know it was right? The agent wrote tests, and they passed. Then it ran 103 listings from David Ahl’s BASIC Computer Games of 1978, which nobody involved had written, and every one loads and runs without changes, as the coding-horror collection has them; that collection was normalised for Vintage BASIC, so they are not the printed book line for line. Then it ran test programs through PC-BASIC, an independent emulation of Microsoft’s GW-BASIC. Twenty-two of them print the same on standard output in both, byte for byte once PC-BASIC’s line endings and closing prompt are set aside, and the comparison found one real mistake. Error messages were not compared. Everything agreed. All of it was BASIC from fourteen years or more after the manual.

body.label: 07 / LINE 40
body.text: Then I asked for pages of the 1964 manual, for this note, and the example programs came with them. Programs 1 and 3 gave the page’s figures. Program 2 solves quadratic equations, and on its third set of numbers it stopped: Illegal function call: SQR, in line 40. Line 40 takes a square root before the program has looked at whether the number is negative. Page 5 says why that was fine in 1964: “SQR(A) stands for √A, where the square-root is always taken of the absolute value of A.” The games and the second interpreter come from later BASICs, where, in the two I could run, the square root of a negative number is an error. They agreed with each other, and my interpreter agreed with them. The oldest page disagreed with all of it.

references.label: First BASIC instruction manual, Dartmouth, May 1964

body.text: Program number 2, as later BASICs run it. Press RUN: it stops at line 40. Switch on AS IN 1964 and run it again, and the last result reads IMAGINARY PART= 1.41421, as the page does. It goes back for more numbers until there are none, and then, as page 15 says the computer does when READ runs out of data, it stops.

Source, tutorial and the scanned pages

body.label: 08 / OCTOBER 1964
body.text: Dartmouth’s second manual, dated 1 October 1964, describes what the beginners’ part left out, and settles some of what this note had guessed. Page 34 gives the rules for printing a number: no more than six significant figures, and “if the number is an exact integer, the decimal point is not printed”. So a point after a whole number means the figure only rounds to one. The May page prints program 2’s roots as 3. and −1.: the 1964 square root of 16 was not exactly 4. This interpreter’s is, so in 1964 mode it prints 3 and −1. Page 31 gives five zones of fifteen columns, and “each number occupies one zone”, which is why the May page puts −1. under the third coefficient; 1964 mode now does too. Page 39 says that INT chops, “INT(-7.8) is -7, not -8”, and that RND’s argument “has no significance”: the note had taken both from Thomas Kurtz’s account of 2005. Its appendix lists fifteen statements, one more than the May manual’s fourteen. The manual prints 26 programs. Typed in, those with printed results agree in their figures, except where 1964’s arithmetic was inexact, where its random numbers differ, where its system caught a mistake before the run that this interpreter lets through, and where the page puts a space inside a number, which this interpreter refuses.

The table of cubes from page 35, in 1964 mode. A semicolon packs the numbers, and the page prints eleven on the first line, eight on each line after, and 1000000 alone at the end. This prints the same thirteen lines. The study has nine of the October programs beside their pages.

The 26 programs, and where they disagree

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This is not Dartmouth’s 1964 BASIC. It is an interpreter written sixty-two years later. In 1964 mode it follows the May manual on square roots, powers and the end of the data, the October manual on printing, LOG, INT and RND, and Thomas Kurtz’s later account on a leading minus sign, which neither manual covers. Taking the October manual, or Kurtz, as a description of May 1964 is a reading.

Its printing follows the October manual’s rules; its arithmetic is not 1964’s. Its powers and square roots are exact where 1964’s were not, so where a page prints 4. or 3., with the point that marks an inexact figure, this prints 4 and 3. Its random numbers are not 1964’s.

In 1964 mode it still accepts everything the later BASICs added. It does not refuse INPUT or a variable called NAME$, nor stop on the mistakes the October manual’s session shows the 1964 system catching before a run.

The manuals’ programs agree in their figures and, under the October rules, their columns; the pages’ TIME: lines, and the May page’s READ PART where the program says REAL PART, are not reproduced. The rule for square roots turned up because one program happened to need it. Other differences may be waiting for a program that needs them.
The checks were run by the coding agent and reported to me. It also miscounted its own tests twice, saying 120 and then 122 when there were 88, and corrected itself when it ran them again.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, later reviewed the repository independently. It found that 1964 mode differed from Kurtz’s account on INT, RND and a leading minus, that RANDOMIZE could change numbers the playground had already shown, and that the games were described as unmodified. These are put right, and its review, with what was done about each point, is in the repository.
body.principle: Sources that agree with each other are evidence about those sources.

body.text: Which BASIC is the reference for BASIC?
body.detail: The interpreter now has a switch: later BASIC unless asked, Dartmouth’s 1964 arithmetic and printing on request. That is a decision, not a discovery. Every check I had was a later BASIC agreeing with a later BASIC, and the manual was on Dartmouth’s website the whole time.

record.title: The program in the Atlas Autocode manual does not compile. Its printout shows what ran.
record.dek: Atlas Autocode rebuilt from its 1965 manual, with both compilers and the Flexowriter it was typed on, prints the words of all 29 lines of the one full page COMPILER AB printed that survives with its program. The program printed beside it would have stopped at line 12.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding Atlas Autocode, the language of the Ferranti Atlas at Manchester, from Brooker and Rohl’s Reference Manual of 1965 with a coding agent: both of its compilers, AA and AB, the Atlas arithmetic, and the Friden Flexowriter on which its programs were typed, underlined word by word with the backspace key. The compilers are lost. Two pages that COMPILER AB printed survive with the programs that produced them: a program map and run-time monitor in the manual’s Amendments, and a table of binomial coefficients in the Mini-Manual of July 1965. The rebuilt compiler prints the same words as all 29 lines of the first, and the second’s table number for number. It also shows that the program printed beside the first page would not have compiled: it declares a′ and assigns a″. The printout lists a″ where a′ is declared, so the program that ran was most likely not quite the program that was printed. The second page’s map counts a line its listing does not have, and the first program in the manual prints a sum of squares of −125.3.
record.lineage: REFERENCE MANUAL → FLEXOWRITER → AGENT → COMPILERS AA AND AB → 1965 PRINTOUTS

body.label: 01 / TYPED ON A FLEXOWRITER
body.text: Atlas Autocode was the language of the Ferranti Atlas, which Manchester University and Ferranti put into service in 1962. Tony Brooker’s group wrote it, and Brooker and J. S. Rohl’s Reference Manual of March 1965 defines it. It is close kin to ALGOL 60, with blocks, recursive routines and arrays sized when the block is entered, but it was written for the keyboard it was typed on: a Friden Flexowriter, an electric typewriter that punched paper tape. The keyboard had no underlined letters and no ≠. The words of the language were underlined by typing the word, backspacing, and typing underlines over it; ≠ was = with / struck over it, and even the semicolon was a colon struck over a comma. Atlas rebuilt each line as the paper showed it, and spaces did not count at all. I asked a coding agent to build the language from the manual, with the Flexowriter as its input: a line is a row of positions, each holding the symbols struck there.

references.label: Brooker and Rohl, Atlas Autocode Reference Manual, 1965 (scan)

body.label: 02 / TWO COMPILERS, AND ATLAS ARITHMETIC
body.text: In 1965 there were two compilers. COMPILER AA is the language of the Reference Manual. COMPILER AB, described in Amendments bound into the same manual and in Lunnon and Riding’s Mini-Manual of July 1965, dropped complex numbers, own variables and some checks, and rounded a real put into an integer where AA refused it when compiling. The job description at the head of the tape chose between them, and does here. The arithmetic is Atlas’s, from Ferranti’s description of the machine: a 40-bit fraction and an octal exponent, each result formed exactly and then rounded “by forcing a one into the least significant bit” if anything was lost. So .1 added ten times is not 1. The store is a model of the Atlas stack, word by word, and as the manual warns, nothing is cleared between one routine and the next.

references.label: Lunnon and Riding, The Atlas Autocode Mini-Manual, July 1965

body.label: 03 / WHAT COMPILER AB PRINTED
body.text: The compilers do not survive, so there is nothing to run the rebuilt one against. What survives is output. The Amendments end with a short program, a routine that calls a routine that calls a function that takes the square root of −2, and the page COMPILER AB printed for it: a program map, then the run-time monitor, which lists every block and routine that was running, with its variables and its cycles. The rebuilt compiler prints the same words in the same order, all 29 lines, apart from the machine addresses and code sizes in the map, which belong to machine code it does not write. The page was typed again for the manual, so its spacing is not compared. The serial numbers, 91 to 94, follow the order of the routine specifications, not of the routines. The line numbers count from 1 and leave blank lines out, so line 33 is the square root. The monitor shows only the variables declared in each routine that are not zero, not the parameters, and says the function’s first cycle has gone round 0 times and its second was never entered.

body.label: 04 / ONE PRIME
body.text: Run as printed, the program on the facing page does not reach the square root. Its second line declares a′, with one prime, and its twelfth sets a″, with two. To the compiler they are different names, so it stops at line 12 with NAME a″ NOT SET, and the program is never entered. The printout points to which was meant: the monitor lists a″ = 21.6 sixth among the reals of the main block, exactly where a′ is declared. The likely reading is that the program COMPILER AB ran declared a″, and the listing, typed out again for the manual, dropped a prime. The tape is lost, so that cannot be proved; the printout could have been edited instead. Neither page could have caught it alone: the listing looks right, and the printout has no listing. The interpreter caught it only because it was given both.

body.label: 05 / A LINE THE LISTING DOES NOT HAVE
body.text: The Mini-Manual’s sample program tabulates binomial coefficients, and its next page shows what COMPILER AB printed. The table comes out character for character. The program map agrees as far as line 9, where an inner block begins; after that every line number on the page is one more than the listing gives, 27 where the listing has 26, through to the end of the program. The listing was redrawn for the Mini-Manual with boxes round its blocks, and may have lost a line on the way; or the map may have been edited. The pages do not say which.

body.label: 06 / THE FIRST PROGRAM IN THE MANUAL
body.text: The Reference Manual opens with a program that fits a straight line to sets of points and prints, it says, “the sum of the squares of the deviations”. Its formula has + 2abΣX; its program has − 2a*b*Sx. For five points near y = 2x + 1 the program prints −1.253α 2, a sum of squares of −125.3; with the sign put right it is 0.107. The manual printed no output for this program, so nothing on the page shows the mistake. Both scans that could be read have the minus sign. The manual also says that the constant 'a' is 33, which its own table gives to A.

The compiler runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Type a program on the Flexowriter, see the tape it punches, and run it as COMPILER AA or AB. For the two programs of 1965, the page that was printed then is beside the one printed now.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: Two pages are the whole of the evidence about what the compilers printed, and both are COMPILER AB. No output of COMPILER AA survives with its program; its map and monitor follow the manual’s description and examples, which are illustrations, not runs.

The layout of the AB monitor, which variables it shows and how many to a line, was read off the same page it is tested against. Agreement there is not independent. What is independent is what comes from running the program: the line and serial numbers, the values, the counts of each cycle.

The arithmetic follows Ferranti’s description of the machine. The pages show four or five digits of each number, which does not test the last bits. The standard functions are computed in modern double precision, because the Atlas routines for them have not been found.
Both pages were retyped for the documents they are printed in, so they are compared word for word, not character for character, and they may have been changed in retyping, as the listings were.
Everything here, including the transcriptions of the programs from the scans, was read and built by a coding agent over one day. The scans are linked so that they can be checked by eye.

A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository independently before this note was published. It found eighteen problems, among them a tab stop misread from the Mini-Manual, large constants turned into wrong numbers, and claims of agreement “to the character” where the test compares words. All are fixed or reworded, and each is now a test; the review is in the repository.
Nothing here is claimed as new. The manuals were kept and put online by the Edinburgh computer history project and others; the language’s history is well told elsewhere.
body.principle: A listing typed for a manual is a copy. Where the listing and the machine’s own page disagree, the page is the better witness to what ran.

record.title: A 1954 manual asked for trouble reports. So I sent some.
record.dek: Algebra typed on tape for MIT’s Whirlwind in 1953, rebuilt from its manual by a coding agent. The one page of 1954 output I found agrees to the last digit or two. Its rules find a slip in its arithmetic, a 1954 copy that would not run, and a forbidden zero index in Knuth’s TPK.
record.abstract: A note about rebuilding the algebraic system J. H. Laning Jr. and N. Zierler wrote for MIT’s Whirlwind I, from the manual they published in January 1954, with a coding agent. You typed equations on a Flexowriter and the answers came back typewritten. The manual ends by admitting that “exhaustive tests have not been made” and asking for information about “any troubles encountered in the use of this program”. Its three complete programs run on the reconstruction, and their answers check against mathematics. One program of the time can be checked against Whirlwind itself: the lead-pursuit problem of early 1954, whose tape and first page of output Laning sent Knuth in 1976. Its 62 values agree with that page to within 4.2 parts in ten million, except two from the arcsine, within 7.2 parts in a million. Its rules mean what they say: a/b/c is ac over b, and a zero has two signs, which its own loops step round. The troubles worth reporting are elsewhere. The manual’s decimal for its largest number is wrong in the fifth place. The 1954 summer school’s version of its differential-equation program would not have been accepted. And Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s 1976 example in the language is incompatible with the 1954 specification: it reads its numbers with v|N, which was not yet working, and on its last number it uses a computed zero as an index, which the manual forbids whatever the zero’s sign. An earlier, smaller version of the translator survives, as a hand-written listing of March 1953 in Knuth’s papers; the reconstruction was not built from it. A second model reviewed the reconstruction independently, twice. The system runs in the browser.

body.label: 01 / A COMPUTER WITHIN A COMPUTER
body.text: In 1952 J. H. Laning Jr. of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory wrote a program that let Whirlwind I take mathematics typed as mathematics, and with N. Zierler made it a usable system by May 1953. Equations typed on a Flexowriter were punched on paper tape, translated into Whirlwind’s own instructions, and the answers typed back. “The effect of our program is to create a computer within a computer …” In 1954 John Backus came to MIT with two colleagues to see it run. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the system from its manual, Engineering Memorandum E-364, and to run the manual’s programs under the manual’s own rules.

body.label: 02 / EXHAUSTIVE TESTS HAVE NOT BEEN MADE
body.text: The manual ends with Temporary Rules and Restrictions, among them “The x|N is not yet in operation.” Then: “All other portions of the program are believed to be operating satisfactorily but exhaustive tests have not been made. Information relative to any troubles encountered in the use of this program would be appreciated by the authors.” A progress report for the first quarter of 1954 says every routine had been tested and worked except the x|N routine. I have not found Zierler’s report on the program’s inner workings, and that summer it was said that “there are no annotated copies of the conversion routine”. A hand-written listing of an earlier version, dated March 1953, does survive, in Knuth’s papers. It has no superscript variables, no drum, no D equations, no SR or CR, and treats −x as 1 − x. So for the system of 1954 the manual is the specification, and what it does not say is this reconstruction’s choice.

references.label: Project Whirlwind Summary Report No. 37, first quarter 1954

body.label: 03 / A PERFECTLY REASONABLE EXPRESSION
body.text: Multiplication is writing things side by side: 2ay is 2 times a times y, and a space between two digits is a multiplication sign, so 2 3 is six. Inside a term a slash sends everything after it to the other side of the fraction, until the next slash. So cd/a(b + c) is cd over a(b + c), and “a/b/c is properly interpreted as the product ac divided by b”, not a over bc, as FORTRAN would have it. In 1976 Laning wrote: “The notion of operator precedence as a formal concept did not occur to me at the time; I lived in fear that someone would write a perfectly reasonable algebraic expression that my system would not analyze correctly.”

body.label: 04 / TWO ZEROS
body.text: Numbers have 24 binary digits and an exponent, about seven decimal places, and zero has a sign. CP jumps if the last quantity computed was negative, and on a zero “the CP may or may not behave like an SP since 0 may appear as +0 or −0.” The manual’s loops step round this: to go round ten times one tests n − 9.5, never n − 10, and another counts down in twos, so its test never comes to zero. The reconstruction has to decide, and my inference is a one’s-complement adder’s: a zero typed as 0 is +0, and the difference of two equal numbers is −0. So n − 5 with n equal to 5 is typed −.00000000+00, and CP jumps.

body.label: 05 / KNUTH’S EXAMPLE AND THE 1954 RULES
body.text: Knuth and Trabb Pardo’s 1976 example in the language, TPK, reads eleven numbers with v|N, copies them to a|0 to a|10, and works back down with i = i − 1. Page 13 allows a letter as an index, but: “Negative values of n are not permitted in this connection, nor are values between zero and one half inclusive, with the exception that the value zero is permissible if assigned by the specific equation n = 0,.” The last time round, i is zero, and it got there by i = i − 1, not by i = 0. Page 13 forbids that whatever the zero’s sign, so the 1976 example and the 1954 specification are incompatible. Under the rules of January 1954 it could not have run at all, because it begins with v|N, and “The x|N is not yet in operation.” What the reconstruction does about it is a separate matter. It approximates page 13 by the sign of zero, refusing −0 and allowing +0, and since my inference is that a computed zero is −0, it types ten lines and then ALARM EQUATION 2 PRECEDED BY 109. That alarm rests on the inference, not on the manual, which names no alarm for it. Make every zero +0 and TPK runs to the end, still breaking the rule. Its checker points at i = i − 1 before anything runs.

body.label: 06 / THE INNOCUOUS CHANGE
body.text: Write dy/dt as D y = …, and the stretch from the first D equation to the last is gone through four times a step, by “the method of Gill - a variation of the 4th order Runge-Kutta technique”. The manual’s example has the answers sin(t − 2) and cos(t − 2) − 1, and the reconstruction is within about .004 of them at every t it prints: what a step of one half costs. Then the manual warns. Move y|2 + 1 into a helper, a = y|2 + 1, just before the first D equation, and the change “would appear to be innocuous”. It is not, because the later passes start at the first D equation and never recompute a. At t = 10, y|1 is 2.58 where sin 8 is .99. The checker warns about it, quoting the page.

body.label: 07 / A PROGRAM THAT WOULD NOT HAVE RUN
body.text: The MIT summer school notes of 1954 give their own, shorter version of the manual’s differential-equation program. As printed, its last two lines lack the commas the rules require, so the translator would not have accepted it. It also has no PRINT, so with the commas put back it integrates from t = 2 to past t = 10 and types nothing; it may have been meant to leave its answers in storage. The manual’s own examples have three smaller slips: a missing comma on page 8, a semicolon for a comma on page 11, and a figure on page 7 that types a ninth value nobody asked for. The manual has a slip of its own, on page 6. Its largest number, 2⁶³ − 2³⁹, is “(or, roughly, 9.2233995 · 10¹⁸)”. It is 9.2233715 · 10¹⁸, wrong in the fifth decimal place. And the manual prints .05 as +.50000000−01, which the nearest 24-bit number to .05 gives only if the digits are cut off rather than rounded. So the reconstruction cuts them off: a choice that fits the page, not something the page proves.

body.label: 08 / IT RAN THE FIRST TIME
body.text: These are the troubles the authors asked for, seventy years late: slips in the manual, one in a copy of it, and the rest its rules doing what they say. The system itself did real work. Laning recalled a three-dimensional lead-pursuit problem, coded with its sceptical owners “in a 2-1/2 hour coding session, at least half of which was spent in defining notation”, which “ran successfully the first time”: 79 statements, with seven uses of the differential-equation feature. The summer school heard that “with a single exception, all programs coded in the Laning-Zierler system have been completed successfully on their first run”. The price was speed: “a reduction of computing speed of the order of magnitude of ten to one from an efficient computer program”, as C. W. Adams put it in May 1954, and six to eight times the Laboratory’s usual interpretive system, as the summer school did.

body.label: 09 / WHAT WHIRLWIND TYPED
body.text: In 1976 Laning sent Knuth that lead-pursuit program as the Flexowriter typed it, with the first page of what it printed: “the first effort to use the Whirlwind compiler on a serious engineering problem”, from “very early 1954”, he guessed. It has 79 statements, seven of them D equations, as he had said. It is the only output of the 1954 system I have found, and it exercises most of the system: superscript variables, eighteen function calls, Gill’s method, SR and CP, and the slash. Typed into the reconstruction, it prints the same variables in the same order, and all 62 values on the page agree to within 4.2 parts in ten million, except the two of a|0, which come from the arcsine, one of the routines the reconstruction had to choose, and are out by 7.2 parts in a million. One line of the program runs off the edge of the sheet; of the endings tried, only one makes the numbers agree. The page also shows what the reconstruction does not do: a zero set by t = 0 was typed +.16155871−27, a zero exponent −00, and 6400 came back +.64000003+04. And it shows the minus sign working. The listing of March 1953 treats −x as 1 − x, “the problem you mentioned about unary minus”, Knuth wrote to Laning; this program uses unary minus throughout, and with that bug it would have typed d as about .1 at its first step, not .00052. It never uses x|N, so whether that ever worked is still open.

body.text: The system runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version, with the manual’s programs among its tapes. Type a tape, feed it, and the printer types the answers, as slowly as ten characters a second if you like. The translation shows each equation’s block of orders, and the same tape can be fed with each kind of zero side by side.
