body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: I have not found the translator of 1954. This is built from a programmer’s manual, which says what the system does and not how. The listing that survives is of a smaller version of March 1953, and the reconstruction was not built from it. Larry Stabile has transcribed that listing and runs it on Guy Fedorkow’s Whirlwind simulator; I have read that work, not checked it.

The manual prints almost none of what its programs typed. Three numbers on page 6, 5, .05 and −π, can be compared digit for digit, and match; its programs are checked against mathematics. One later page, the lead-pursuit program’s, is checked against Whirlwind, but only as far as it goes: to t = .6, before the program changes its step, with no x|N and no rule broken.

The sign of a computed zero is an inference from the manual’s warning on page 8 and from the arithmetic of the time, not from a listing. The reconstruction uses that sign to approximate the rule of page 13, so it lets through some computed zeros the rule forbids, such as n = 0·5, and the TPK alarm rests on the inference. The alarm’s wording is this reconstruction’s.
TPK was never run on Whirlwind, as far as I know. Knuth and Trabb Pardo wrote it to show what the language looked like, not to test it.

How Gill’s method was arranged inside the system, the rounding of each operation, the function routines, and what happened to a number too small to hold are this reconstruction’s choices, each listed in the repository. Nothing is timed.

The pages were read by the same coding agent that wrote the interpreter, from the page images. No person has checked the reading against the scans by eye. A second model, OpenAI’s Codex, reviewed the repository independently and checked twenty places against the page images: seventeen matched, and three were repairs that had not been disclosed, the three slips in the manual’s examples, which are now listed. It also found that the option making every zero +0 left a negated zero as −0, which is fixed. Its review, and what was done about each point, is in the repository. The lead-pursuit program and its page were read the same way, and a second review by Codex found no error in either reading; it found ten things to put right in the claims and the test, and they were.
No search has been made for earlier discussion of these troubles. Someone may well have noticed them before.
body.principle: When only the manual survives, its rules are the program. Running them shows what the rules say, not what Whirlwind did.

body.text: If a manual is all that survives, can you tell what the program did?
body.detail: The three complete programs in E-364 run on the reconstruction and give answers that check against mathematics. That shows the manual is consistent with itself and with arithmetic. It does not show that Whirlwind typed the same eight digits, or did the same thing when a tape broke a rule. One printout from 1954 has now been found, and where it exercises the system the reconstruction agrees with it to the last digit or two. What Whirlwind did with x|N, or with a tape that broke a rule, is still not shown.

record.title: Absys did not unify two unknowns. It waited.
record.dek: Absys, built at Aberdeen around 1967 and rebuilt here from its designers’ papers, prints the binding environments of Elcock’s examples variable for variable, suspended equations included. One of his examples also favours one order in which Absys may have taken its steps.
record.abstract: A note about reconstructing Absys, the language J. M. Foster, E. W. Elcock and their colleagues built for the Elliott 4120 at the University of Aberdeen, which Elcock argued in 1990 was the first logic programming language. No program text or listing of it is known to survive. With a coding agent, the language was rebuilt from three papers: Foster’s Assertions of 1968, extracts of Foster and Elcock’s introduction to Absys 1 of 1969, and Elcock’s retrospective of 1990, read from its page scans. An equation between two unknowns is not solved but suspended until one of them is known; an or splits the computation into derivations that are all pursued, fairly, until each fails or hibernates; and each assertion is accepted as it is typed. Run on the papers’ own examples, the reconstruction gives every result they print, the binding environments of the append and reverse examples variable for variable and Absys 1’s three triples in the paper’s order, and the expected answers for Clark’s students and for setdiff, whose results the paper does not print. Run on inputs chosen here, setdiff gives the right answer if each applied body takes the place of its literal, or if not waits for its variables; taking literals strictly in turn without such a delay, one fair rule among several, gives the wrong one.
record.lineage: FOSTER 1968 → FOSTER AND ELCOCK 1969 → ELCOCK 1990 → AGENT → THE MACHINE THE PAPERS DESCRIBE → THEIR EXAMPLES RUN

body.label: 01 / ASSERTIONS, NOT INSTRUCTIONS
body.text: In a paper given in 1967, Michael Foster, of the Computer Research Group at Aberdeen, described a system in which “the basic elements … are not instructions to do something, as are the statements of Algol, but assertions about the data, such as a=b or a+b=c.” His paper was called Assertions: Programs Written without Specifying Unnecessary Order. By 1968 the group had “a working on-line incremental compiler” for it on the university’s Elliott 4120: Absys, the Aberdeen System. A text is a conjunction of assertions, typed one at a time, and as each is accepted, “whatever processing can be done on the basis of data already present in the system is done.” In 1990 Elcock argued that Absys, “essentially completed in 1967”, had been a logic programming language in the full sense, some five years before the first Prolog, in Marseilles around 1972. The program was tied to the machine’s own code, the machine was retired in the mid-1970s and later dismantled, and no listing of the program is known to us. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the language from what its designers published, and to run every example they printed.

references.label: J. M. Foster, “Assertions: programs written without specifying unnecessary order”, Machine Intelligence 3, 1968
J. M. Foster and E. W. Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)
E. W. Elcock, “Absys: the first logic programming language”, J. Logic Programming 9, 1990

body.label: 02 / AN EQUATION THAT WAITS
body.text: Elcock describes equality in Absys as a process. Two lists: equate their heads and their tails. A variable and a term: the variable takes the term, and anything that was waiting on it is taken up again. Two different unknowns: the equation is “suspended” and associated with both, until one is known. Prolog would make the two variables one. Absys kept the equation, and waited. So a computation can end with equations still suspended, a “partially solved form”, and Elcock gives one: reversing [1,2,U] into [V|L] ends with L/[2,1] and the suspended equations U = X₃ and X₃ = V. The reconstruction prints that binding environment variable for variable, X₁/1, L₁/[2,U], X₂/2, L₂/[U], L₃/[], L/[2,1], with the same two equations suspended. Typing rev([5],[V]) afterwards wakes them: V becomes 5, then X₃, then U, and the environment is again Elcock’s, down to the names X₄ and L₄ of the variables the new assertion made. Elcock gives no rule for the subscripts; here each alternative of a procedure makes its variables new when it is chosen, a derivation numbers them as it goes, and that reproduces his.

references.label: Elcock 1990, pp. 10–13: the treatment of equality, and the reverse example

body.label: 03 / EVERY ALTERNATIVE AT ONCE
body.text: An or in Absys does not choose. It “is distributed through the goal conjunct”, Elcock writes, “essentially creating two new goals which can notionally be regarded as initiating parallel derivations”; in Foster and Elcock’s words of 1969, “unsatisfiable conjunctions disappear when unsatisfiability is detected”, and the conjunctions “in effect constitute parallel non-interacting programs.” Absys pursued them all: “all derivations continue to be incrementally elaborated until found unsatisfiable”, which Elcock calls a fair search rule. A procedure is a relation, so the one definition of append splits [1,2] three ways, or joins two lists, or finds what is missing. The 1969 paper, in its own quite different notation of begin and end, primes and [a;b], gives a problem with its answer: pick r, s and t from three lists so that r+s=t. The result “would be three distinct conjunctions … 1, 3, 4, 1, 1, 2 and 6, 1, 7 respectively.” The reconstruction gives those three, in that order. Where one alternative never ends and the next succeeds at once, the fair search finds the answer; a depth-first search, as Prolog’s is, never reaches it.

references.label: Foster and Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)

body.label: 04 / THE ORDER DOES NOT MATTER, EXCEPT FOR NOT
body.text: Foster and Elcock claimed that if data can be found to satisfy all the assertions, “these data are independent of the order in which the operations are performed.” The reconstruction can test that. A text of seven assertions, in which a procedure is applied before it is defined and a list reversed before its members are known, was accepted in all 5,040 orders. Every order gave the same result. In 1,260 of them some assertion ran past its budget of 20,000 steps until a later one cut it short. The cost is not independent of the order: it ran from 34 steps to 22,021. In a smaller text of three assertions, the same three answers of append cost 25 steps in one order and 22,868 in another, most of them an unbounded search stopped by the budget. Of what was tested, the one thing that makes the order matter is not. Here it is decided on the bindings as they stand, and Elcock concedes the point beneath that: “both Absys and PROLOG have the shortcoming that they do not use a safe computation rule.” not(X = 1) then X = 2 leaves no answer; X = 2 then not(X = 1) leaves X = 2. set is built the same way, and presumably behaves the same.

body.label: 05 / HIS OWN EXAMPLE PREFERS ONE ORDER
body.text: On the order in which a derivation takes its next step, Elcock says only that “Absys does not guarantee a particular order of processing of conjuncts”, and what else he says points two ways. An applied goal is “replaced by” the procedure’s body, which suggests the body takes the goal’s place; and “Absys used a fair computation rule”, of which taking every literal strictly in turn is one. His example of Absys-4’s set operator, from “a demonstration of Absys-4 circa 1968”, is printed as a definition only, with no query and no result, and the mem it uses is not defined; the inputs and mem here are ours. Run on [1,2,3,4] and [2,4,6], setdiff gives [1,3] if the body takes the goal’s place. Taken strictly in turn, it gives [1]: the not is decided before the recursion has given its variable a value. Strictly in turn but with not waiting for its variables, it gives [1,3] again, and Elcock mentions delays he does not describe. So the example favours the body in the goal’s place, without proving it. The reconstruction follows it, and keeps the other rules as options, so the difference can be run. Permuting the student example found a second gap: a not applied before a procedure it used was defined counted a derivation that was only waiting as a success. Elcock counts a derivation that ends with suspended equations between variables as a success because “the constraint is always satisfiable”; a waiting application has no such guarantee, so here a not that cannot be decided waits too, and all 120 orders of that text now agree.

body.label: 06 / THREE MISPRINTS
body.text: Elcock renders Clark’s student database in Absys, as a completion. As printed, one alternative of takes reads X - 'SMITH', C - 'C101', with minus signs for equals, and the procedure that asks who is not a maths major applies maths-course, where the one defined is math-course. Typed in as printed, the second leaves the query here waiting for ever for a procedure that is never defined; corrected, Brown, who takes C101 and not C301, is a non-maths-major and Smith is not. The application of append on page 9 has a third, [T₁ = [X₁|N₁]] where [1,2] = [X₁|N₁] is meant. The OCR of the paper garbles every program, so all of them were read from the page images.

The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Type assertions and step through them: each derivation, its bindings and its suspended equations, the tree of alternatives the ors made, and every step on the way.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: No Absys program text, listing or manual from Aberdeen is known to survive. This is the language as its designers described it, not the program they wrote; where they are silent, the choice made is listed as a decision.

No Prolog was run. What Prolog would do is from its standard behaviour, not from a comparison made here.

Everything was read and built by one coding agent in one day, from scans and OCR, and has not been checked by a person. A separate fact-check of this note against the papers, by another model, found three quotations, attributions and claims wrong and nine overstated; all are corrected.

record.title: Absys did not unify two unknowns. It waited.
record.dek: Absys, built at Aberdeen around 1967 and rebuilt here from its designers’ papers, prints the binding environments of Elcock’s examples variable for variable, suspended equations included. One of his examples also favours one order in which Absys may have taken its steps.
record.abstract: A note about reconstructing Absys, the language J. M. Foster, E. W. Elcock and their colleagues built for the Elliott 4120 at the University of Aberdeen, which Elcock argued in 1990 was the first logic programming language. No program text or listing of it is known to survive. With a coding agent, the language was rebuilt from three papers: Foster’s Assertions of 1968, extracts of Foster and Elcock’s introduction to Absys 1 of 1969, and Elcock’s retrospective of 1990, read from its page scans. An equation between two unknowns is not solved but suspended until one of them is known; an or splits the computation into derivations that are all pursued, fairly, until each fails or hibernates; and each assertion is accepted as it is typed. Run on the papers’ own examples, the reconstruction gives every result they print, the binding environments of the append and reverse examples variable for variable and Absys 1’s three triples in the paper’s order, and the expected answers for Clark’s students and for setdiff, whose results the paper does not print. Run on inputs chosen here, setdiff gives the right answer if each applied body takes the place of its literal, or if not waits for its variables; taking literals strictly in turn without such a delay, one fair rule among several, gives the wrong one. A paper of 1982, found after version 1.0 of this note, prints Absys’s list of relations awaiting elaboration step by step; the reconstruction prints every list it shows once two of its rules follow the paper, one of them against the paper’s own word “appended”.
record.lineage: FOSTER 1968 → FOSTER AND ELCOCK 1969 → ELCOCK 1990 → AGENT → THE MACHINE THE PAPERS DESCRIBE → THEIR EXAMPLES RUN

body.label: 01 / ASSERTIONS, NOT INSTRUCTIONS
body.text: In a paper given in 1967, Michael Foster, of the Computer Research Group at Aberdeen, described a system in which “the basic elements … are not instructions to do something, as are the statements of Algol, but assertions about the data, such as a=b or a+b=c.” His paper was called Assertions: Programs Written without Specifying Unnecessary Order. By 1968 the group had “a working on-line incremental compiler” for it on the university’s Elliott 4120: Absys, the Aberdeen System. A text is a conjunction of assertions, typed one at a time, and as each is accepted, “whatever processing can be done on the basis of data already present in the system is done.” In 1990 Elcock argued that Absys, “essentially completed in 1967”, had been a logic programming language in the full sense, some five years before the first Prolog, in Marseilles around 1972. The program was tied to the machine’s own code, the machine was retired in the mid-1970s and later dismantled, and no listing of the program is known to us. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the language from what its designers published, and to run every example they printed.

references.label: J. M. Foster, “Assertions: programs written without specifying unnecessary order”, Machine Intelligence 3, 1968
J. M. Foster and E. W. Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)
E. W. Elcock, “Absys: the first logic programming language”, J. Logic Programming 9, 1990

body.label: 02 / AN EQUATION THAT WAITS
body.text: Elcock describes equality in Absys as a process. Two lists: equate their heads and their tails. A variable and a term: the variable takes the term, and anything that was waiting on it is taken up again. Two different unknowns: the equation is “suspended” and associated with both, until one is known. Prolog would make the two variables one. Absys kept the equation, and waited. So a computation can end with equations still suspended, a “partially solved form”, and Elcock gives one: reversing [1,2,U] into [V|L] ends with L/[2,1] and the suspended equations U = X₃ and X₃ = V. The reconstruction prints that binding environment variable for variable, X₁/1, L₁/[2,U], X₂/2, L₂/[U], L₃/[], L/[2,1], with the same two equations suspended. Typing rev([5],[V]) afterwards wakes them: V becomes 5, then X₃, then U, and the environment is again Elcock’s, down to the names X₄ and L₄ of the variables the new assertion made. Elcock gives no rule for the subscripts; here each alternative of a procedure makes its variables new when it is chosen, a derivation numbers them as it goes, and that reproduces his.

references.label: Elcock 1990, pp. 10–13: the treatment of equality, and the reverse example

body.label: 03 / EVERY ALTERNATIVE AT ONCE
body.text: An or in Absys does not choose. It “is distributed through the goal conjunct”, Elcock writes, “essentially creating two new goals which can notionally be regarded as initiating parallel derivations”; in Foster and Elcock’s words of 1969, “unsatisfiable conjunctions disappear when unsatisfiability is detected”, and the conjunctions “in effect constitute parallel non-interacting programs.” Absys pursued them all: “all derivations continue to be incrementally elaborated until found unsatisfiable”, which Elcock calls a fair search rule. A procedure is a relation, so the one definition of append splits [1,2] three ways, or joins two lists, or finds what is missing. The 1969 paper, in its own quite different notation of begin and end, primes and [a;b], gives a problem with its answer: pick r, s and t from three lists so that r+s=t. The result “would be three distinct conjunctions … 1, 3, 4, 1, 1, 2 and 6, 1, 7 respectively.” The reconstruction gives those three, in that order. Where one alternative never ends and the next succeeds at once, the fair search finds the answer; a depth-first search, as Prolog’s is, never reaches it.

references.label: Foster and Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)

body.label: 04 / THE ORDER DOES NOT MATTER, EXCEPT FOR NOT
body.text: Foster and Elcock claimed that if data can be found to satisfy all the assertions, “these data are independent of the order in which the operations are performed.” The reconstruction can test that. A text of seven assertions, in which a procedure is applied before it is defined and a list reversed before its members are known, was accepted in all 5,040 orders. Every order gave the same result. In 1,260 of them some assertion ran past its budget of 20,000 steps until a later one cut it short. The cost is not independent of the order: it ran from 34 steps to 22,021. In a smaller text of three assertions, the same three answers of append cost 25 steps in one order and 22,868 in another, most of them an unbounded search stopped by the budget. Of what was tested, the one thing that makes the order matter is not. Here it is decided on the bindings as they stand, and Elcock concedes the point beneath that: “both Absys and PROLOG have the shortcoming that they do not use a safe computation rule.” not(X = 1) then X = 2 leaves no answer; X = 2 then not(X = 1) leaves X = 2. set is built the same way, and presumably behaves the same.

body.label: 05 / HIS OWN EXAMPLE PREFERS ONE ORDER
body.text: On the order in which a derivation takes its next step, Elcock says only that “Absys does not guarantee a particular order of processing of conjuncts”, and what else he says points two ways. An applied goal is “replaced by” the procedure’s body, which suggests the body takes the goal’s place; and “Absys used a fair computation rule”, of which taking every literal strictly in turn is one. His example of Absys-4’s set operator, from “a demonstration of Absys-4 circa 1968”, is printed as a definition only, with no query and no result, and the mem it uses is not defined; the inputs and mem here are ours. Run on [1,2,3,4] and [2,4,6], setdiff gives [1,3] if the body takes the goal’s place. Taken strictly in turn, it gives [1]: the not is decided before the recursion has given its variable a value. Strictly in turn but with not waiting for its variables, it gives [1,3] again, and Elcock mentions delays he does not describe. So the example favours the body in the goal’s place, without proving it. The reconstruction follows it, and keeps the other rules as options, so the difference can be run. Permuting the student example found a second gap: a not applied before a procedure it used was defined counted a derivation that was only waiting as a success. Elcock counts a derivation that ends with suspended equations between variables as a success because “the constraint is always satisfiable”; a waiting application has no such guarantee, so here a not that cannot be decided waits too, and all 120 orders of that text now agree.

body.label: 06 / THREE MISPRINTS
body.text: Elcock renders Clark’s student database in Absys, as a completion. As printed, one alternative of takes reads X - 'SMITH', C - 'C101', with minus signs for equals, and the procedure that asks who is not a maths major applies maths-course, where the one defined is math-course. Typed in as printed, the second leaves the query here waiting for ever for a procedure that is never defined; corrected, Brown, who takes C101 and not C301, is a non-maths-major and Smith is not. The application of append on page 9 has a third, [T₁ = [X₁|N₁]] where [1,2] = [X₁|N₁] is meant. The OCR of the paper garbles every program, so all of them were read from the page images.

body.label: 07 / THE LIST OF RELATIONS, 1982
body.text: In a short paper of 1982 comparing Absys with Prolog, found after version 1.0 of this note, Elcock walks through Absys’s “list of relations still to be elaborated” for u+v = 16 and w*u = v and u+10 = 12: the relations u’s binding returns, (2+v = 16; w*2 = v), then the list after v is bound, (2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14; w*2 = 14), then (7*2 = 14; 7*2 = 14). For the mechanism “in detail” it points to a paper of 1972 by Elcock, McGregor and Murray. The reconstruction returned a waiting relation only once, which cannot give his lists. It now returns one for each of its variables that is bound, and puts returned relations at the head of the list. So a relation goes back on the list for each of its variables that is bound, even after it has run: w*2 = 14 is there twice, and 2+14 = 16 is examined again and “found satisfied”. And the relations that come back go to the head of the list, although the paper says they are “appended”: appended to the end, the list after v is bound would read (w*2 = 14; 2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14), and the next relation examined would bind w instead of being found satisfied. Either way u is 2, v is 14 and w is 7. The same paper says the alternatives, “notionally” parallel, were “in practice … handled by appropriate differential record keeping and backtracking in a similar spirit to Prolog implementations”, where the retrospective says the search was fair; and it dates Absys “essentially completed in 1968”, where the retrospective has 1967. It also says where this kind of evaluation stops: a general set of linear equations needs “much more sophisticated aggregation and solution methods”. Here x + y = 10 and x − y = 4 leave both relations waiting, each for a second number.

references.label: E. W. Elcock, “Goal selection strategies in Horn clause programming”, Proceedings of the CSCSI, 1982, pp. 121–124

body.text: The interpreter runs in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Type assertions and step through them: each derivation, its bindings and its suspended equations, the tree of alternatives the ors made, and every step on the way.

record.title: A Q-system rule never replaced anything.
record.dek: Colmerauer’s Q-systems, the Montréal translation project’s rule language, rebuilt from his report of 1970. Sixteen rules analyse a French sentence into its tree; run the other way, they write its eighteen paraphrases into one graph that matches his printout.
record.abstract: A note about reconstructing the Q-systems, the rule language Alain Colmerauer designed at the Université de Montréal for the TAUM machine-translation project, in use from October 1969. No program text of it is known to survive. With a coding agent, the language was rebuilt from Colmerauer’s report of September 1970, read from its page scans. A Q-system rewrites a graph of strings, not a string: a rule adds a path beside every path it matches and replaces nothing, and the arrows it rewrote are removed only when no rule applies any more. So one graph holds every alternative, with the shared parts shared. Run on the report’s examples, the reconstruction gives every result the report prints, with two exceptions. Its French example runs both ways: the sixteen rules, inverted, analyse a sentence into its normalised tree, and as written they synthesise its eighteen paraphrases into one graph of nineteen vertices, which is the report’s printout line for line, vertex numbers and all; each of the eighteen analyses back to the one tree. The exceptions: the report’s rules for turning a tree into a string do not stop as printed, and the eighteen sentences of the last printout come out in exactly the reverse of the report’s order. And the rules for removing one string remove its neighbours too.
record.lineage: COLMERAUER 1970 → AGENT → THE MACHINE THE REPORT DESCRIBES → ITS EXAMPLES RUN → ITS PRINTOUT COMPARED

body.label: 01 / A GRAPH OF EVERY GROUPING
body.text: In October 1969 a program written in ALGOL by Alain Colmerauer was running on the CDC 6400 of the Université de Montréal. It ran his Q-systems, the rule language of TAUM, the university’s project to translate English into French by computer. In the project’s chain, his report says, an English sentence went through no fewer than fifteen Q-systems before it came out in French. The Computer History Museum’s Prolog archive says that Colmerauer considered the Q-systems the ancestor of Prolog. The report opens on the problem they were made for. To analyse a sentence you must try every partial grouping of its words, and to hold that multitude economically Colmerauer used a directed graph, each arrow carrying a tree. A Q-system is a set of rules that turns one such graph into another. No program text of the Q-systems is known to us. The report, Les systèmes-Q ou un formalisme pour analyser et synthétiser des phrases sur ordinateur, of September 1970, gives the whole grammar, the meaning of every construct and the printed results of its examples. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the language from it, and to run every example it prints.

references.label: A. Colmerauer, Les systèmes-Q, publication interne no 43, Université de Montréal, September 1970, pp. 4–5
Computer History Museum, History of Prolog: Université de Montréal

body.label: 02 / A RULE ADDS A PATH
body.text: Every path from the entry of the graph to its exit is one string, and a rule a1 + … + ap == b1 + … + bq. is applied to a path, not a string. For every path whose trees match its left side, the first phase adds a new path, carrying the right side, between the same two vertices. Nothing is replaced: “on ajoute donc au graphe le tout nouveau chemin”, so the old path and the new one sit side by side, and later rules match paths through either. This goes on until no rule applies to a path it has not been applied to. Only then does the second phase remove every arrow some rule was applied to, and after it every arrow no longer on a way from entry to exit. The example of the report’s section 8 recognises AⁿBⁿCⁿ in two rules. On A + A + A + B + B + B + C + C + C, the first phase grows nine arrows into nineteen: two A(1), one A(1,1), the same for B and C, and one S(1,1,1), exactly the arrows of the figure on page 29. The second phase leaves S(1,1,1). The report says the result of a phase that converges does not depend on the order in which the rules were applied. The rules of the report’s largest example were put in 32 orders (its last two phases have one rule each, so the orders differ in the first two); every order printed the same graphs. The printout is sorted, so this compares what was made, not the order it was made in. It follows from the definition: every rule is applied to every path, whatever the order.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 22: the two phases; pp. 27–29: the example of section 8 and its figure

body.label: 03 / ONE SYSTEM, BOTH WAYS
body.text: Colmerauer called reversibility one of the originalities of the Q-systems: practically the same system can describe a transformation and its inverse, analysis and synthesis. His last section shows it. Sixteen rules take a normalised sentence, a tree of verbs and their subjects and objects, to French: active or passive, each embedded clause as a clause or as a noun. -INV- exchanges the two sides of every rule. The treatment runs the system inverted, then as written. Inverted, it analyses RICHARD CONSTATE QUE LA DESTRUCTION DE BEAUCEVILLE PAR BENOIT ETONNE GAETANE into the tree drawn on page 36; along the way it makes 38 arrows of partial groupings and keeps one. As written, it synthesises from that tree every paraphrase: eighteen sentences in one graph of nineteen vertices and 139 arrows, where written out one to a line they take 282. Pages 38 to 40 print that graph as 35 lines. The reconstruction prints the same 35 lines, with Colmerauer’s vertex numbers, and page 42 draws the same graph. Then each of the eighteen sentences was put back through the inverted system. Every one gives the one tree.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 4: reversibility; pp. 35–42: the paraphrase treatment and its results

body.label: 04 / THE RULES OF PAGE 30 DO NOT STOP
body.text: Page 30 gives two rules to take a tree apart into a “structured” string: A*(U*) == [(A*) + ](U*) / U* ≠ -NUL-. and ](I*,U*) == I* + ](U*). Applied to A(B,C(A,E(F))), the report says, they would produce [(A) + B + [(C) + A + [(E) + F + ] + ] + ]. Applied as the report’s own section 7 defines, they never stop. The [(A) they make is itself a tree of the form A*(U*), with [ for A* and A for U*, and nothing stops the first rule matching it again: it becomes [([) + ](A), then [([) + ]([), and so on. Every path is matched, including the new ones, so a rule that matches its own output goes on for ever. With one condition the report does not have, that A* is neither [ nor ], they produce exactly the printed string. The inverse pair, on the same page, works as printed, because its condition already keeps the brackets out. So as printed these rules run only one way.

body.label: 05 / A RULE REWRITES ARROWS, NOT STRINGS
body.text: The same page gives three rules to delete from a graph “tout chemin portant une chaîne donnée”, every path carrying a given string, here LE + FAIT + QUE + LE + FAIT + QUE. The first rewrites it as /CUL + /DE + /SAC, and the other two add /CULDE and /DESAC beside the pairs they match. When the rewritten arrows are removed, /CULDE and /DESAC are left leading nowhere, and “à la fin de cette dernière phase il ne reste plus rien”, page 31 says. That is what happens. But the second phase removes arrows, and an arrow can belong to many strings. Given a graph that carries LE + FAIT + QUE + LE + FAIT + QUE and also LE + FAIT + QUE + BENOIT, sharing their first three arrows, the rules remove both: nothing is left of either. A shared prefix belongs to every string through it, and it cannot be taken from one and left to the others. The same holds for every rule, not only these: an arrow some rule used is gone from every string that ran through it. In analysis that is usually harmless, because every string through such an arrow was rewritten too.

body.label: 06 / AMBIGUITY COSTS NOTHING
body.text: The French grammar of the last section is recursive, and allows infinitely many sentences. Every normalised sentence with at most one embedded clause was synthesised, with its three verbs and four names: 8,112 trees give 131,424 different sentences, and no sentence comes from two trees. Then every one of the 131,424 was put back through the inverted system, and each gives back its one tree. The report’s own example has two embedded clauses, so it is not among them; its eighteen paraphrases analyse back too. The many groupings of the introduction exist only during the first phase, as partial analyses that the second throws away. What a graph does with a sentence that is ambiguous needed a grammar of our own, not the report’s. In it AVEC LE TELESCOPE can go with the seeing or with the man. Analysed, JEAN VOIT L HOMME AVEC LE TELESCOPE gives one graph with both readings, as two arrows between the same two vertices. Nothing chooses between them; a later phase can work on both at once.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 35: the normalised sentences; p. 4: the combinatorial problem

body.label: 07 / THE ORDER THAT DOES NOT MATCH
body.text: Every computation the report gives a result for comes out as it says, with two exceptions: the rules of page 30, above, and this one. The last two phases of the paraphrase treatment pack each sentence into one tree and unpack it again, so that each of the eighteen is printed on a line of its own, from -01- to -02-. Pages 40 and 41 print them in one order. The reconstruction prints the same eighteen lines in exactly the reverse order. The report does not say how its program ordered the paths leaving a vertex. At all fourteen vertices of the synthesis graph with more than one path leaving them, the printed paths are in ascending order of their trees, and that order reproduces pages 38 to 40; the same order puts pages 40 and 41 backwards. No simple order of making or keeping arrows was found that fits both pages. The order was most likely a side effect of the lists of the lost program. The test for pages 40 and 41 checks the reversal, so that it stays a recorded difference and not a hidden one.

The Q-systems run in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Choose a treatment and step through a phase one rule application at a time: the path each rule matched, the path it added beside it, then what the second phase removes and what is left, drawn as the report draws its figure on page 29.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: No program text of the Q-systems is known to us. This is the formalism as Colmerauer’s report describes it, not the program he wrote; where the report is silent, the choice made is listed as a decision.

The scan of the report is missing printed page 23, which most likely held a first, simplified example. The system of section 8 is therefore called an example here, not the first. A 1972 TAUM printout was used only for the form of the output.
The order in which paths are printed is a decision fitted to pages 38 to 40, and it puts pages 40 and 41 in reverse. The form of the details printed for -DET- is our own.

The two-readings grammar is ours, not the report’s. The TAUM grammars, the earliest large Q-system programs, have not been seen, nor has METEO, written later in Q-systems, nor any later version of the formalism.
Everything was read and built by one coding agent, from scans, and has not been checked by a person. No literature search was made, so nothing here is claimed as new.

body.text: What did the TAUM grammars look like?
body.detail: Colmerauer and Roussel name the TAUM grammars written in Q-systems: English morphology, the analysis of English, transfer, French synthesis and French morphology. TAUM 71, edited by Colmerauer in January 1971, is listed by the Computer History Museum as holding the English morphology, and may hold the others. They are the earliest large Q-system programs. Run here, they would test the decisions made from a 45-page report, and show what the graph of every grouping cost on real English.

record.title: Absys did not unify two unknowns. It waited.
record.dek: Absys, built at Aberdeen around 1967 and rebuilt here from its designers’ papers, prints the binding environments of Elcock’s examples variable for variable, suspended equations included. One of his examples also favours one order in which Absys may have taken its steps.
record.abstract: A note about reconstructing Absys, the language J. M. Foster, E. W. Elcock and their colleagues built for the Elliott 4120 at the University of Aberdeen, which Elcock argued in 1990 was the first logic programming language. No program text or listing of it is known to survive. With a coding agent, the language was rebuilt from three papers: Foster’s Assertions of 1968, extracts of Foster and Elcock’s introduction to Absys 1 of 1969, and Elcock’s retrospective of 1990, read from its page scans. An equation between two unknowns is not solved but suspended until one of them is known; an or splits the computation into derivations that are all pursued, fairly, until each fails or hibernates; and each assertion is accepted as it is typed. Run on the papers’ own examples, the reconstruction gives every result they print, the binding environments of the append and reverse examples variable for variable and Absys 1’s three triples in the paper’s order, and the expected answers for Clark’s students and for setdiff, whose results the paper does not print. Run on inputs chosen here, setdiff gives the right answer if each applied body takes the place of its literal, or if not waits for its variables; taking literals strictly in turn without such a delay, one fair rule among several, gives the wrong one. A paper of 1982, found after version 1.0 of this note, prints Absys’s list of relations awaiting elaboration step by step; the reconstruction prints every list it shows once two of its rules follow the paper, one of them against the paper’s own word “appended”. That settles the order only if the lists were copied from a run. Run on SWI-Prolog, the same programs give the same answers where both answer, and Absys’s session, assertions fed one at a time into one open computation, can be rebuilt there from engines and coroutines, with a layer written here to make a procedure applied before its definition wait.
record.lineage: FOSTER 1968 → FOSTER AND ELCOCK 1969 → ELCOCK 1990 → AGENT → THE MACHINE THE PAPERS DESCRIBE → THEIR EXAMPLES RUN

body.label: 01 / ASSERTIONS, NOT INSTRUCTIONS
body.text: In a paper given in 1967, Michael Foster, of the Computer Research Group at Aberdeen, described a system in which “the basic elements … are not instructions to do something, as are the statements of Algol, but assertions about the data, such as a=b or a+b=c.” His paper was called Assertions: Programs Written without Specifying Unnecessary Order. By 1968 the group had “a working on-line incremental compiler” for it on the university’s Elliott 4120: Absys, the Aberdeen System. A text is a conjunction of assertions, typed one at a time, and as each is accepted, “whatever processing can be done on the basis of data already present in the system is done.” In 1990 Elcock argued that Absys, “essentially completed in 1967”, had been a logic programming language in the full sense, some five years before the first Prolog, in Marseilles around 1972. The program was tied to the machine’s own code, the machine was retired in the mid-1970s and later dismantled, and no listing of the program is known to us. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the language from what its designers published, and to run every example they printed.

references.label: J. M. Foster, “Assertions: programs written without specifying unnecessary order”, Machine Intelligence 3, 1968
J. M. Foster and E. W. Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)
E. W. Elcock, “Absys: the first logic programming language”, J. Logic Programming 9, 1990

body.label: 02 / AN EQUATION THAT WAITS
body.text: Elcock describes equality in Absys as a process. Two lists: equate their heads and their tails. A variable and a term: the variable takes the term, and anything that was waiting on it is taken up again. Two different unknowns: the equation is “suspended” and associated with both, until one is known. Prolog would make the two variables one. Absys kept the equation, and waited. So a computation can end with equations still suspended, a “partially solved form”, and Elcock gives one: reversing [1,2,U] into [V|L] ends with L/[2,1] and the suspended equations U = X₃ and X₃ = V. The reconstruction prints that binding environment variable for variable, X₁/1, L₁/[2,U], X₂/2, L₂/[U], L₃/[], L/[2,1], with the same two equations suspended. Typing rev([5],[V]) afterwards wakes them: V becomes 5, then X₃, then U, and the environment is again Elcock’s, down to the names X₄ and L₄ of the variables the new assertion made. Elcock gives no rule for the subscripts; here each alternative of a procedure makes its variables new when it is chosen, a derivation numbers them as it goes, and that reproduces his.

references.label: Elcock 1990, pp. 10–13: the treatment of equality, and the reverse example

body.label: 03 / EVERY ALTERNATIVE AT ONCE
body.text: An or in Absys does not choose. It “is distributed through the goal conjunct”, Elcock writes, “essentially creating two new goals which can notionally be regarded as initiating parallel derivations”; in Foster and Elcock’s words of 1969, “unsatisfiable conjunctions disappear when unsatisfiability is detected”, and the conjunctions “in effect constitute parallel non-interacting programs.” Absys pursued them all: “all derivations continue to be incrementally elaborated until found unsatisfiable”, which Elcock calls a fair search rule. A procedure is a relation, so the one definition of append splits [1,2] three ways, or joins two lists, or finds what is missing. The 1969 paper, in its own quite different notation of begin and end, primes and [a;b], gives a problem with its answer: pick r, s and t from three lists so that r+s=t. The result “would be three distinct conjunctions … 1, 3, 4, 1, 1, 2 and 6, 1, 7 respectively.” The reconstruction gives those three, in that order. Where one alternative never ends and the next succeeds at once, the fair search finds the answer; a depth-first search, as Prolog’s is, never reaches it.

references.label: Foster and Elcock, “Absys 1: an incremental compiler for assertions”, Machine Intelligence 4, 1969 (extracts)

body.label: 04 / THE ORDER DOES NOT MATTER, EXCEPT FOR NOT
body.text: Foster and Elcock claimed that if data can be found to satisfy all the assertions, “these data are independent of the order in which the operations are performed.” The reconstruction can test that. A text of seven assertions, in which a procedure is applied before it is defined and a list reversed before its members are known, was accepted in all 5,040 orders. Every order gave the same result. In 1,260 of them some assertion ran past its budget of 20,000 steps until a later one cut it short. The cost is not independent of the order: it ran from 34 steps to 22,021. In a smaller text of three assertions, the same three answers of append cost 25 steps in one order and 22,868 in another, most of them an unbounded search stopped by the budget. Of what was tested, the one thing that makes the order matter is not. Here it is decided on the bindings as they stand, and Elcock concedes the point beneath that: “both Absys and PROLOG have the shortcoming that they do not use a safe computation rule.” not(X = 1) then X = 2 leaves no answer; X = 2 then not(X = 1) leaves X = 2. set is built the same way, and presumably behaves the same.

body.label: 05 / HIS OWN EXAMPLE PREFERS ONE ORDER
body.text: On the order in which a derivation takes its next step, Elcock says only that “Absys does not guarantee a particular order of processing of conjuncts”, and what else he says points two ways. An applied goal is “replaced by” the procedure’s body, which suggests the body takes the goal’s place; and “Absys used a fair computation rule”, of which taking every literal strictly in turn is one. His example of Absys-4’s set operator, from “a demonstration of Absys-4 circa 1968”, is printed as a definition only, with no query and no result, and the mem it uses is not defined; the inputs and mem here are ours. Run on [1,2,3,4] and [2,4,6], setdiff gives [1,3] if the body takes the goal’s place. Taken strictly in turn, it gives [1]: the not is decided before the recursion has given its variable a value. Strictly in turn but with not waiting for its variables, it gives [1,3] again, and Elcock mentions delays he does not describe. So the example favours the body in the goal’s place, without proving it. The reconstruction follows it, and keeps the other rules as options, so the difference can be run. Permuting the student example found a second gap: a not applied before a procedure it used was defined counted a derivation that was only waiting as a success. Elcock counts a derivation that ends with suspended equations between variables as a success because “the constraint is always satisfiable”; a waiting application has no such guarantee, so here a not that cannot be decided waits too, and all 120 orders of that text now agree.

body.label: 06 / THREE MISPRINTS
body.text: Elcock renders Clark’s student database in Absys, as a completion. As printed, one alternative of takes reads X - 'SMITH', C - 'C101', with minus signs for equals, and the procedure that asks who is not a maths major applies maths-course, where the one defined is math-course. Typed in as printed, the second leaves the query here waiting for ever for a procedure that is never defined; corrected, Brown, who takes C101 and not C301, is a non-maths-major and Smith is not. The application of append on page 9 has a third, [T₁ = [X₁|N₁]] where [1,2] = [X₁|N₁] is meant. The OCR of the paper garbles every program, so all of them were read from the page images.

body.label: 07 / THE LIST OF RELATIONS, 1982
body.text: In a short paper of 1982 comparing Absys with Prolog, found after version 1.0 of this note, Elcock walks through Absys’s “list of relations still to be elaborated” for u+v = 16 and w*u = v and u+10 = 12: the relations u’s binding returns, (2+v = 16; w*2 = v), then the list after v is bound, (2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14; w*2 = 14), then (7*2 = 14; 7*2 = 14). For the mechanism “in detail” it points to a paper of 1972 by Elcock, McGregor and Murray. The reconstruction returned a waiting relation only once, which cannot give his lists. It now returns one for each of its variables that is bound, and puts returned relations at the head of the list. So a relation goes back on the list for each of its variables that is bound, even after it has run: w*2 = 14 is there twice, and 2+14 = 16 is examined again and “found satisfied”. And the relations that come back go to the head of the list, although the paper says they are “appended”: appended to the end, the list after v is bound would read (w*2 = 14; 2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14), and the next relation examined would bind w instead of being found satisfied. Either way u is 2, v is 14 and w is 7. The same paper says the alternatives, “notionally” parallel, were “in practice … handled by appropriate differential record keeping and backtracking in a similar spirit to Prolog implementations”, where the retrospective says the search was fair; and it dates Absys “essentially completed in 1968”, where the retrospective has 1967. It also says where this kind of evaluation stops: a general set of linear equations needs “much more sophisticated aggregation and solution methods”. Here x + y = 10 and x − y = 4 leave both relations waiting, each for a second number.

references.label: E. W. Elcock, “Goal selection strategies in Horn clause programming”, Proceedings of the CSCSI, 1982, pp. 121–124

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: No Absys program text, listing or manual from Aberdeen is known to survive. This is the language as its designers described it, not the program they wrote; where they are silent, the choice made is listed as a decision.

Elcock’s retrospective, the main source, describes “a subset of the language Absys-4” in syntax that takes “some slight liberties” with the original. The 1969 notation was read only from OCR extracts of that paper; its last pages, and Elcock and Gray’s fuller description of 1988, have not been seen.

The order in which a derivation takes its next step is chosen on the evidence of one published example, setdiff, run on inputs chosen here; a fair rule with delayed negation would also run it correctly. The rule that a not or set waits when it cannot be decided was added here, after permuting the texts showed it was needed; it is not in the papers.

Elcock’s two accounts disagree about the search: fair in 1990, backtracking in 1982. Nothing printed in either tells the two apart, so the fair search is kept, and the backtracking reading is an option. The rule that returned relations go to the head of the list follows the lists the 1982 paper prints, against the word it uses. That is evidence from a printed trace, not proof of what the program did: if Elcock wrote the lists out by hand, the word may be the better witness.
The arithmetic of the 1969 notation follows the paper’s examples and Foster’s “pass sets” of 1968; the retrospective shows none.

The comparison with Prolog was run on SWI-Prolog 11.0.1 alone, with programs written here; no Prolog of the 1970s was run. Where both answer, the answers agree; Prolog’s left-to-right rule loses the three cases above that Absys’s order of elaboration gets through, and coroutines or CLP(FD) get them back. Version 1.1 implied that Prolog has nothing like Absys’s incremental session. That was wrong. A SWI-Prolog engine fed one assertion at a time keeps its bindings, choice points and waiting coroutines between them, and reproduces the reverse example and the 1982 relations posted one by one. What it lacks is a wait for a procedure not yet defined, which is an error there; a dozen lines written here supply it. So Prolog can be made to work this way; in Absys it was the ordinary way a program ran. Both comparisons run in the repository’s CI on a pinned SWI-Prolog.

Everything was read and built by one coding agent in one day, from scans and OCR, and has not been checked by a person. Nothing here is claimed as new: Elcock made the case himself, and the history is told elsewhere. A separate fact-check of this note against the papers, by another model, found three quotations, attributions and claims wrong and nine overstated; all are corrected.
body.principle: A language that survives only as a description can be rebuilt as that description; where the description is silent, its own examples are the best witness.

body.text: What did the rest of Absys-4 look like?
body.detail: Elcock says the full language, described in a technical report of 1988 with P. M. D. Gray, had higher-order features and simple control mechanisms, and that Absys had user-declared delays. That report, the end of the 1969 paper, and Elcock’s Problem Solving Compilers of 1971, with its “more complex examples”, would test the decisions made here.

record.title: A Q-system rule never replaced anything.
record.dek: Colmerauer’s Q-systems, the Montréal translation project’s rule language, rebuilt from his report of 1970. Sixteen rules analyse a French sentence into its tree; run the other way, they write its eighteen paraphrases into one graph that matches his printout.
record.abstract: A note about reconstructing the Q-systems, the rule language Alain Colmerauer designed at the Université de Montréal for the TAUM machine-translation project, in use from October 1969. No program text of it is known to survive. With a coding agent, the language was rebuilt from Colmerauer’s report of September 1970, read from its page scans. A Q-system rewrites a graph of strings, not a string: a rule adds a path beside every path it matches and replaces nothing, and the arrows it rewrote are removed only when no rule applies any more. So one graph holds every alternative, with the shared parts shared. Run on the report’s examples, the reconstruction gives every result the report prints, with two exceptions. Its French example runs both ways: the sixteen rules, inverted, analyse a sentence into its normalised tree, and as written they synthesise its eighteen paraphrases into one graph of nineteen vertices, which is the report’s printout line for line, vertex numbers and all; each of the eighteen analyses back to the one tree. The exceptions: the report’s rules for turning a tree into a string do not stop as printed, and the eighteen sentences of the last printout come out in exactly the reverse of the report’s order. And the rules for removing one string remove its neighbours too.
record.lineage: COLMERAUER 1970 → AGENT → THE MACHINE THE REPORT DESCRIBES → ITS EXAMPLES RUN → ITS PRINTOUT COMPARED

body.label: 01 / A GRAPH OF EVERY GROUPING
body.text: In October 1969 a program written in ALGOL by Alain Colmerauer was running on the CDC 6400 of the Université de Montréal. It ran his Q-systems, the rule language of TAUM, the university’s project to translate English into French by computer. In the project’s chain, his report says, an English sentence went through no fewer than fifteen Q-systems before it came out in French. The Computer History Museum’s Prolog archive says that Colmerauer considered the Q-systems the ancestor of Prolog. The report opens on the problem they were made for. To analyse a sentence you must try every partial grouping of its words, and to hold that multitude economically Colmerauer used a directed graph, each arrow carrying a tree. A Q-system is a set of rules that turns one such graph into another. No program text of the Q-systems is known to us. The report, Les systèmes-Q ou un formalisme pour analyser et synthétiser des phrases sur ordinateur, of September 1970, gives the whole grammar, the meaning of every construct and the printed results of its examples. I asked a coding agent to rebuild the language from it, and to run every example it prints.

references.label: A. Colmerauer, Les systèmes-Q, publication interne no 43, Université de Montréal, September 1970, pp. 4–5
Computer History Museum, History of Prolog: Université de Montréal

body.label: 02 / A RULE ADDS A PATH
body.text: Every path from the entry of the graph to its exit is one string, and a rule a1 + … + ap == b1 + … + bq. is applied to a path, not a string. For every path whose trees match its left side, the first phase adds a new path, carrying the right side, between the same two vertices. Nothing is replaced: “on ajoute donc au graphe le tout nouveau chemin”, so the old path and the new one sit side by side, and later rules match paths through either. This goes on until no rule applies to a path it has not been applied to. Only then does the second phase remove every arrow some rule was applied to, and after it every arrow no longer on a way from entry to exit. The example of the report’s section 8 recognises AⁿBⁿCⁿ in two rules. On A + A + A + B + B + B + C + C + C, the first phase grows nine arrows into nineteen: two A(1), one A(1,1), the same for B and C, and one S(1,1,1), exactly the arrows of the figure on page 29. The second phase leaves S(1,1,1). The report says the result of a phase that converges does not depend on the order in which the rules were applied. The rules of the report’s largest example were put in 32 orders (its last two phases have one rule each, so the orders differ in the first two); every order printed the same graphs. The printout is sorted, so this compares what was made, not the order it was made in. It follows from the definition: every rule is applied to every path, whatever the order.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 22: the two phases; pp. 27–29: the example of section 8 and its figure

body.label: 03 / ONE SYSTEM, BOTH WAYS
body.text: Colmerauer called reversibility one of the originalities of the Q-systems: practically the same system can describe a transformation and its inverse, analysis and synthesis. His last section shows it. Sixteen rules take a normalised sentence, a tree of verbs and their subjects and objects, to French: active or passive, each embedded clause as a clause or as a noun. -INV- exchanges the two sides of every rule. The treatment runs the system inverted, then as written. Inverted, it analyses RICHARD CONSTATE QUE LA DESTRUCTION DE BEAUCEVILLE PAR BENOIT ETONNE GAETANE into the tree drawn on page 36; along the way it makes 38 arrows of partial groupings and keeps one. As written, it synthesises from that tree every paraphrase: eighteen sentences in one graph of nineteen vertices and 139 arrows, where written out one to a line they take 282. Pages 38 to 40 print that graph as 35 lines. The reconstruction prints the same 35 lines, with Colmerauer’s vertex numbers, and page 42 draws the same graph. Then each of the eighteen sentences was put back through the inverted system. Every one gives the one tree.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 4: reversibility; pp. 35–42: the paraphrase treatment and its results

body.label: 04 / THE RULES OF PAGE 30 DO NOT STOP
body.text: Page 30 gives two rules to take a tree apart into a “structured” string: A*(U*) == [(A*) + ](U*) / U* ≠ -NUL-. and ](I*,U*) == I* + ](U*). Applied to A(B,C(A,E(F))), the report says, they would produce [(A) + B + [(C) + A + [(E) + F + ] + ] + ]. Applied as the report’s own section 7 defines, they never stop. The [(A) they make is itself a tree of the form A*(U*), with [ for A* and A for U*, and nothing stops the first rule matching it again: it becomes [([) + ](A), then [([) + ]([), and so on. Every path is matched, including the new ones, so a rule that matches its own output goes on for ever. With one condition the report does not have, that A* is neither [ nor ], they produce exactly the printed string. The inverse pair, on the same page, works as printed, because its condition already keeps the brackets out. So as printed these rules run only one way.

body.label: 05 / A RULE REWRITES ARROWS, NOT STRINGS
body.text: The same page gives three rules to delete from a graph “tout chemin portant une chaîne donnée”, every path carrying a given string, here LE + FAIT + QUE + LE + FAIT + QUE. The first rewrites it as /CUL + /DE + /SAC, and the other two add /CULDE and /DESAC beside the pairs they match. When the rewritten arrows are removed, /CULDE and /DESAC are left leading nowhere, and “à la fin de cette dernière phase il ne reste plus rien”, page 31 says. That is what happens. But the second phase removes arrows, and an arrow can belong to many strings. Given a graph that carries LE + FAIT + QUE + LE + FAIT + QUE and also LE + FAIT + QUE + BENOIT, sharing their first three arrows, the rules remove both: nothing is left of either. A shared prefix belongs to every string through it, and it cannot be taken from one and left to the others. The same holds for every rule, not only these: an arrow some rule used is gone from every string that ran through it. In analysis that is usually harmless, because every string through such an arrow was rewritten too.

body.label: 06 / AMBIGUITY COSTS NOTHING
body.text: The French grammar of the last section is recursive, and allows infinitely many sentences. Every normalised sentence with at most one level of embedding, a clause in either argument but none inside another, was synthesised, with its three verbs and four names: 8,112 trees give 131,424 different sentences, and no sentence comes from two trees. Then every one of the 131,424 was put back through the inverted system, and each gives back its one tree. The report’s own example has a clause inside a clause, two levels of embedding, so it is not among them; its eighteen paraphrases analyse back too. The many groupings of the introduction exist only during the first phase, as partial analyses that the second throws away. What a graph does with a sentence that is ambiguous needed a grammar of our own, not the report’s. In it AVEC LE TELESCOPE can go with the seeing or with the man. Analysed, JEAN VOIT L HOMME AVEC LE TELESCOPE gives one graph with both readings, as two arrows between the same two vertices. Nothing chooses between them; a later phase can work on both at once.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 35: the normalised sentences; p. 4: the combinatorial problem

body.label: 07 / THE ORDER THAT DOES NOT MATCH
body.text: Every computation the report gives a result for comes out as it says, with two exceptions: the rules of page 30, above, and this one. The last two phases of the paraphrase treatment pack each sentence into one tree and unpack it again, so that each of the eighteen is printed on a line of its own, from -01- to -02-. Pages 40 and 41 print them in one order. The reconstruction prints the same eighteen lines in exactly the reverse order. The report does not say how its program ordered the paths leaving a vertex. At all fourteen vertices of the synthesis graph with more than one path leaving them, the printed paths are in ascending order of their trees, and that order reproduces pages 38 to 40; the same order puts pages 40 and 41 backwards. No simple order of making or keeping arrows was found that fits both pages. The order was most likely a side effect of the lists of the lost program. The test for pages 40 and 41 checks the reversal, so that it stays a recorded difference and not a hidden one.

The Q-systems run in the browser, compiled from the same Rust source as the command-line version. Choose a treatment and step through a phase one rule application at a time: the path each rule matched, the path it added beside it, then what the second phase removes and what is left, drawn as the report draws its figure on page 29.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: No program text of the Q-systems is known to us. This is the formalism as Colmerauer’s report describes it, not the program he wrote; where the report is silent, the choice made is listed as a decision.

The scan of the report is missing printed page 23, which most likely held a first, simplified example. The system of section 8 is therefore called an example here, not the first. A 1972 TAUM printout was used only for the form of the output.
The order in which paths are printed is a decision fitted to pages 38 to 40, and it puts pages 40 and 41 in reverse. The form of the details printed for -DET- is our own.

The two-readings grammar is ours, not the report’s. The TAUM grammars, the earliest large Q-system programs, have not been seen, nor has METEO, written later in Q-systems, nor any later version of the formalism.
Everything was read and built by one coding agent, from scans, and has not been checked by a person. No literature search was made, so nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: A language that survives only as a description can be rebuilt as that description; its own printed results are the test, including the one that does not match.

body.text: What did the TAUM grammars look like?
body.detail: Colmerauer and Roussel name the TAUM grammars written in Q-systems: English morphology, the analysis of English, transfer, French synthesis and French morphology. TAUM 71, edited by Colmerauer in January 1971, is listed by the Computer History Museum as holding the English morphology, and may hold the others. They are the earliest large Q-system programs. Run here, they would test the decisions made from a 45-page report, and show what the graph of every grouping cost on real English.

record.title: A Q-system can hold a trillion strings, but never sees two become one.
record.dek: Colmerauer’s Q-systems, rebuilt from his report of 1970, measured. One graph holds 2⁴⁰ strings in 80 arrows, and a rule can work on all of them at once. A result that comes out the same along many paths is made once for each path.
record.abstract: A second note on the Q-systems, Alain Colmerauer’s rule language of 1969 for the TAUM translation project, reconstructed with a coding agent from his report of 1970. The first note checked the reconstruction against every result the report prints. This one measures the machine on graphs built to test it. Forty independent choices give 1,099,511,627,776 strings in 80 arrows, and a rule that looks at one or two words at a time works on all of them in 80 applications or fewer. So does a rule that fans one word out into two, which is how the report’s grammar writes 9,565,938 French sentences in 2,760 arrows. But a result carried along a string is made once for every path that reaches it. The parity of twelve choices has two possible values and costs 8,190 applications, exactly what writing each of the 4,096 strings out as a tree costs. The report adds a brand-new path for every application and says nothing of merging, so read literally two equal arrows are kept; and no rule can merge them, because a rule matches one path and two alternatives are never on one path. A variant of the machine that merges them, kept apart from the historical one, does parity in 46 applications and can still count every derivation, but it changes what some rules mean. The second phase, which removes every arrow a rule used, removes strings no rule touched; purifying by strings instead keeps them, but breaks the report’s own analysis and its recipe for deleting a string. Whether or not Colmerauer saw that loss, his systems depend on it: it is what makes an analysis return only complete analyses.
record.lineage: THE RECONSTRUCTED MACHINE → GRAPHS BUILT TO TEST IT → WHAT IT COSTS → WHAT IT LOSES → A VARIANT, KEPT APART

body.label: 01 / A TRILLION STRINGS IN 80 ARROWS
body.text: Colmerauer made the Q-systems to hold every partial grouping of a sentence at once, economically, in one graph: each path from its entry to its exit carries one string, and paths that share words share arrows. The first note rebuilt the machine from his report of 1970 and checked it against every result the report prints. This note asks what the machine can do with the economy. Take n independent choices between A and B: n + 1 vertices with two arrows between each pair, carrying 2ⁿ strings. Forty choices carry 1,099,511,627,776 strings in 80 arrows. The rules A == X. and B == Y. rewrite every one of them in 80 applications, and the graph after has 80 arrows and 2⁴⁰ strings. A rule matches paths, and here there are only 80 paths of one arrow. A rule that reads two words, A + B == C., applies 39 times. Fanning out costs as little: A == X. and A == Y. on one string of forty As give 2⁴⁰ strings in 80 arrows. This is how the report’s grammar works. Synthesising a sentence with fourteen embedded clauses, three levels deep on both sides, writes its 9,565,938 paraphrases into 2,760 arrows in 3,108 applications. Every sentence tried, 500 walks through that graph, analysed back to its one tree.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 4: the economy of the graph; p. 35: the grammar

body.label: 02 / TWO RESULTS, 8,190 APPLICATIONS
body.text: Now carry something along the string. Put an arrow S before twelve choices, and six rules that keep the parity of the number of As: S + A == O., E + A == O., O + A == E., and so on. There are two possible results, and the phase makes 8,190 arrows to reach them, one for every prefix of every string: 2¹³ − 2. Of those, 8,166 repeat an arrow already made, with the same two ends and the same tree. The graph after holds 4,096 arrows, each O or E, from the entry to the exit. Packing each whole string into one tree, P(A,B,B,…), whose 4,096 results really are all different, costs exactly the same, 8,190. The cost is set by the number of derivations, not by the number of results. That is the report’s definition read literally. Each application adds “le tout nouveau chemin”, a brand-new path, and the report says nothing of merging one with an equal arrow already there, so equal arrows are kept. And no rule can merge them. A rule’s left side matches one path, and two alternatives never lie on one path: a rule never sees both. Composing a relation along seven facts in a row, R(A*,B*) + R(B*,C*) == R(A*,C*)., makes the one fact R(A,H) 132 times, once for each way of bracketing the chain. The graph shares what is the same before a rule. It cannot share what becomes the same after one. None of the report’s own examples ever makes two equal arrows, so its printed results cannot say whether the lost program merged them.

references.label: Colmerauer 1970, p. 22: “on ajoute donc au graphe le tout nouveau chemin”

body.label: 03 / A MACHINE THAT MERGES
body.text: What would merging buy? A second machine, kept apart from the historical one in the repository, reuses an equal arrow, or an equal path the phase has already made, instead of adding another. With its merging turned off, it gives the historical machine’s graphs and application counts on every example of the report whose phases stop, and a test checks that. Merged, parity takes 46 applications instead of 8,190, and leaves two arrows, O and E. Composing the seven facts takes 56 instead of 294, and leaves R(A,H) once. Packing does not change, because its results really are all different. A third setting merges in the same way but records every application that made each arrow. From those records the number of derivations can still be counted, 4,096 for parity and 132 for the facts, without the copies. The count is what is kept, not everything: the order the copies would have been made in, the separate arrows and vertices each would have had, and the 8,190 applications a -DET- listing would show are gone. It is the same idea as the shared forests of later chart parsers. On every one of those examples the merged machine prints exactly what the historical one prints; that is a result about those examples, not about every Q-system that stops. But merging is not harmless. Under the report’s definition A == A. never stops: the arrow it adds is a new path it applies to. Merged, its one application adds nothing, finds the data’s own arrow, and the second phase removes that arrow as rewritten, leaving an empty graph. Others behave the same, A + B == A + B. and A == X. X == A. among them: each gives back an arrow equal to one it read, never stops under the report’s definition, and leaves an empty graph when merged. In every change found, the report’s result was undefined to begin with.

body.label: 04 / A RULE TAKES ITS NEIGHBOURS
body.text: The second phase removes every arrow of every path a rule was applied to, and then every arrow left leading nowhere. The first note found that the report’s recipe for deleting one string deletes its neighbours too. Measured on the choices, the effect is complete. A + B == C. on ten choices leaves two strings, of 1,024. Eleven of the 1,024 have no A + B in them, so the rule applied to none of them, and none of the eleven survives. Every arrow except the first B and the last A is on some path the rule was applied to. On three choices, A + A + A has no A + B, but its first arrow is also the first arrow of A + B + A, so it goes; from three choices on, no untouched string survives. Add a copy of every word to a new label, A == X. and B == Y., and every one of the original strings comes through, relabelled, beside every string with C in it: 5, 12, 29, 169, 985 and 5,741 strings for 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 choices, the Pell numbers. The copy has to go to a new label. A == A. never stops.

body.label: 05 / THE LOSS IS THE POINT
body.text: So the second phase could keep strings instead: keep every string from entry to exit that does not run through a path some rule was applied to. The second machine does this too. To keep one string and drop another that shares an arrow with it, the graph has to be unshared, each vertex split by the arrows just crossed to reach it. On the ten choices, nothing is lost. All 1,024 strings come through, each A + B rewritten as C, in 69 arrows where the report’s phase keeps 11. On the report’s own systems it breaks them. The analysis of the French sentence keeps 72 strings, the tree and every partial analysis no rule took further, where the report keeps one. The example of section 8 keeps eight, S(1,1,1) and seven partial analyses, where the report keeps one. And the recipe for deleting a string no longer empties the graph: the string goes, but the dead ends it builds, /CUL + /DESAC and /CULDE + /SAC, survive, because the recipe works by having the second phase remove their arrows. Nothing in the report says the loss of neighbours was known or wanted; its recipe is offered for deleting every path carrying one given string, and it deletes more. But whether or not Colmerauer saw the loss, his systems depend on what causes it. A second phase that kept the neighbours would return partial analyses and keep the dead ends.

body.label: 06 / WHAT -INV- CAN UNDO
body.text: The report’s grammar runs both ways: inverted with -INV-, the rules that wrote eighteen paraphrases analyse each back to its tree, and so do all 131,424 sentences with at most one level of embedding. That is a property of the grammar, not of -INV-. Three systems were run on all 64 strings of six choices, then inverted and run on the result. A == X. and B == Y. give back each string exactly. A == X. and B == X. give back all 64 strings for every input: each one does give X + … + X, and nothing records which was there. Parity’s inverse never stops, because E + B == E., inverted, is E == E + B., which applies to its own result. Phases in sequence lose in another way. The report’s last two phases pack each sentence into one tree and unpack it, “pour sortir les résultats en clair”, to print the results plainly. They give back exactly the eighteen sentences, and 282 arrows where the synthesis had 139: the identity on strings, and the undoing of the sharing. And phases do not commute: on A + B, A == B. and A + B == D. give D in one phase, B + B as two phases in that order, and D in the other.

body.label: 07 / OTHER COMPUTATIONS
body.text: Written in the report’s language and run by the historical machine, lists make data easy. Unary addition is N(U*) + PLUS + N(V*) == N(U*,V*)., and a parameter used twice tests equality: N(U*) + EGAL + N(U*) == VRAI. Multiplication, adding one in binary with a carry that moves right, reversing a list, and one step of the cellular automaton rule 110 all work, in one to nine rules. Each repeated step is a scan from left to right with an accumulator, because a rule reads its whole left side and replaces it: it cannot read a neighbour as context and leave it, so the overlapping windows of the automaton cannot all be rewritten at once. Facts are joined only when they are next to each other. R(B,C) + R(A,B) is never composed. A rule that lets facts change places joins them, but never stops, and two facts held side by side as alternatives are never joined at all, since no path runs through both. That is the same limit again.
Every count is asserted by a test in the repository, and the historical machine is unchanged by any of it. Parity and the pair rule run in the playground, one application at a time.

body.title: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW
lines: This is the machine as the report describes it, rebuilt; no program text of the Q-systems is known to us. The lost ALGOL program, its FORTRAN translation, the machine-code version Colmerauer and Roussel mention, and the later Q-systems of METEO may have merged equal arrows. None of the report’s examples could show it.
Two arrows are called equal here when they have the same two ends and the same tree. Merging is about that, not about strings or meanings that are equivalent in some wider sense.

The merging and string-purifying machines are experiments of our own, not Colmerauer’s. They were run on the systems named here and on the report’s examples, nothing more. That merging left every one of those examples unchanged does not show it leaves every Q-system that stops unchanged, and keeping the count of derivations is not keeping every property of the derivations. The only changes merging was found to make were in systems like A == A., which never stop under the report’s definition; others may exist.
Beyond one level of embedding the grammar was sampled, not exhausted: of 9,565,938 sentences of one tree, 500 tried. That no sentence tried was ambiguous is not a proof that none is.

The graphs of choices were built to test the machine, not taken from any use of it. Everything was built and measured by one coding agent and checked by no person. No literature search was made, and merging equal results is the familiar idea of tabulation and chart parsing, so nothing here is claimed as new.
body.principle: A rebuilt machine can be measured where its designer never ran it, so long as what was measured is kept apart from what was changed.

body.text: Did any later Q-system merge equal arrows?
body.detail: The report defines a phase by adding a whole new path for every application, and none of its examples meets the case where that matters. The FORTRAN translation of the ALGOL program, the machine-code version Colmerauer and Roussel mention, and the Q-systems METEO was written in may have done otherwise. A manual or listing of any of them would say whether the cost of fanning in measured here was ever paid in practice.
